abstract: We present a simplified model of the micromechanics of the human cochlea, realized with electrical elements. Simulation of the model shows that it retains four signal processing features whose importance we argue on the basis of engineering logic and evolutionary evidence. Furthermore, just as the cochlea does, the model achieves massively parallel signal processing in a structurally economic way, by means of shared elements. By extracting what we believe are the five essential features of the cochlea, we hope to design a useful front-end filter to process acoustic images and to obtain a better understanding of the auditory system.

paragraphs: This paper presents a simplified electrical model of the human cochlea’s micromechanics. The authors seek to preserve features they consider essential to its signal processing while expressing the model through electrical elements. The project connects an account of biological hearing with a possible design for acoustic preprocessing.

Simulations show that the model retains four signal-processing features whose importance the authors justify through engineering arguments and evolutionary evidence. The model also uses shared elements to achieve extensive parallel processing with an economical structure. Sharing is central to the approach because the physical organization contributes to how the processing is implemented.

The authors frame the design around five features they regard as essential to the cochlea. Their goals are a useful front-end filter for acoustic images and a clearer understanding of the auditory system. The stated simulation result supports preservation of selected processing properties in the simplified model. Its broader significance is the attempt to make biological organization informative for both an electrical implementation and an explanation of hearing.
summary.tldr: A simplified electrical cochlea preserves selected signal-processing properties while using shared components for economical parallel processing.

title: A Passive Shared Element Analog Electrical Cochlea

paragraphs: The paper derives Value and Policy Search, or VAPS, as a learning rule that generates a broad family of reinforcement-learning algorithms. Its aim is to place value-based learning and direct policy search within one theory. These approaches can then be used individually or combined through the same general construction.

The generated algorithms include modifications of Q-learning, SARSA, and advantage learning. Their original forms can fail to converge on simple Markov decision processes when using parameterized value-function approximators. The paper reports convergence guarantees for the algorithms produced by its framework. It also includes pure policy-search methods that learn optimal policies without first learning a value function.

The framework extends to partially observable Markov decision processes, where the stated convergence does not require a proper belief state. Simulations accompany the theoretical development. The main significance is a common route to constructing and combining learning algorithms with convergence guarantees; convergence and optimal-policy learning are distinct claims in the abstract and should not be collapsed into one universal guarantee.
summary.tldr: VAPS unifies value-based learning and policy search through a general learning rule that produces algorithms with convergence guarantees.

title: Gradient Descent for General Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We propose a new approach to the problem of searching a space of stochastic controllers for a Markov decision process (MDP) or a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). Following several other authors, our approach is based on searching in parameterized families of policies (for example, via gradient descent) to optimize solution qual(cid:173) ity. However, rather than trying to estimate the values and derivatives of a policy directly, we do so indirectly using estimates for the proba(cid:173) bility densities that the policy induces on states at the different points in time. This enables our algorithms to exploit the many techniques for efficient and robust approximate density propagation in stochastic sys(cid:173) tems. We show how our techniques can be applied both to deterministic propagation schemes (where the MDP's dynamics are given explicitly in compact form,) and to stochastic propagation schemes (where we have access only to a generative model, or simulator, of the MDP). We present empirical results for both of these variants on complex problems.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the search for a good stochastic controller in a Markov decision process or its partially observable counterpart. It searches within parameterized policy families, using methods such as gradient descent to improve solution quality. The main innovation concerns how the information needed for that search is estimated.

Rather than estimating policy values and derivatives directly, the method first estimates the probability distributions over states induced by the policy at different times. Policy evaluation and improvement information are then obtained indirectly through those distributions. This makes techniques for efficient, robust approximate density propagation available to the policy-search problem.

The authors describe two variants. Deterministic propagation applies when the system dynamics have an explicit, compact representation. Stochastic propagation applies when access is through a generative model or simulator. Both variants are evaluated empirically on complex problems. The contribution is a route from modeling the distribution of possible system states to optimizing a controller, with implementations suited to two different forms of access to the dynamics.
summary.tldr: Policy search can estimate values and gradients indirectly by propagating the state distributions induced by a controller.

title: Policy Search via Density Estimation

abstract: We consider the problem of modeling a helicopter's dynamics based on state-action trajectories collected from it. The contribution of this paper is two-fold. First, we consider the linear models such as learned by C I F E R (the industry standard in helicopter identification), and show that the linear parameterization makes certain properties of dynamical systems, such as inertia, fundamentally difficult to capture. We propose an alternative, acceleration based, parameterization that does not suffer from this deficiency, and that can be learned as efficiently from data. Second, a Markov decision process model of a helicopter's dynamics would explicitly model only the one-step transitions, but we are often interested in a model's predictive performance over longer timescales. In this paper, we present an efficient algorithm for (approximately) minimizing the prediction error over long time scales. We present empirical results on two different helicopters. Although this work was motivated by the problem of modeling helicopters, the ideas presented here are general, and can be applied to modeling large classes of vehicular dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper learns helicopter dynamics from recorded sequences of states and actions. It addresses two questions: how to represent the vehicle's motion and how to train a model for predictions extending beyond the next time step. Both matter when the goal is to predict how a vehicle will evolve over an extended sequence.

The authors show that the linear parameterization used in models such as those learned by CIFER makes properties including inertia fundamentally difficult to capture. They propose an acceleration-based parameterization that avoids this deficiency while remaining equally efficient to learn from data. The contribution changes the representation of the dynamics without requiring a less efficient learning procedure.

The second contribution is an efficient algorithm that approximately minimizes prediction error over long time scales. This targets a different objective from explicitly modeling only one-step transitions in a Markov decision process. The paper presents empirical results on two helicopters and argues that the ideas also apply to broad classes of vehicle dynamics, although the reported applications concern those helicopters.
summary.tldr: An acceleration-based dynamics model addresses inertia-related shortcomings of linear parameterizations, while a second algorithm targets longer-term prediction error.

title: Learning vehicular dynamics, with application to modeling helicopters

abstract: Standard statistical models of language fail to capture one of the most striking properties of natural languages: the power-law distribution in the frequencies of word tokens. We present a framework for developing statistical models that generically produce power-laws, augmenting stan- dard generative models with an adaptor that produces the appropriate pattern of token frequencies. We show that taking a particular stochastic process – the Pitman-Yor process – as an adaptor justiﬁes the appearance of type frequencies in formal analyses of natural language, and improves the performance of a model for unsupervised learning of morphology.
originalAbstract: Standard statistical models of language fail to capture one of the most striking properties of natural languages: the power-law distribution in the frequencies of word tokens. We present a framework for developing statistical models that generically produce power-laws, augmenting stan- dard generative models with an adaptor that produces the appropriate pattern of token frequencies. We show that taking a particular stochastic process – the Pitman-Yor process – as an adaptor justiﬁes the appearance of type frequencies in formal analyses of natural language, and improves the performance of a model for unsupervised learning of morphology.

paragraphs: Word frequencies in natural language follow a strikingly uneven pattern: some words occur often, while many others occur rarely. The paper argues that standard statistical language models fail to capture this power-law behavior. It proposes a framework that changes how a generative model produces repeated word occurrences while retaining the underlying generative model.

The key addition is an adaptor that produces the desired pattern of token frequencies. Tokens are individual occurrences, whereas types are distinct forms. The authors show that using a particular stochastic process, the Pitman–Yor process, as the adaptor provides a justification for the appearance of type frequencies in formal language analysis.

This connects a modeling choice about repetition to the question of how distinct forms should influence statistical learning. The authors also report improved performance for an unsupervised morphology model, which learns aspects of word structure without labeled examples. The contribution thus combines a framework for producing power-law frequencies, an explanation of type-based quantities, and an empirical improvement in the stated language-learning task.
summary.tldr: A Pitman–Yor adaptor models power-law word frequencies, explains the role of type counts, and improves unsupervised morphology learning.

title: Interpolating between types and tokens by estimating power-law generators

abstract: The problem of resource allocation in sparse graphs with real variables is studied using methods of statistical physics. An efﬁcient distributed algorithm is devised on the basis of insight gained from the analysis and is examined using numerical simulations, showing excellent performance and full agreement with the theoretical results.
originalAbstract: The problem of resource allocation in sparse graphs with real variables is studied using methods of statistical physics. An efﬁcient distributed algorithm is devised on the basis of insight gained from the analysis and is examined using numerical simulations, showing excellent performance and full agreement with the theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies resource allocation on sparse graphs, with task redistribution providing the problem context. The allocation variables are real-valued, so the problem concerns quantities that can vary continuously. The graph supplies the structure within which allocation is studied, making the relationships between connected parts of the system relevant to the solution.

The authors use methods from statistical physics to analyze the problem. Insights from that analysis then guide the design of an efficient distributed algorithm. The title identifies message passing as the computational approach. A central contribution is therefore the connection between a theoretical treatment of allocation and an algorithm organized for distributed computation on the graph.

Numerical simulations examine the resulting algorithm. The authors report excellent performance and full agreement between the simulations and their theoretical results. This agreement supports the link between the analysis and the implemented procedure in the investigated setting. The paper's stated outcome combines an effective allocation algorithm with numerical evidence that its behavior matches the theory used to develop it.
summary.tldr: Statistical-physics analysis yields a distributed resource-allocation algorithm whose simulated behavior agrees with the theory.

title: Message passing for task redistribution on sparse graphs

abstract: We show that an important and computationally challenging solution space feature of the graph coloring problem (COL), namely the number of clusters of solutions, can be accurately estimated by a technique very similar to one for counting the number of solutions. This cluster counting approach can be naturally written in terms of a new factor graph derived from the factor graph representing the COL instance. Using a variant of the Belief Propagation inference framework, we can efﬁciently approximate cluster counts in random COL problems over a large range of graph densities. We illustrate the algorithm on instances with up to 100, 000 vertices. Moreover, we supply a methodology for computing the number of clus- ters exactly using advanced techniques from the knowledge compilation literature. This methodology scales up to several hundred variables.

This cluster counting approach can be naturally written in terms of a new factor graph derived from the factor graph representing the COL instance. Using a variant of the Belief Propagation inference framework, we can efﬁciently approximate cluster counts in random COL problems over a large range of graph densities. paragraphs: For graph coloring, knowing how many valid solutions exist does not fully describe how those solutions are organized. This paper studies the number of clusters within the solution space. Counting these groups is computationally difficult, but it reveals a different structural property from simply counting all valid colorings individually.

The authors show that cluster counts can be estimated with a technique closely related to solution counting. They construct a new factor graph from the factor graph describing the original coloring problem. A variant of belief propagation then operates on this transformed representation, providing an efficient way to approximate the number of solution clusters.

The approximate method produces accurate estimates for random coloring problems across a broad range of graph densities, with examples containing up to 100,000 vertices. The paper also provides an exact counting methodology based on knowledge compilation, which scales to several hundred variables. Together, these contributions offer approximate cluster counts for large instances and exact counts at a smaller scale, making solution-space organization more accessible to computation.
summary.tldr: A transformed factor graph enables belief propagation to estimate graph-coloring solution clusters, alongside an exact method for smaller instances.

title: Counting Solution Clusters in Graph Coloring Problems Using Belief Propagation

abstract: We investigate how well Gaussian process regression can learn functions defined on graphs, using large regular random graphs as a paradigmatic example. Random-walk based kernels are shown to have some surprising properties: within the standard approximation of a locally tree-like graph structure, the kernel does not become constant, i.e.neighbouring function values do not become fully correlated, when the lengthscale $\sigma$ of the kernel is made large. Instead the kernel attains a non-trivial limiting form, which we calculate. The fully correlated limit is reached only once loops become relevant, and we estimate where the crossover to this regime occurs. Our main subject are learning curves of Bayes error versus training set size. We show that these are qualitatively well predicted by a simple approximation using only the spectrum of a large tree as input, and generically scale with $n/V$, the number of training examples per vertex. We also explore how this behaviour changes once kernel lengthscales are large enough for loops to become important.

paragraphs: The paper investigates Gaussian process regression for functions defined on graph vertices, using large regular random graphs as its main example. It examines random-walk kernels, which specify relationships between function values across the graph. A central question is how those relationships change as the kernel's lengthscale grows.

Under a locally tree-like approximation, increasing the lengthscale does not make neighboring values fully correlated. Instead, the kernel approaches a nonconstant limiting form that the authors calculate. Full correlation appears only when graph loops become relevant. The paper estimates the crossover to that regime, showing why the tree approximation changes the expected large-lengthscale behavior.

The authors also study learning curves relating Bayes error to training-set size. A simple approximation based only on the spectrum of a large tree predicts their qualitative behavior. These curves generally scale with the number of training examples per vertex. The paper then explores how this behavior changes when larger lengthscales make loops important.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how graph loops affect random-walk kernels and how Gaussian process learning curves generally scale with examples per vertex.

title: Kernels and learning curves for Gaussian process regression on random graphs

abstract: When animals repeatedly choose actions from multiple alternatives, they can allocate their choices stochastically depending on past actions and outcomes. It is commonly assumed that this ability is achieved by modifications in synaptic weights related to decision making. Choice behavior has been empirically found to follow Herrnstein’s matching law. Loewenstein & Seung (2006) demonstrated that matching behavior is a steady state of learning in neural networks if the synaptic weights change proportionally to the covariance between reward and neural activities. However, their proof did not take into account the change in entire synaptic distributions. In this study, we show that matching behavior is not necessarily a steady state of the covariance-based learning rule when the synaptic strength is sufficiently strong so that the fluctuations in input from individual sensory neurons influence the net input to output neurons. This is caused by the increasing variance in the input potential due to the diffusion of synaptic weights. This effect causes an undermatching phenomenon, which has been observed in many behavioral experiments. We suggest that the synaptic diffusion effects provide a robust neural mechanism for stochastic choice behavior.

However, their proof did not take into account the change in entire synaptic distributions. In this study, we show that matching behavior is not necessarily a steady state of the covariance-based learning rule when the synaptic strength is sufficiently strong so that the fluctuations in input from individual sensory neurons influence the net input to output neurons. paragraphs: Animals can distribute their choices probabilistically according to previous actions and rewards. Matching behavior describes an observed relationship between choice allocation and rewards. Earlier theoretical work showed that matching could be a steady state when synaptic changes follow the covariance between reward and neural activity. This paper examines a feature that analysis omitted: changes in the entire distribution of synaptic weights.

The authors show that matching need not remain a steady state when synapses are strong enough for fluctuations from individual sensory neurons to affect the total input to output neurons. As synaptic weights diffuse, the variance of the input potential increases. Accounting for this changing variability alters the behavior predicted by the covariance-based learning rule.

The resulting effect produces undermatching, a phenomenon observed in many behavioral experiments. This connects a property of synaptic dynamics to a recognizable pattern in action selection. The authors suggest that diffusion of synaptic weights could provide a robust neural mechanism for stochastic choice, with the steady-state conclusion depending on the stated strength and fluctuation conditions.
summary.tldr: Synaptic weight diffusion can disrupt matching behavior under sufficiently strong synapses and produce undermatching in decision-making networks.

title: Effects of Synaptic Weight Diffusion on Learning in Decision Making Networks

abstract: This paper introduces the first set of PAC-Bayesian bounds for the batch reinforcement learning problem in finite state spaces. These bounds hold regardless of the correctness of the prior distribution. We demonstrate how such bounds can be used for model-selection in control problems where prior information is available either on the dynamics of the environment, or on the value of actions. Our empirical results confirm that PAC-Bayesian model-selection is able to leverage prior distributions when they are informative and, unlike standard Bayesian RL approaches, ignores them when they are misleading.
originalAbstract: This paper introduces the first set of PAC-Bayesian bounds for the batch reinforcement learning problem in finite state spaces. These bounds hold regardless of the correctness of the prior distribution. We demonstrate how such bounds can be used for model-selection in control problems where prior information is available either on the dynamics of the environment, or on the value of actions. Our empirical results confirm that PAC-Bayesian model-selection is able to leverage prior distributions when they are informative and, unlike standard Bayesian RL approaches, ignores them when they are misleading.

paragraphs: Prior information can help a reinforcement-learning system choose a model, but that information may be wrong. This paper develops PAC-Bayesian bounds for batch reinforcement learning in finite state spaces. A central property is that the bounds remain valid regardless of whether the prior distribution correctly describes the problem.

The authors show how these bounds can guide model selection in control tasks. Prior information may concern the environment’s dynamics or the values of actions, so the framework accommodates knowledge about either how the world changes or how useful actions are. The bounds provide a basis for using that information without requiring its correctness.

The empirical results show model selection benefiting from informative priors and ignoring misleading ones, in contrast with the standard Bayesian reinforcement-learning approaches discussed in the paper. The theoretical and empirical claims serve different roles: the bounds tolerate incorrect priors, while the experiments demonstrate selective use of prior information. Together they support a way to make prior knowledge useful without depending on its reliability.
summary.tldr: PAC-Bayesian bounds support batch reinforcement-learning model selection with priors that may be informative or misleading.

title: PAC-Bayesian Model Selection for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Heavy-tailed distributions naturally occur in many real life problems. Unfortunately, it is typically not possible to compute inference in closed-form in graphical models which involve such heavy tailed distributions. In this work, we propose a novel simple linear graphical model for independent latent random variables, called linear characteristic model (LCM), defined in the characteristic function domain. Using stable distributions, a heavy-tailed family of distributions which is a generalization of Cauchy, L\'evy and Gaussian distributions, we show for the first time, how to compute both exact and approximate inference in such a linear multivariate graphical model. LCMs are not limited to only stable distributions, in fact LCMs are always defined for any random variables (discrete, continuous or a mixture of both). We provide a realistic problem from the field of computer networks to demonstrate the applicability of our construction. Other potential application is iterative decoding of linear channels with non-Gaussian noise.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed distributions appear in many practical problems, but graphical models containing them often resist closed-form inference. This paper introduces the linear characteristic model, a linear graphical model built from independent latent random variables. Its defining move is to represent the model in the characteristic function domain, providing a different mathematical setting for inference.

The authors develop exact and approximate inference using stable distributions. This family encompasses Cauchy, Lévy, and Gaussian distributions, giving the construction access to several forms of distributional behavior. The contribution is an inference treatment for this linear multivariate setting. The model's definition is broader still: it exists for arbitrary random variables, including discrete, continuous, and mixed variables, although that broader definability is distinct from the stated stable-distribution inference results.

A realistic computer networking problem demonstrates the construction's applicability. The authors also identify iterative decoding over linear channels with non-Gaussian noise as a potential use. The paper thus links a general representation for linear random-variable models with concrete inference methods and an application beyond a purely mathematical formulation.
summary.tldr: Linear characteristic models enable exact and approximate inference for a linear multivariate setting using stable distributions.

title: Inference with Multivariate Heavy-Tails in Linear Models

abstract: Machine Learning competitions such as the Netflix Prize have proven reasonably successful as a method of “crowdsourcing” prediction tasks. But these compe- titions have a number of weaknesses, particularly in the incentive structure they create for the participants. We propose a new approach, called a Crowdsourced Learning Mechanism, in which participants collaboratively “learn” a hypothesis for a given prediction task. The approach draws heavily from the concept of a prediction market, where traders bet on the likelihood of a future event. In our framework, the mechanism continues to publish the current hypothesis, and par- ticipants can modify this hypothesis by wagering on an update. The critical in- centive property is that a participant will profit an amount that scales according to how much her update improves performance on a released test set.
originalAbstract: Machine Learning competitions such as the Netflix Prize have proven reasonably successful as a method of “crowdsourcing” prediction tasks. But these compe- titions have a number of weaknesses, particularly in the incentive structure they create for the participants. We propose a new approach, called a Crowdsourced Learning Mechanism, in which participants collaboratively “learn” a hypothesis for a given prediction task. The approach draws heavily from the concept of a prediction market, where traders bet on the likelihood of a future event. In our framework, the mechanism continues to publish the current hypothesis, and par- ticipants can modify this hypothesis by wagering on an update. The critical in- centive property is that a participant will profit an amount that scales according to how much her update improves performance on a released test set.

paragraphs: Prediction competitions recruit many people to improve a model, but their reward structures can create weaknesses in participants’ incentives. This paper proposes a Crowdsourced Learning Mechanism that makes collaboration part of the competition itself. Participants work on a shared prediction hypothesis, giving them a common object to improve as the process continues.

The mechanism borrows from prediction markets, where participants put money behind judgments about future events. Here, the mechanism continually publishes its current hypothesis, and a participant can wager on a proposed modification. The contribution being evaluated is therefore an update to the shared predictor, with a financial stake attached to that update.

The central incentive property connects a participant’s profit to how much the update improves performance on a released test set. This makes the reward sensitive to the contribution’s measured value. The paper’s contribution is a mechanism for organizing collaborative prediction work: it connects public, incremental model development with payments that scale according to the improvement each participant supplies.
summary.tldr: A prediction-market-inspired mechanism rewards participants according to how much their updates improve a shared predictor on a released test set.

title: A Collaborative Mechanism for Crowdsourcing Prediction Problems

abstract: We consider unsupervised estimation of mixtures of discrete graphical models, where the class variable is hidden and each mixture component can have a potentially different Markov graph structure and parameters over the observed variables. We propose a novel method for estimating the mixture components with provable guarantees. Our output is a tree-mixture model which serves as a good approximation to the underlying graphical model mixture. The sample and computational requirements for our method scale as $\poly(p, r)$, for an $r$-component mixture of $p$-variate graphical models, for a wide class of models which includes tree mixtures and mixtures over bounded degree graphs.
originalAbstract: We consider unsupervised estimation of mixtures of discrete graphical models, where the class variable is hidden and each mixture component can have a potentially different Markov graph structure and parameters over the observed variables. We propose a novel method for estimating the mixture components with provable guarantees. Our output is a tree-mixture model which serves as a good approximation to the underlying graphical model mixture. The sample and computational requirements for our method scale as $\poly(p, r)$, for an $r$-component mixture of $p$-variate graphical models, for a wide class of models which includes tree mixtures and mixtures over bounded degree graphs.

paragraphs: The paper studies data generated by a mixture of discrete graphical models. The component responsible for each observation is hidden, and different components may have different dependency graphs as well as different parameters. Learning therefore requires disentangling several underlying models without being told which observations belong to which component.

The authors propose a method with provable guarantees for estimating the mixture components. Its output is a mixture of tree models that provides a good approximation to the underlying graphical-model mixture. This distinction matters because the original components need not all be trees: the learned tree mixture is also an approximation tool for a broader class of structures.

For a mixture with r components and p variables, both sample requirements and computation scale polynomially in p and r over the stated model class. That class includes tree mixtures and mixtures of bounded-degree graphs. The result connects theoretical learnability with computational feasibility, showing that hidden component assignments and differing structures can be handled together for this range of models.
summary.tldr: A provably supported method learns tree-mixture approximations of discrete graphical-model mixtures with polynomial sample and computational requirements.

title: Learning Mixtures of Tree Graphical Models

abstract: We investigate a curious relationship between the structure of a discrete graphical model and the support of the inverse of a generalized covariance matrix. We show that for certain graph structures, the support of the inverse covariance matrix of indicator variables on the vertices of a graph reﬂects the conditional independence structure of the graph. Our work extends results that have previously been es- tablished only in the context of multivariate Gaussian graphical models, thereby addressing an open question about the signiﬁcance of the inverse covariance ma- trix of a non-Gaussian distribution. Based on our population-level results, we show how the graphical Lasso may be used to recover the edge structure of cer- tain classes of discrete graphical models, and present simulations to verify our theoretical results.

We show that for certain graph structures, the support of the inverse covariance matrix of indicator variables on the vertices of a graph reﬂects the conditional independence structure of the graph. Our work extends results that have previously been es- tablished only in the context of multivariate Gaussian graphical models, thereby addressing an open question about the signiﬁcance of the inverse covariance ma- trix of a non-Gaussian distribution. Based on our population-level results, we show how the graphical Lasso may be used to recover the edge structure of cer- tain classes of discrete graphical models, and present simulations to verify our theoretical results.

paragraphs: A graphical model represents patterns of conditional independence among variables. This paper investigates whether those patterns can be read from the nonzero entries of an inverse generalized covariance matrix for discrete variables. Such a relationship was already established for multivariate Gaussian models, but its significance outside the Gaussian setting was an open question addressed by this work.

The authors show that, for certain graph structures, the inverse covariance matrix of vertex indicator variables reflects the graph's conditional independence structure. Indicator variables encode discrete outcomes in a form suitable for covariance calculations. The restriction to particular graph structures is essential to the stated result; the paper does not claim the relationship for every discrete graphical model.

Using these population-level results, the authors show how graphical Lasso can recover edges for certain classes of discrete models. Simulations provide supporting verification of the theory. The contribution connects a matrix-based representation of statistical dependence to graph recovery beyond Gaussian distributions, while identifying a setting in which an established estimation tool can be used for discrete data.
summary.tldr: For certain discrete graphical models, inverse covariance structure reveals conditional independences and supports edge recovery with graphical Lasso.

title: Structure estimation for discrete graphical models: Generalized covariance matrices and their inverses

abstract: Probabilistic approaches to computer vision typically assume a centralized setting, with the algorithm granted access to all observed data points. However, many problems in wide-area surveillance can benefit from distributed modeling, either because of physical or computational constraints. Most distributed models to date use algebraic approaches (such as distributed SVD) and as a result cannot explicitly deal with missing data. In this work we present an approach to estimation and learning of generative probabilistic models in a distributed context where certain sensor data can be missing. In particular, we show how traditional centralized models, such as probabilistic PCA and missing-data PPCA, can be learned when the data is distributed across a network of sensors. We demonstrate the utility of this approach on the problem of distributed affine structure from motion. Our experiments suggest that the accuracy of the learned probabilistic structure and motion models rivals that of traditional centralized factorization methods while being able to handle challenging situations such as missing or noisy observations.

paragraphs: This paper studies probabilistic learning when observations are spread across a sensor network and some measurements are unavailable. Centralized vision algorithms assume access to all observed data, but physical or computational constraints can make distributed processing desirable. The authors also identify missing data as a difficulty for existing distributed approaches based primarily on algebraic factorization.

Their contribution is a distributed approach to estimating generative probabilistic models. In particular, they show how probabilistic principal component analysis and its missing-data version can be learned with observations distributed across sensors. This extends models usually learned centrally to a setting where the data reside at different network locations.

The application is distributed affine structure from motion, which estimates structure and motion from visual observations. Experiments suggest that the learned models achieve accuracy comparable to traditional centralized factorization methods while handling challenging missing or noisy measurements. The findings support distributed probabilistic modeling as a practical option for camera networks facing incomplete observations.
summary.tldr: Distributed probabilistic learning extends PCA-based camera-network models to missing observations, with accuracy reported to rival centralized factorization.

title: Distributed Probabilistic Learning for Camera Networks with Missing Data

abstract: Bandit Convex Optimization (BCO) is a fundamental framework for decision making under uncertainty, which generalizes many problems from the realm of online and statistical learning. While the special case of linear cost functions is well understood, a gap on the attainable regret for BCO with nonlinear losses remains an important open question. In this paper we take a step towards understanding the best attainable regret bounds for BCO: we give an efficient and near-optimal regret algorithm for BCO with strongly-convex and smooth loss functions. In contrast to previous works on BCO that use time invariant exploration schemes, our method employs an exploration scheme that shrinks with time.

While the special case of linear cost functions is well understood, a gap on the attainable regret for BCO with nonlinear losses remains an important open question. In this paper we take a step towards understanding the best attainable regret bounds for BCO: we give an efficient and near-optimal regret algorithm for BCO with strongly-convex and smooth loss functions. In contrast to previous works on BCO that use time invariant exploration schemes, our method employs an exploration scheme that shrinks with time.

paragraphs: Bandit convex optimization provides a framework for making decisions under uncertainty. A central question is how much regret an algorithm must incur as it learns to make those decisions. The paper focuses on nonlinear losses, where the best attainable regret was less well understood than in the special case of linear costs.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm with a near-optimal regret guarantee for losses that are both strongly convex and smooth. Those two requirements define the setting of the result. The contribution therefore advances understanding of a structured nonlinear case, while leaving the broader question for nonlinear bandit convex optimization open.

The distinguishing design choice is an exploration scheme that shrinks over time. Earlier approaches discussed in the abstract use exploration schemes that remain unchanged over time. Here, the exploration schedule becomes part of the route to the regret guarantee. The stated finding connects this changing exploration strategy with efficient, near-optimal performance under the specified assumptions on the loss functions.
summary.tldr: A shrinking exploration scheme gives efficient, near-optimal regret guarantees for bandit convex optimization with strongly convex, smooth losses.

title: Bandit Convex Optimization: Towards Tight Bounds

abstract: We introduce a new sequential Monte Carlo algorithm we call the particle cascade. The particle cascade is an asynchronous, anytime alternative to traditional sequential Monte Carlo algorithms that is amenable to parallel and distributed implementations. It uses no barrier synchronizations which leads to improved particle throughput and memory efficiency. It is an anytime algorithm in the sense that it can be run forever to emit an unbounded number of particles while keeping within a fixed memory budget. We prove that the particle cascade provides an unbiased marginal likelihood estimator which can be straightforwardly plugged into existing pseudo-marginal methods.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new sequential Monte Carlo algorithm we call the particle cascade. The particle cascade is an asynchronous, anytime alternative to traditional sequential Monte Carlo algorithms that is amenable to parallel and distributed implementations. It uses no barrier synchronizations which leads to improved particle throughput and memory efficiency. It is an anytime algorithm in the sense that it can be run forever to emit an unbounded number of particles while keeping within a fixed memory budget. We prove that the particle cascade provides an unbiased marginal likelihood estimator which can be straightforwardly plugged into existing pseudo-marginal methods.

paragraphs: Sequential Monte Carlo represents an inference problem using a collection of particles. This paper introduces the particle cascade, an alternative designed to support asynchronous computation. Its central organizational change is to remove barrier synchronizations, so execution does not require all participating work to reach a shared checkpoint before proceeding.

That organization makes the method suitable for parallel and distributed implementations. The authors report improved particle throughput and memory efficiency from avoiding these barriers. The algorithm is also anytime in a specific sense: it can continue generating particles indefinitely while remaining within a fixed memory budget. Producing more particles therefore does not require retaining an ever-growing collection in memory.

The paper also proves a statistical property beyond these computational advantages: the particle cascade yields an unbiased estimator of marginal likelihood. Unbiasedness concerns the estimator's average over repeated randomness, rather than exactness of each individual estimate. This guarantee lets the estimator be inserted into existing pseudo-marginal methods, connecting a different execution strategy with established approaches to probabilistic inference.
summary.tldr: The particle cascade enables asynchronous, fixed-memory sequential Monte Carlo while providing an unbiased marginal-likelihood estimator.

title: Asynchronous Anytime Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: We investigate the problem of stochastic network design in bidirected trees. In this problem, an underlying phenomenon (e.g., a behavior, rumor, or disease) starts at multiple sources in a tree and spreads in both directions along its edges. Actions can be taken to increase the probability of propagation on edges, and the goal is to maximize the total amount of spread away from all sources. Our main result is a rounded dynamic programming approach that leads to a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS), that is, an algorithm that can find (1−ε)-optimal solutions for any problem instance in time polynomial in the input size and 1/ε. Our algorithm outperforms competing approaches on a motivating problem from computational sustainability to remove barriers in river networks to restore the health of aquatic ecosystems.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to improve spreading through a tree when propagation is probabilistic and can travel in both directions along edges. Spread begins at multiple sources, and available actions can increase edge propagation probabilities. The objective is to maximize the total spread away from all those sources.

The authors develop a rounded dynamic-programming approach that yields a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. For any chosen ε, it finds a solution worth at least 1−ε times the optimum in time polynomial in the input size and 1/ε. This gives a formal relationship between computational effort and the desired closeness to the best possible solution.

A motivating application is removing barriers in river networks to support aquatic ecosystems. In that setting, the algorithm outperforms competing approaches. The result connects a provable approximation method with a practical network-design problem involving multiple starting locations and two-way movement. The guarantee applies to the bidirected-tree problem studied here, and the river-network experiments provide evidence of its usefulness in that application.
summary.tldr: Rounded dynamic programming gives a fully polynomial approximation scheme for maximizing stochastic spread in bidirected trees.

title: Stochastic Network Design in Bidirected Trees

abstract: We present two approaches to use unlabeled data to improve Sequence Learningwith recurrent networks. The first approach is to predict what comes next in asequence, which is a language model in NLP. The second approach is to use asequence autoencoder, which reads the input sequence into a vector and predictsthe input sequence again. These two algorithms can be used as a “pretraining”algorithm for a later supervised sequence learning algorithm. In other words, theparameters obtained from the pretraining step can then be used as a starting pointfor other supervised training models. In our experiments, we find that long shortterm memory recurrent networks after pretrained with the two approaches becomemore stable to train and generalize better. With pretraining, we were able toachieve strong performance in many classification tasks, such as text classificationwith IMDB, DBpedia or image recognition in CIFAR-10.

paragraphs: This paper explores how recurrent networks can learn from unlabeled sequences before being trained for a supervised task. The central idea is to use an initial learning problem that does not need labels, then transfer the resulting network parameters as the starting point for supervised training.

The authors study two pretraining objectives. One predicts the next element in a sequence, corresponding to language modeling when applied to text. The other uses a sequence autoencoder: it reads a sequence into a vector and then attempts to reconstruct the original sequence. These objectives provide different ways to learn from the structure already present in unlabeled inputs.

In the reported experiments, long short-term memory networks pretrained through these approaches are more stable to train and generalize better. The authors report strong classification performance on tasks involving IMDB, DBpedia, and CIFAR-10. The findings support using unlabeled sequence learning to prepare recurrent networks for later supervised optimization, with benefits observed in both training behavior and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Predicting or reconstructing unlabeled sequences provides pretraining that improves LSTM training stability and generalization in the reported experiments.

title: Semi-supervised Sequence Learning

abstract: We consider Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) in the context of stochastic optimization with exp-concave and smooth losses---a general optimization framework that captures several important learning problems including linear and logistic regression, learning SVMs with the squared hinge-loss, portfolio selection and more. In this setting, we establish the first evidence that ERM is able to attain fast generalization rates, and show that the expected loss of the ERM solution in $d$ dimensions converges to the optimal expected loss in a rate of $d/n$. This rate matches existing lower bounds up to constants and improves by a $\log{n}$ factor upon the state-of-the-art, which is only known to be attained by an online-to-batch conversion of computationally expensive online algorithms.
originalAbstract: We consider Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) in the context of stochastic optimization with exp-concave and smooth losses---a general optimization framework that captures several important learning problems including linear and logistic regression, learning SVMs with the squared hinge-loss, portfolio selection and more. In this setting, we establish the first evidence that ERM is able to attain fast generalization rates, and show that the expected loss of the ERM solution in $d$ dimensions converges to the optimal expected loss in a rate of $d/n$. This rate matches existing lower bounds up to constants and improves by a $\log{n}$ factor upon the state-of-the-art, which is only known to be attained by an online-to-batch conversion of computationally expensive online algorithms.

paragraphs: Empirical risk minimization chooses a model by minimizing loss on observed data. The statistical question is how close that model's expected loss comes to the best achievable expected loss. This paper studies that question for smooth, exp-concave losses, a framework covering important problems such as regression, squared-hinge-loss classification, and portfolio selection.

Under this framework, the authors show that empirical risk minimization achieves an expected-loss convergence rate of d/n, where d is the dimension and n is the sample size. The rate makes the dependence on both quantities explicit: the guarantee improves with more observations and accounts for the number of dimensions being learned.

The bound matches existing lower bounds up to constant factors and removes a logarithmic factor from the previous state of the art. Earlier guarantees were associated with converting computationally expensive online algorithms into batch predictors. The contribution establishes that ERM itself can attain the faster statistical rate for the stated loss class, strengthening the theoretical case for this direct learning principle.
summary.tldr: For smooth, exp-concave losses, empirical risk minimization achieves a d/n generalization rate that matches lower bounds up to constants.

title: Fast Rates for Exp-concave Empirical Risk Minimization

abstract: We propose Confusions over Time (CoT), a novel generative framework which facilitates a multi-granular analysis of the decision making process. The CoT not only models the confusions or error properties of individual decision makers and their evolution over time, but also allows us to obtain diagnostic insights into the collective decision making process in an interpretable manner. To this end, the CoT models the confusions of the decision makers and their evolution over time via time-dependent confusion matrices. Interpretable insights are obtained by grouping similar decision makers (and items being judged) into clusters and representing each such cluster with an appropriate prototype and identifying the most important features characterizing the cluster via a subspace feature indicator vector. Experimentation with real world data on bail decisions, asthma treatments, and insurance policy approval decisions demonstrates that CoT can accurately model and explain the confusions of decision makers and their evolution over time.

To this end, the CoT models the confusions of the decision makers and their evolution over time via time-dependent confusion matrices. paragraphs: Decision makers can make different kinds of mistakes, and those patterns can change over time. Confusions over Time, or CoT, is a Bayesian generative framework for describing both individual error patterns and broader trends across a collection of decision makers. Its goal includes making those patterns interpretable.

The model represents errors through time-dependent confusion matrices, which describe how decisions confuse one category with another as time passes. It groups similar decision makers and judged items into clusters. Each cluster receives a representative prototype and a feature indicator identifying the attributes most important to characterizing that group.

Together, these components connect individual behavior with collective patterns at multiple levels of detail. The prototype describes a representative member, while the selected features explain what distinguishes the cluster. Experiments use real-world data involving bail decisions, asthma treatments, and insurance policy approvals. The reported results show that CoT can accurately model and explain changing confusion patterns in those settings, supporting the framework's combination of temporal modeling and interpretable grouping.
summary.tldr: CoT models changing decision errors with time-dependent confusion matrices and explains collective patterns through interpretable clusters.

title: Confusions over Time: An Interpretable Bayesian Model to Characterize Trends in Decision Making

abstract: This paper proposes an adaptive neural-compilation framework to address the problem of learning efficient program. Traditional code optimisation strategies used in compilers are based on applying pre-specified set of transformations that make the code faster to execute without changing its semantics. In contrast, our work involves adapting programs to make them more efficient while considering correctness only on a target input distribution. Our approach is inspired by the recent works on differentiable representations of programs. We show that it is possible to compile programs written in a low-level language to a differentiable representation. We also show how programs in this representation can be optimised to make them efficient on a target distribution of inputs. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach enables learning specifically-tuned algorithms for given data distributions with a high success rate.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to make programs more efficient by adapting them to the inputs they are expected to receive. Conventional compiler optimization applies predefined transformations while preserving a program's semantics. Here, correctness is considered on a target input distribution, making specialization to that distribution part of the optimization objective.

The authors show that programs written in a low-level language can be compiled into a differentiable representation. This provides a form in which the program can be optimized through a learning process. They also show how to optimize programs in that representation for efficiency on the chosen input distribution, connecting program compilation with learned adaptation.

Experiments demonstrate a high success rate in learning algorithms tuned to particular data distributions. The significance is that useful program specialization can be learned rather than supplied entirely through a fixed collection of compiler transformations. The scope of correctness remains essential: the framework targets the specified distribution of inputs, so the reported success does not establish preservation of behavior on every possible input.
summary.tldr: Adaptive neural compilation learns efficient program specializations by optimizing differentiable representations for a target input distribution.

title: Adaptive Neural Compilation

abstract: We develop a class of algorithms, as variants of the stochastically controlled stochastic gradient (SCSG) methods , for the smooth nonconvex finite-sum optimization problem. Only assuming the smoothness of each component, the complexity of SCSG to reach a stationary point with $E \|\nabla f(x)\|^{2}\le \epsilon$ is $O(\min\{\epsilon^{-5/3}, \epsilon^{-1}n^{2/3}\})$, which strictly outperforms the stochastic gradient descent. Moreover, SCSG is never worse than the state-of-the-art methods based on variance reduction and it significantly outperforms them when the target accuracy is low. A similar acceleration is also achieved when the functions satisfy the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition. Empirical experiments demonstrate that SCSG outperforms stochastic gradient methods on training multi-layers neural networks in terms of both training and validation loss.

paragraphs: This paper develops variants of stochastically controlled stochastic gradient methods for smooth, nonconvex objectives expressed as finite sums. The target is a point whose expected squared gradient norm is at most ε. That criterion measures approximate stationarity, so the theoretical result concerns reaching a small gradient rather than identifying a global optimum.

Assuming smoothness of each component, the stated complexity is O(min{ε^(-5/3), ε^(-1)n^(2/3)}), where n is the number of components. The bound improves on SGD and is no worse than the state-of-the-art variance-reduction methods considered in the paper. Its advantage over those methods is particularly strong when only a relatively low target accuracy is required.

The authors also obtain a similar acceleration when the objective satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. This supplies a further result under an additional structural condition on the function. Experiments training multilayer neural networks show better training and validation losses than stochastic gradient methods, adding empirical support to the theoretical improvements in the cost of reaching the stated optimization criterion.
summary.tldr: SCSG variants improve complexity guarantees for approximate stationarity in smooth nonconvex finite-sum problems, especially at low target accuracy.

title: Non-convex Finite-Sum Optimization Via SCSG Methods

abstract: Recommendation for e-commerce with a mix of durable and nondurable goods has characteristics that distinguish it from the well-studied media recommendation problem. The demand for items is a combined effect of form utility and time utility, i.e., a product must both be intrinsically appealing to a consumer and the time must be right for purchase. In particular for durable goods, time utility is a function of inter-purchase duration within product category because consumers are unlikely to purchase two items in the same category in close temporal succession. Moreover, purchase data, in contrast to rating data, is implicit with non-purchases not necessarily indicating dislike. Together, these issues give rise to the positive-unlabeled demand-aware recommendation problem that we pose via joint low-rank tensor completion and product category inter-purchase duration vector estimation. We further relax this problem and propose a highly scalable alternating minimization approach with which we can solve problems with millions of users and millions of items in a single thread. We also show superior prediction accuracies on multiple real-world datasets.

paragraphs: An appealing product is not necessarily a timely purchase. This paper models e-commerce demand as a combination of a product's intrinsic appeal and the suitability of the purchase time. For durable goods, timing depends on the interval between purchases within a category, because consumers are unlikely to buy two such items close together.

The method also accounts for the ambiguity of purchase records: buying an item supplies positive evidence, but not buying it does not necessarily indicate dislike. The authors formulate this as a positive-unlabeled recommendation problem. They jointly estimate a low-rank tensor representation and a vector of category-specific inter-purchase durations, connecting preference estimation with the timing of demand.

A relaxation of the problem leads to an alternating minimization algorithm that handles millions of users and millions of items on a single thread. The authors also report superior prediction accuracy on multiple real-world datasets. The findings support treating purchase timing and implicit feedback as central parts of recommendation, with a formulation designed to remain computationally scalable.
summary.tldr: Demand-aware recommendation jointly models product appeal, purchase timing, and ambiguous non-purchases at large scale.

title: Scalable Demand-Aware Recommendation

abstract: Generative moment matching network (GMMN) is a deep generative model that differs from Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) by replacing the discriminator in GAN with a two-sample test based on kernel maximum mean discrepancy (MMD). Although some theoretical guarantees of MMD have been studied, the empirical performance of GMMN is still not as competitive as that of GAN on challenging and large benchmark datasets. The computational efficiency of GMMN is also less desirable in comparison with GAN, partially due to its requirement for a rather large batch size during the training. In this paper, we propose to improve both the model expressiveness of GMMN and its computational efficiency by introducing {\it adversarial kernel learning} techniques, as the replacement of a fixed Gaussian kernel in the original GMMN. The new approach combines the key ideas in both GMMN and GAN, hence we name it MMD-GAN. The new distance measure in MMD-GAN is a meaningful loss that enjoys the advantage of weak$^*$ topology and can be optimized via gradient descent with relatively small batch sizes. In our evaluation on multiple benchmark datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA and LSUN, the performance of MMD-GAN significantly outperforms GMMN, and is competitive with other representative GAN works.

paragraphs: Generative moment matching networks compare generated and real samples using maximum mean discrepancy, a kernel-based two-sample measure. Their fixed-kernel formulation has struggled to match GAN performance on challenging datasets and can require large training batches. This paper replaces the fixed Gaussian kernel with adversarial kernel learning to improve expressiveness and computational efficiency.

The resulting MMD-GAN combines moment matching with adversarial learning. The comparison used to train the generator is itself learned, making the discrepancy responsive to differences between the two distributions. The authors describe the resulting distance as a meaningful loss with favorable weak-star topology properties, and show that gradient descent can optimize it using relatively small batches.

Evaluations cover MNIST, CIFAR-10, CelebA, and LSUN. MMD-GAN substantially outperforms the original moment matching approach and is competitive with representative GAN methods. The findings support learning the kernel as a useful way to improve both the practical training requirements and generative performance of moment matching networks, while retaining a distribution-comparison objective.
summary.tldr: MMD-GAN learns an adversarial kernel to improve moment matching generation and enable training with smaller batches.

title: MMD GAN: Towards Deeper Understanding of Moment Matching Network

abstract: Hiererachical clustering, that is computing a recursive partitioning of a dataset to obtain clusters at increasingly finer granularity is a fundamental problem in data analysis. Although hierarchical clustering has mostly been studied through procedures such as linkage algorithms, or top-down heuristics, rather than as optimization problems, recently Dasgupta [1] proposed an objective function for hierarchical clustering and initiated a line of work developing algorithms that explicitly optimize an objective (see also [2, 3, 4]). In this paper, we consider a fairly general random graph model for hierarchical clustering, called the hierarchical stochastic blockmodel (HSBM), and show that in certain regimes the SVD approach of McSherry [5] combined with specific linkage methods results in a clustering that give an O(1)-approximation to Dasgupta’s cost function. We also show that an approach based on SDP relaxations for balanced cuts based on the work of Makarychev et al. [6], combined with the recursive sparsest cut algorithm of Dasgupta, yields an O(1) approximation in slightly larger regimes and also in the semi-random setting, where an adversary may remove edges from the random graph generated according to an HSBM. Finally, we report empirical evaluation on synthetic and real-world data showing that our proposed SVD-based method does indeed achieve a better cost than other widely-used heurstics and also results in a better classification accuracy when the underlying problem was that of multi-class classification.

In certain regimes of that model, combining a singular value decomposition approach with particular linkage methods gives a constant-factor approximation to the clustering objective. These guarantees depend on the stated graph settings, making the model assumptions central to the result. For problems involving multiclass classification, it also produces better classification accuracy, linking improvement in the clustering objective to a downstream task.
summary.tldr: Under hierarchical random graph assumptions, spectral and semidefinite approaches achieve constant-factor clustering guarantees, with empirical benefits for the spectral method.

title: Hierarchical Clustering Beyond the Worst-Case

abstract: Optimization algorithms that leverage gradient covariance information, such as variants of natural gradient descent (Amari, 1998), offer the prospect of yielding more effective descent directions. For models with many parameters, the covari- ance matrix they are based on becomes gigantic, making them inapplicable in their original form. This has motivated research into both simple diagonal approxima- tions and more sophisticated factored approximations such as KFAC (Heskes, 2000; Martens & Grosse, 2015; Grosse & Martens, 2016). In the present work we draw inspiration from both to propose a novel approximation that is provably better than KFAC and amendable to cheap partial updates. It consists in tracking a diagonal variance, not in parameter coordinates, but in a Kronecker-factored eigenbasis, in which the diagonal approximation is likely to be more effective. Experiments show improvements over KFAC in optimization speed for several deep network architectures.

paragraphs: Natural-gradient-style optimization uses information about gradient covariance to choose potentially more effective update directions. For large neural networks, however, the full covariance matrix is too large to use directly. This motivates compact approximations, including simple diagonal representations and more structured factorizations such as KFAC.

The paper combines ideas from these approaches by tracking diagonal variance in a Kronecker-factored eigenbasis. The choice of coordinates is central: a diagonal approximation in this basis is expected to capture useful information more effectively than one in the original parameter coordinates. The construction also permits inexpensive partial updates, addressing the practical cost of maintaining the approximation during training.

The authors prove that their proposed approximation is better than KFAC and report faster optimization than KFAC across several deep network architectures. The theoretical comparison concerns the approximation, while the experiments establish the observed optimization-speed improvements. Together, they support changing the basis in which diagonal information is maintained as a useful way to improve scalable covariance-based optimization.
summary.tldr: Tracking diagonal variance in a Kronecker-factored eigenbasis yields a provably improved approximation over KFAC and faster optimization in reported experiments.

title: Fast Approximate Natural Gradient Descent in a Kronecker Factored Eigenbasis

abstract: We consider a high dimensional linear regression problem where the goal is to efficiently recover an unknown vector \beta^* from n noisy linear observations Y=X \beta^ +W in R^n, for known X in R^{n \times p} and unknown W in R^n. Unlike most of the literature on this model we make no sparsity assumption on \beta^ . Instead we adopt a regularization based on assuming that the underlying vectors \beta^* have rational entries with the same denominator Q. We call this Q-rationality assumption. We propose a new polynomial-time algorithm for this task which is based on the seminal Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovasz (LLL) lattice basis reduction algorithm. We establish that under the Q-rationality assumption, our algorithm recovers exactly the vector \beta^* for a large class of distributions for the iid entries of X and non-zero noise W. We prove that it is successful under small noise, even when the learner has access to only one observation (n=1). Furthermore, we prove that in the case of the Gaussian white noise for W, n=o(p/\log p) and Q sufficiently large, our algorithm tolerates a nearly optimal information-theoretic level of the noise.

paragraphs: This paper asks when an unknown coefficient vector can be recovered efficiently from noisy linear observations in high dimensions. It replaces the usual sparsity assumption with an arithmetic one: every coefficient is rational, and all share a denominator Q. This Q-rationality condition supplies the structure used to make recovery possible.

The proposed polynomial-time algorithm builds on LLL lattice basis reduction. Under Q-rationality, the authors establish exact recovery for a broad class of distributions with independent, identically distributed entries in the observation matrix, even with nonzero noise. They also prove recovery from a single observation when the noise is sufficiently small.

A further result concerns Gaussian white noise. When the observation count satisfies n = o(p/log p) and Q is sufficiently large, the algorithm tolerates a noise level close to the information-theoretic limit. These are conditional recovery results: their significance is that shared rational structure can support efficient, exact estimation without assuming most coefficients are zero.
summary.tldr: A lattice-reduction algorithm exactly recovers nonsparse regression coefficients under shared-denominator rationality and stated design and noise conditions.

title: High Dimensional Linear Regression using Lattice Basis Reduction

abstract: A property or statistic of a distribution is said to be elicitable if it can be expressed as the minimizer of some loss function in expectation. Recent work shows that continuous real-valued properties are elicitable if and only if they are identifiable, meaning the set of distributions with the same property value can be described by linear constraints. From a practical standpoint, one may ask for which such properties do there exist convex loss functions. In this paper, in a finite-outcome setting, we show that in fact every elicitable real-valued property can be elicited by a convex loss function. Our proof is constructive, and leads to convex loss functions for new properties.

paragraphs: A statistic is elicitable when minimizing an expected loss returns that statistic's value for the underlying distribution. This connects a quantity one wants to estimate with a learning objective that targets it. The paper asks whether such an objective can be chosen to be convex, a useful structural property for optimization.

The starting point is a connection between elicitation and identifiability for continuous real-valued properties. Identifiability means that distributions sharing a property value can be characterized through linear constraints. This provides a way to reason about the property through the sets of distributions on which it takes the same value, rather than through a particular loss alone.

Within a finite-outcome setting, the authors show that every elicitable continuous real-valued property admits a convex loss that elicits it. Their proof is constructive: it provides a route to obtaining losses, not merely an existence statement. The construction yields convex losses for new properties, extending the set of statistical targets that can be paired with explicitly designed convex objectives.
summary.tldr: For finite outcomes, the paper constructively shows that elicitable continuous real-valued properties can be elicited by convex losses.

title: Convex Elicitation of Continuous Properties

abstract: Imagine a large firm with multiple departments that plans a large recruitment. Candidates arrive one-by-one, and for each candidate the firm decides, based on her data (CV, skills, experience, etc), whether to summon her for an interview. The firm wants to recruit the best candidates while minimizing the number of interviews. We model such scenarios as an assignment problem between items (candidates) and categories (departments): the items arrive one-by-one in an online manner, and upon processing each item the algorithm decides, based on its value and the categories it can be matched with, whether to retain or discard it (this decision is irrevocable). The goal is to retain as few items as possible while guaranteeing that the set of retained items contains an optimal matching. We consider two variants of this problem: (i) in the first variant it is assumed that the $n$ items are drawn independently from an unknown distribution $D$. (ii) In the second variant it is assumed that before the process starts, the algorithm has an access to a training set of $n$ items drawn independently from the same unknown distribution (e.g.\ data of candidates from previous recruitment seasons). We give tight bounds on the minimum possible number of retained items in each of these variants. These results demonstrate that one can retain exponentially less items in the second variant (with the training set). Our algorithms and analysis utilize ideas and techniques from statistical learning theory and from discrete algorithms.

paragraphs: Screening requires deciding which arriving items deserve further consideration before seeing everything that will arrive. The paper illustrates this with recruitment across several departments. Each candidate has a value and a set of departments they could join. A screening decision retains or discards the candidate permanently, while the final goal involves assigning candidates to departments.

The objective is to retain as few items as possible while ensuring that the retained collection contains an optimal matching. The authors study independently drawn items from an unknown distribution. They compare a setting without prior training data against one with a training set of the same size, independently drawn from that same unknown distribution.

The paper establishes tight bounds on the minimum number of retained items in both variants. These bounds show that access to the training set permits retaining exponentially fewer items. The result quantifies the value of prior examples for irrevocable screening decisions under the stated sampling assumptions. Its algorithms and analysis combine statistical learning theory with discrete algorithmic techniques.
summary.tldr: For the studied online matching problem, prior training examples allow exponentially fewer items to be retained while preserving an optimal matching.

title: Learning to Screen

abstract: Recent progress in natural language generation has raised dual-use concerns. While applications like summarization and translation are positive, the underlying technology also might enable adversaries to generate neural fake news: targeted propaganda that closely mimics the style of real news. Modern computer security relies on careful threat modeling: identifying potential threats and vulnerabilities from an adversary's point of view, and exploring potential mitigations to these threats. Likewise, developing robust defenses against neural fake news requires us first to carefully investigate and characterize the risks of these models. We thus present a model for controllable text generation called Grover. Given a headline like 'Link Found Between Vaccines and Autism,' Grover can generate the rest of the article; humans find these generations to be more trustworthy than human-written disinformation. Developing robust verification techniques against generators like Grover is critical. We find that best current discriminators can classify neural fake news from real, human-written, news with 73% accuracy, assuming access to a moderate level of training data. Counterintuitively, the best defense against Grover turns out to be Grover itself, with 92% accuracy, demonstrating the importance of public release of strong generators. We investigate these results further, showing that exposure bias -- and sampling strategies that alleviate its effects -- both leave artifacts that similar discriminators can pick up on. We conclude by discussing ethical issues regarding the technology, and plan to release Grover publicly, helping pave the way for better detection of neural fake news.

paragraphs: The paper investigates automatically generated disinformation by developing Grover, a controllable text generator that can produce an article from a headline. summary.tldr: Grover demonstrates both risks of generated news and the value of generator-based detection.

title: Defending Against Neural Fake News

abstract: Despite the empirical success of the actor-critic algorithm, its theoretical understanding lags behind. In a broader context, actor-critic can be viewed as an online alternating update algorithm for bilevel optimization, whose convergence is known to be fragile. To understand the instability of actor-critic, we focus on its application to linear quadratic regulators, a simple yet fundamental setting of reinforcement learning. We establish a nonasymptotic convergence analysis of actor- critic in this setting. In particular, we prove that actor-critic finds a globally optimal pair of actor (policy) and critic (action-value function) at a linear rate of convergence. Our analysis may serve as a preliminary step towards a complete theoretical understanding of bilevel optimization with nonconvex subproblems, which is NP-hard in the worst case and is often solved using heuristics.
