paragraphs: Actor-critic methods alternate between updating a policy and updating an action-value estimate that guides the policy. Despite their empirical success, these coupled updates can be theoretically fragile. The paper views them as an online alternating procedure for bilevel optimization and studies their convergence in the linear quadratic regulator setting with ergodic cost.

The authors establish a nonasymptotic analysis, meaning the result describes convergence behavior rather than only an eventual limiting outcome. In this setting, they prove that actor-critic reaches a globally optimal policy and action-value function pair at a linear convergence rate. The guarantee addresses both interacting components, which is central to understanding the alternating learning process.

The result gives a rigorous positive case within a simple but fundamental reinforcement learning problem. Its scope is the analyzed regulator setting. The authors present it as a possible preliminary step toward understanding broader bilevel problems with nonconvex subproblems, whose worst-case difficulty prevents treating this specific guarantee as a general solution.
summary.tldr: For the studied linear quadratic regulator setting, actor-critic provably converges linearly to a globally optimal policy and critic pair.

title: Provably Global Convergence of Actor-Critic: A Case for Linear Quadratic Regulator with Ergodic Cost

abstract: Network pruning reduces the computation costs of an over-parameterized network without performance damage. Prevailing pruning algorithms pre-define the width and depth of the pruned networks, and then transfer parameters from the unpruned network to pruned networks. To break the structure limitation of the pruned networks, we propose to apply neural architecture search to search directly for a network with flexible channel and layer sizes. The number of the channels/layers is learned by minimizing the loss of the pruned networks. The feature map of the pruned network is an aggregation of K feature map fragments (generated by K networks of different sizes), which are sampled based on the probability distribution. The loss can be back-propagated not only to the network weights, but also to the parameterized distribution to explicitly tune the size of the channels/layers. Specifically, we apply channel-wise interpolation to keep the feature map with different channel sizes aligned in the aggregation procedure. The maximum probability for the size in each distribution serves as the width and depth of the pruned network, whose parameters are learned by knowledge transfer, e.g., knowledge distillation, from the original networks. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet demonstrate the effectiveness of our new perspective of network pruning compared to traditional network pruning algorithms. Various searching and knowledge transfer approaches are conducted to show the effectiveness of the two components. Code is at: https://github.com/D-X-Y/NAS-Projects

paragraphs: Network pruning aims to reduce the computation of an oversized network while preserving predictive performance. Many pruning methods choose the smaller network's width and depth beforehand. This paper instead treats those dimensions as quantities to learn, using neural architecture search to select flexible numbers of channels and layers.

During search, the method aggregates feature-map fragments from K differently sized networks sampled from a parameterized distribution. Channel-wise interpolation aligns fragments with different channel counts so they can be combined. The prediction loss updates both network weights and the sampling distribution, allowing training to influence the architecture sizes as well as the parameters within them.

The most probable sizes determine the final network's width and depth. Its parameters are then learned through knowledge transfer from the original network, including knowledge distillation. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet support this approach compared with traditional pruning algorithms. Additional evaluations of search and transfer methods examine the contribution of both components, linking architecture selection with learning an effective smaller model.
summary.tldr: The method learns a pruned network's width and depth through architecture search, then trains it using knowledge transferred from the original network.

title: Network Pruning via Transformable Architecture Search

abstract: We consider a new family of stochastic operators for reinforcement learning with the goal of alleviating negative effects and becoming more robust to approximation or estimation errors. Various theoretical results are established, which include showing that our family of operators preserve optimality and increase the action gap in a stochastic sense. Our empirical results illustrate the strong benefits of our robust stochastic operators, significantly outperforming the classical Bellman operator and recently proposed operators.
originalAbstract: We consider a new family of stochastic operators for reinforcement learning with the goal of alleviating negative effects and becoming more robust to approximation or estimation errors. Various theoretical results are established, which include showing that our family of operators preserve optimality and increase the action gap in a stochastic sense. Our empirical results illustrate the strong benefits of our robust stochastic operators, significantly outperforming the classical Bellman operator and recently proposed operators.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning depends on repeated updates to estimates of how valuable different actions are. When those estimates contain approximation or estimation errors, the updates can make action selection less reliable. This paper introduces a family of stochastic operators designed to reduce the negative effects of those errors. The proposed change concerns the rule used to update values.

The theoretical results establish two properties: the operators preserve optimality and enlarge the action gap in a stochastic sense. The action gap is the separation between the values of better and worse actions. Increasing that separation can make the preferred action easier to distinguish when estimates are imperfect. The stochastic qualification matters: the stated result concerns randomized operators rather than an unconditional increase at every individual update.

The experiments report substantial improvements over the classical Bellman operator and other recently proposed operators. Together, the theory and empirical findings support the approach of designing value updates around robustness to error while retaining optimality.
summary.tldr: A family of randomized value-update rules preserves optimality and increases action gaps in a stochastic sense, with strong empirical improvements.

title: A Family of Robust Stochastic Operators for Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study two time-scale linear stochastic approximation algorithms, which can be used to model well-known reinforcement learning algorithms such as GTD, GTD2, and TDC. We present finite-time performance bounds for the case where the learning rate is fixed. The key idea in obtaining these bounds is to use a Lyapunov function motivated by singular perturbation theory for linear differential equations. We use the bound to design an adaptive learning rate scheme which significantly improves the convergence rate over the known optimal polynomial decay rule in our experiments, and can be used to potentially improve the performance of any other schedule where the learning rate is changed at pre-determined time instants.

We use the bound to design an adaptive learning rate scheme which significantly improves the convergence rate over the known optimal polynomial decay rule in our experiments, and can be used to potentially improve the performance of any other schedule where the learning rate is changed at pre-determined time instants.

paragraphs: Some reinforcement learning algorithms involve two coupled learning processes operating on different time scales. This paper studies linear stochastic approximation models of that kind, which can represent algorithms including GTD, GTD2, and TDC. Its focus is performance after a finite amount of learning, rather than only behavior after indefinitely many updates.

The authors derive finite-time performance bounds when the learning rate is fixed. Their main analytical tool is a Lyapunov function motivated by singular perturbation theory for linear differential equations. This provides a way to analyze the coupled dynamics and turn that analysis into bounds relevant to the learning process.

The resulting bound also guides an adaptive learning rate scheme. In experiments, this scheme substantially improves convergence over the known optimal polynomial decay rule. The authors further describe potential improvements to other schedules that change learning rates at predetermined times. The distinction is important: the fixed-rate bounds are theoretical results, while the reported adaptive advantage is experimental and the broader scheduling benefit is presented as a possibility.
summary.tldr: Finite-time bounds for two-time-scale learning motivate an adaptive learning rate scheme that improves convergence over polynomial decay in experiments.

title: Finite-Time Performance Bounds and Adaptive Learning Rate Selection for Two Time-Scale Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) algorithm, which optimises a set of particles to approximate a target probability distribution $\pi\propto e^{-V}$ on $\R^d$. In the population limit, SVGD performs gradient descent in the space of probability distributions on the KL divergence with respect to $\pi$, where the gradient is smoothed through a kernel integral operator. In this paper, we provide a novel finite time analysis for the SVGD algorithm. We provide a descent lemma establishing that the algorithm decreases the objective at each iteration, and rates of convergence for the averaged Stein Fisher divergence (also referred to as Kernel Stein Discrepancy) . We also provide a convergence result of the finite particle system corresponding to the practical implementation of SVGD to its population version.

In the population limit, SVGD performs gradient descent in the space of probability distributions on the KL divergence with respect to $\pi$, where the gradient is smoothed through a kernel integral operator. In this paper, we provide a novel finite time analysis for the SVGD algorithm. We provide a descent lemma establishing that the algorithm decreases the objective at each iteration, and rates of convergence for the averaged Stein Fisher divergence (also referred to as Kernel Stein Discrepancy) . paragraphs: Stein Variational Gradient Descent approximates a probability distribution by moving a collection of representative points, called particles. This paper studies how the algorithm progresses after a finite number of updates. That focus makes the analysis relevant to understanding an algorithm that must be stopped after some amount of computation.

The analysis connects particle movement to optimization over probability distributions. In the population limit, the method descends on KL divergence, an objective measuring discrepancy from the target distribution, using a gradient smoothed by a kernel. The authors establish a descent lemma showing that the analyzed updates decrease this objective, and give convergence rates for an averaged discrepancy known as Stein Fisher divergence or Kernel Stein Discrepancy.

The paper also connects the population description to the finite collection of particles used in practice through a convergence result. Together, these contributions explain both progress within the idealized distributional formulation and how a practical particle system relates to it. The stated rates concern the averaged Stein discrepancy, so that particular quantity is central to interpreting the guarantee.
summary.tldr: The paper gives finite-time descent and convergence results for SVGD and connects its practical particle implementation to its population formulation.

title: A Non-Asymptotic Analysis for Stein Variational Gradient Descent

abstract: Bayesian quadrature (BQ) is a method for solving numerical integration problems in a Bayesian manner, which allows users to quantify their uncertainty about the solution. The standard approach to BQ is based on a Gaussian process (GP) approximation of the integrand. As a result, BQ is inherently limited to cases where GP approximations can be done in an efficient manner, thus often prohibiting very high-dimensional or non-smooth target functions. This paper proposes to tackle this issue with a new Bayesian numerical integration algorithm based on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) priors, which we call BART-Int. BART priors are easy to tune and well-suited for discontinuous functions. We demonstrate that they also lend themselves naturally to a sequential design setting and that explicit convergence rates can be obtained in a variety of settings. The advantages and disadvantages of this new methodology are highlighted on a set of benchmark tests including the Genz functions, on a rare-event simulation problem and on a Bayesian survey design problem.
originalAbstract: Bayesian quadrature (BQ) is a method for solving numerical integration problems in a Bayesian manner, which allows users to quantify their uncertainty about the solution. The standard approach to BQ is based on a Gaussian process (GP) approximation of the integrand. As a result, BQ is inherently limited to cases where GP approximations can be done in an efficient manner, thus often prohibiting very high-dimensional or non-smooth target functions. This paper proposes to tackle this issue with a new Bayesian numerical integration algorithm based on Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART) priors, which we call BART-Int. BART priors are easy to tune and well-suited for discontinuous functions. We demonstrate that they also lend themselves naturally to a sequential design setting and that explicit convergence rates can be obtained in a variety of settings. The advantages and disadvantages of this new methodology are highlighted on a set of benchmark tests including the Genz functions, on a rare-event simulation problem and on a Bayesian survey design problem.

paragraphs: Numerical integration estimates an integral from evaluations of a function. Bayesian quadrature adds a representation of uncertainty about the answer, using a probabilistic approximation of the function being integrated. The usual Gaussian process approach becomes difficult when that approximation is computationally expensive, often restricting its usefulness for very high-dimensional or non-smooth functions.

The paper proposes BART-Int, which instead builds its Bayesian integration procedure around Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. These tree-based priors are easy to tune and suited to functions with discontinuities. The central idea is to change the model of the function while retaining a Bayesian treatment of uncertainty about its integral.

The authors show that the tree-based construction fits naturally into sequential design, where function evaluations are chosen over successive steps. They also obtain explicit convergence rates in several settings. Tests involving Genz benchmark functions, rare-event simulation, and Bayesian survey design illustrate both advantages and disadvantages. The contribution is therefore an alternative integration method with theoretical support and demonstrated tradeoffs, rather than a claim that trees always replace Gaussian processes successfully.
summary.tldr: BART-Int uses Bayesian regression trees for uncertainty-aware numerical integration, offering an alternative suited to discontinuous functions.

title: Bayesian Probabilistic Numerical Integration with Tree-Based Models

abstract: In Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), the graph structure is incorporated into the learning of node representations. This complex structure makes explaining GNNs' predictions become much more challenging. In this paper, we propose PGM-Explainer, a Probabilistic Graphical Model (PGM) model-agnostic explainer for GNNs. Given a prediction to be explained, PGM-Explainer identifies crucial graph components and generates an explanation in form of a PGM approximating that prediction. Different from existing explainers for GNNs where the explanations are drawn from a set of linear functions of explained features, PGM-Explainer is able to demonstrate the dependencies of explained features in form of conditional probabilities. Our theoretical analysis shows that the PGM generated by PGM-Explainer includes the Markov-blanket of the target prediction, i.e. including all its statistical information. We also show that the explanation returned by PGM-Explainer contains the same set of independence statements in the perfect map. Our experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that PGM-Explainer achieves better performance than existing explainers in many benchmark tasks.

PGM-Explainer addresses this by identifying important graph components for a particular prediction and constructing a probabilistic graphical model that approximates it. The method is model-agnostic, so its explanation framework is not tied to one particular graph neural network design.

The explanation represents dependencies between features through conditional probabilities. This provides a way to show how explained features relate to one another, beyond the linear feature explanations discussed in the abstract. The authors' theoretical analysis establishes that the generated model includes the target prediction's Markov blanket, capturing its relevant statistical information.

The analysis also shows that the returned explanation contains the same independence statements as the perfect map. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report better performance than existing explainers on many benchmark tasks. The contribution combines a structured representation of feature relationships with theoretical properties and empirical support for explaining graph-based predictions.
summary.tldr: PGM-Explainer represents important graph components and their statistical dependencies in a probabilistic explanation of a graph neural network prediction.

title: PGM-Explainer: Probabilistic Graphical Model Explanations for Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The feedback data of recommender systems are often subject to what was exposed to the users; however, most learning and evaluation methods do not account for the underlying exposure mechanism. We first show in theory that applying supervised learning to detect user preferences may end up with inconsistent results in the absence of exposure information. The counterfactual propensity-weighting approach from causal inference can account for the exposure mechanism; nevertheless, the partial-observation nature of the feedback data can cause identifiability issues. We propose a principled solution by introducing a minimax empirical risk formulation. We show that the relaxation of the dual problem can be converted to an adversarial game between two recommendation models, where the opponent of the candidate model characterizes the underlying exposure mechanism. We provide learning bounds and conduct extensive simulation studies to illustrate and justify the proposed approach over a broad range of recommendation settings, which shed insights on the various benefits of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Recommendation feedback depends on which items users had an opportunity to see. Consequently, observed responses reflect both preferences and exposure. The paper shows theoretically that supervised learning can produce inconsistent preference estimates when exposure information is absent. This matters for evaluation as well as training, because the observed feedback is shaped by the same selection mechanism.

Counterfactual propensity weighting tries to account for exposure, but partially observed feedback can leave the underlying quantities impossible to identify uniquely. The authors address this problem with a minimax empirical-risk formulation. This makes the uncertainty associated with exposure part of the learning problem instead of treating the observed feedback as a complete account of user preferences.

A relaxation of the formulation's dual becomes an adversarial game between two recommendation models. One is the candidate recommender; its opponent represents the exposure mechanism. The paper supplies learning bounds and extensive simulations across recommendation settings. These results support the proposed formulation as a principled approach to learning and evaluation when exposure complicates the interpretation of feedback.
summary.tldr: An adversarial minimax formulation addresses exposure-related uncertainty in recommendation learning and evaluation.

title: Adversarial Counterfactual Learning and Evaluation for Recommender System

abstract: We consider online convex optimization with time-varying stage costs and additional switching costs. Since the switching costs introduce coupling across all stages, multi-step-ahead (long-term) predictions are incorporated to improve the online performance. However, longer-term predictions tend to suffer from lower quality. Thus, a critical question is: \textit{how to reduce the impact of long-term prediction errors on the online performance?} To address this question, we introduce a gradient-based online algorithm, Receding Horizon Inexact Gradient (RHIG), and analyze its performance by dynamic regrets in terms of the temporal variation of the environment and the prediction errors. RHIG only considers at most $W$-step-ahead predictions to avoid being misled by worse predictions in the longer term. The optimal choice of $W$ suggested by our regret bounds depends on the tradeoff between the variation of the environment and the prediction accuracy. Additionally, we apply RHIG to a well-established stochastic prediction error model and provide expected regret and concentration bounds under correlated prediction errors. Lastly, we numerically test the performance of RHIG on quadrotor tracking problems.

paragraphs: Online decisions can incur both an immediate cost and a cost for changing the previous decision. Those switching costs connect choices across time, making forecasts useful. Yet looking farther ahead can also expose the decision maker to less accurate predictions. This paper studies how to use forecasts while controlling the harm from their errors.

The proposed Receding Horizon Inexact Gradient algorithm, RHIG, uses predictions no more than W steps ahead. The authors analyze dynamic regret in terms of both environmental change and prediction error. Their bounds suggest choosing the forecast horizon by balancing these factors: a longer view can help anticipate changes, but unreliable distant forecasts can undermine that benefit.

The analysis also covers a stochastic prediction-error model with correlated errors, providing expected-regret and concentration bounds. Correlation matters because forecast mistakes need not occur independently across time. Numerical tests apply RHIG to quadrotor tracking. The paper’s contribution is a gradient-based decision rule together with theoretical guidance for selecting how far into an uncertain future to plan.
summary.tldr: RHIG limits its forecast horizon and uses regret analysis to balance changing environments against increasingly unreliable long-term predictions.

title: Leveraging Predictions in Smoothed Online Convex Optimization via Gradient-based Algorithms

abstract: Learning binary classiﬁers only from positive and unlabeled (PU) data is an important and challenging task in many real-world applications, including web text classiﬁcation, disease gene identiﬁcation and fraud detection, where negative samples are difﬁcult to verify experimentally. Most recent PU learning methods are developed based on the misclassiﬁcation risk of the supervised learning type, and they may suffer from inaccurate estimates of class prior probabilities. In this paper, we introduce a variational principle for PU learning that allows us to quantitatively evaluate the modeling error of the Bayesian classiﬁer directly from given data. This leads to a loss function which can be efﬁciently calculated without involving class prior estimation or any other intermediate estimation problems, and the variational learning method can then be employed to optimize the classiﬁer under general conditions. We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed variational method on a number of benchmark examples.

paragraphs: Positive-and-unlabeled learning trains a binary classifier from confirmed positive examples and examples whose class is unknown. The unlabeled group cannot simply be treated as negative. This situation arises when verifying negatives is difficult, including the text classification, disease gene identification, and fraud detection applications discussed in the paper.

Many existing approaches adapt the misclassification-risk objective used in supervised learning. They can depend on estimating class prior probabilities, meaning the overall proportions of the classes, and inaccurate estimates can undermine learning. The paper introduces a variational principle that evaluates the modeling error of the Bayesian classifier directly from the available data.

This principle produces a loss that can be calculated efficiently without estimating class priors or solving other intermediate estimation problems. The classifier can then be optimized through variational learning under general conditions. Benchmark examples illustrate the method's effectiveness. The contribution is a direct training objective for the available positive and unlabeled observations, avoiding an estimation step that can otherwise introduce error.
summary.tldr: A variational objective trains classifiers from positive and unlabeled data without estimating class prior probabilities.

title: A Variational Approach for Learning from Positive and Unlabeled Data

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation methods traditionally assume that all source categories are present in the target domain. In practice, little may be known about the category overlap between the two domains. While some methods address target settings with either partial or open-set categories, they assume that the particular setting is known a priori. We propose a more universally applicable domain adaptation approach that can handle arbitrary category shift, called Domain Adaptative Neighborhood Clustering via Entropy optimization (DANCE). Our approach combines two novel ideas: First, as we cannot fully rely on source categories to learn features discriminative for the target, we propose a novel neighborhood clustering technique to learn the structure of the target domain in a self-supervised way. Second, we use entropy-based feature alignment and rejection to align target features with the source, or reject them as unknown categories based on their entropy. We show through extensive experiments that DANCE outperforms baselines across open-set, open-partial and partial domain adaptation settings.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers a model from a source domain to a target domain, but their categories may overlap only partly. Many approaches assume a particular overlap pattern is known in advance. This paper introduces DANCE to handle arbitrary category shifts without requiring that setting to be specified beforehand.

DANCE combines two mechanisms. Self-supervised neighborhood clustering learns structure from the target data, reducing reliance on source categories as the sole guide to useful features. Entropy-based alignment and rejection then determine whether target features should align with source categories or be treated as belonging to unknown categories.

This combination addresses both learning a useful target representation and deciding which target examples fit the source label space. Extensive experiments show improvements over baselines across open-set, open-partial, and partial adaptation settings. The results support a common approach across several category-overlap situations, with self-supervision supplying target-specific structure and entropy guiding the choice between alignment and rejection.
summary.tldr: DANCE combines target-domain clustering with entropy-based alignment and rejection to adapt across unknown category overlap.

title: Universal Domain Adaptation through Self Supervision

abstract: Despite achieving remarkable performance, deep graph learning models, such as node classification and network embedding, suffer from harassment caused by small adversarial perturbations. However, the vulnerability analysis of graph matching under adversarial attacks has not been fully investigated yet. This paper proposes an adversarial attack model with two novel attack techniques to perturb the graph structure and degrade the quality of deep graph matching: (1) a kernel density estimation approach is utilized to estimate and maximize node densities to derive imperceptible perturbations, by pushing attacked nodes to dense regions in two graphs, such that they are indistinguishable from many neighbors; and (2) a meta learning-based projected gradient descent method is developed to well choose attack starting points and to improve the search performance for producing effective perturbations. We evaluate the effectiveness of the attack model on real datasets and validate that the attacks can be transferable to other graph learning models.
originalAbstract: Despite achieving remarkable performance, deep graph learning models, such as node classification and network embedding, suffer from harassment caused by small adversarial perturbations. However, the vulnerability analysis of graph matching under adversarial attacks has not been fully investigated yet. We evaluate the effectiveness of the attack model on real datasets and validate that the attacks can be transferable to other graph learning models.

paragraphs: Graph matching involves identifying corresponding nodes across graphs. This paper investigates how small, deliberately chosen changes to graph structure can undermine deep learning models that perform this task. Its focus is a vulnerability that had received less attention than attacks on other graph learning tasks, such as node classification.

The attack combines two techniques. First, it estimates node density and pushes attacked nodes toward crowded regions in both graphs. The aim is to make those nodes difficult to distinguish from their neighbors while keeping the perturbations imperceptible. Second, it uses a meta-learning approach to select starting points for projected gradient descent, improving the search for changes that damage matching quality.

Experiments on real datasets support the attack model’s effectiveness. The authors also demonstrate that attacks can transfer to other graph learning models. These findings identify a weakness involving the distinctiveness of nodes: perturbations designed to blur that distinctiveness can interfere with learned matching and may affect models beyond the original target.
summary.tldr: Small structural perturbations can confuse deep graph matching by making attacked nodes resemble crowded neighborhoods.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Deep Graph Matching

abstract: Keypoint detector and descriptor are two main components of point cloud registration. Previous learning-based keypoint detectors rely on saliency estimation for each point or farthest point sample (FPS) for candidate points selection, which are inefficient and not applicable in large scale scenes. This paper proposes Random Sample-based Keypoint Detector and Descriptor Network (RSKDD-Net) for large scale point cloud registration. The key idea is using random sampling to efficiently select candidate points and using a learning-based method to jointly generate keypoints and corresponding descriptors. To tackle the information loss of random sampling, we exploit a novel random dilation cluster strategy to enlarge the receptive field of each sampled point and an attention mechanism to aggregate the positions and features of neighbor points. Furthermore, we propose a matching loss to train the descriptor in a weakly supervised manner. Extensive experiments on two large scale outdoor LiDAR datasets show that the proposed RSKDD-Net achieves state-of-the-art performance with more than 15 times faster than existing methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/ispc-lab/RSKDD-Net.

paragraphs: Point-cloud registration relies on finding useful keypoints and describing them so corresponding locations can be matched. Selecting candidates through per-point saliency or farthest-point sampling can be inefficient in large scenes. RSKDD-Net instead uses random sampling and jointly learns keypoint locations and their descriptors.

Random sampling improves candidate-selection efficiency but loses information. To address that tradeoff, the network uses random dilation clusters to enlarge the region available to each sampled point. An attention mechanism combines neighboring positions and features, and a matching loss trains the descriptors with weak supervision.

Experiments on two large outdoor LiDAR datasets report state-of-the-art performance and speeds more than fifteen times faster than existing methods. The approach therefore combines a cheap sampling step with learned processing intended to recover useful surrounding information. Its contribution lies in making random candidate selection compatible with effective keypoint detection and description, with the reported accuracy and speed results demonstrating that combination in the tested registration settings.
summary.tldr: RSKDD-Net combines random sampling, expanded neighborhoods, and attention to learn fast, effective keypoints and descriptors for large point clouds.

title: RSKDD-Net: Random Sample-based Keypoint Detector and Descriptor

abstract: We consider the problem where $n$ clients transmit $d$-dimensional real-valued vectors using $d(1+o(1))$ bits each, in a manner that allows the receiver to approximately reconstruct their mean. Such compression problems naturally arise in distributed and federated learning. We provide novel mathematical results and derive computationally efficient algorithms that are more accurate than previous compression techniques. We evaluate our methods on a collection of distributed and federated learning tasks, using a variety of datasets, and show a consistent improvement over the state of the art.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem where $n$ clients transmit $d$-dimensional real-valued vectors using $d(1+o(1))$ bits each, in a manner that allows the receiver to approximately reconstruct their mean. Such compression problems naturally arise in distributed and federated learning. We provide novel mathematical results and derive computationally efficient algorithms that are more accurate than previous compression techniques. We evaluate our methods on a collection of distributed and federated learning tasks, using a variety of datasets, and show a consistent improvement over the state of the art.

paragraphs: DRIVE studies how a receiver can estimate the average of vectors held by many clients when communication is tightly restricted. Each client has a real-valued vector with d coordinates but sends only about d bits, with a vanishing relative overhead. The receiver's task is to reconstruct the mean approximately from those compressed messages.

The setting directly concerns distributed and federated learning, where information from separate clients must be combined. The quantity being recovered is their average, so the relevant accuracy question is how well compression preserves that aggregate. The paper develops new mathematical results and uses them to derive computationally efficient algorithms that are more accurate than earlier compression techniques under the studied communication constraints.

The authors evaluate the methods across a collection of distributed and federated learning tasks using several datasets. They report consistent improvements over the state of the art in those evaluations. The contribution therefore joins an extremely small communication budget with practical computation and improved estimation accuracy, making the communication constraint part of the algorithm's design.
summary.tldr: DRIVE improves distributed mean estimation while allowing each client to transmit roughly one bit per vector coordinate.

title: DRIVE: One-bit Distributed Mean Estimation

abstract: The support vector machine (SVM) and minimum Euclidean norm least squares regression are two fundamentally different approaches to fitting linear models, but they have recently been connected in models for very high-dimensional data through a phenomenon of support vector proliferation, where every training example used to fit an SVM becomes a support vector. In this paper, we explore the generality of this phenomenon and make the following contributions. First, we prove a super-linear lower bound on the dimension (in terms of sample size) required for support vector proliferation in independent feature models, matching the upper bounds from previous works. We further identify a sharp phase transition in Gaussian feature models, bound the width of this transition, and give experimental support for its universality. Finally, we hypothesize that this phase transition occurs only in much higher-dimensional settings in the $\ell_1$ variant of the SVM, and we present a new geometric characterization of the problem that may elucidate this phenomenon for the general $\ell_p$ case.

paragraphs: Support vector machines and minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares regression use different fitting principles, yet they can coincide in very high dimensions. This connection involves support vector proliferation: every training example becomes a support vector. The paper investigates how much dimensionality is needed and how broadly the phenomenon occurs.

For independent feature models, the authors prove a super-linear lower bound on dimension as a function of sample size, matching earlier upper bounds. For Gaussian features, they identify a sharp phase transition and bound its width. These results describe both the dimensional scale required and how abruptly the behavior changes around the transition.

Experiments support the possibility that the transition is universal beyond the Gaussian setting. The authors also hypothesize that the l1 version of the SVM needs much higher dimensions for a corresponding transition. A new geometric characterization may help explain the general lp case. The paper thus separates established bounds and Gaussian results from experimentally supported generality and further hypotheses.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the dimensional threshold where every example becomes a support vector, connecting SVMs with minimum-norm regression.

title: Support vector machines and linear regression coincide with very high-dimensional features

abstract: We investigate the optimal design of experimental studies that have pre-treatment outcome data available. The average treatment effect is estimated as the difference between the weighted average outcomes of the treated and control units. A number of commonly used approaches fit this formulation, including the difference-in-means estimator and a variety of synthetic-control techniques. We propose several methods for choosing the set of treated units in conjunction with the weights. Observing the NP-hardness of the problem, we introduce a mixed-integer programming formulation which selects both the treatment and control sets and unit weightings. We prove that these proposed approaches lead to qualitatively different experimental units being selected for treatment. We use simulations based on publicly available data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics that show improvements in terms of mean squared error and statistical power when compared to simple and commonly used alternatives such as randomized trials.

paragraphs: When outcomes are available before an experiment begins, that information can help determine which units receive treatment and how their later outcomes are compared. This paper studies experimental design when treatment effects are estimated by subtracting a weighted control-group outcome from a weighted treated-group outcome.

The formulation includes both simple differences in means and several synthetic-control approaches. The authors propose methods that choose treatment assignments jointly with the weights used in estimation. Because the design problem is NP-hard, they introduce a mixed-integer programming formulation that selects treatment and control sets together with unit weightings.

The authors prove that their proposed approaches select qualitatively different kinds of experimental units for treatment. In simulations based on public US Bureau of Labor Statistics data, the methods improve mean squared error and statistical power relative to simple, commonly used alternatives, including randomized trials. The results illustrate potential gains from coordinating experimental assignment with the eventual estimator when pre-treatment outcome data are available.
summary.tldr: Synthetic Design jointly optimizes treatment assignment and estimation weights, improving error and power in simulations using pre-treatment outcome data.

title: Synthetic Design: An Optimization Approach to Experimental Design with Synthetic Controls

abstract: The neural attention mechanism has been incorporated into deep neural networks to achieve state-of-the-art performance in various domains. Most such models use multi-head self-attention which is appealing for the ability to attend to information from different perspectives. This paper introduces alignment attention that explicitly encourages self-attention to match the distributions of the key and query within each head. The resulting alignment attention networks can be optimized as an unsupervised regularization in the existing attention framework. It is simple to convert any models with self-attention, including pre-trained ones, to the proposed alignment attention. On a variety of language understanding tasks, we show the effectiveness of our method in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, generalization across domains, and robustness to adversarial attacks. We further demonstrate the general applicability of our approach on graph attention and visual question answering, showing the great potential of incorporating our alignment method into various attention-related tasks.

The resulting alignment attention networks can be optimized as an unsupervised regularization in the existing attention framework. paragraphs: Multi-head self-attention allows a neural network to relate information from several learned perspectives. Within each head, keys and queries provide the representations used to determine attention relationships. This paper proposes explicitly encouraging their distributions to match, introducing an additional learning objective called alignment attention.

The alignment objective works as unsupervised regularization within an existing attention framework. This makes it possible to adapt models that already use self-attention, including pretrained models. The approach changes how attention representations are encouraged to organize during optimization, while retaining the broader framework in which those representations are used.

Across language-understanding tasks, the authors report benefits in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, transfer across domains, and resistance to adversarial attacks. They also demonstrate applications to graph attention and visual question answering. These results suggest that distribution matching can be useful across multiple attention-based settings. Its significance extends beyond prediction accuracy: the reported improvements also concern how reliably a model expresses uncertainty and behaves when its inputs or evaluation domain change.
summary.tldr: Alignment attention regularizes each attention head by matching key and query distributions, improving several measures of model reliability in experiments.

title: Alignment Attention by Matching Key and Query Distributions

abstract: We introduce the task of spatially localizing narrated interactions in videos. Key to our approach is the ability to learn to spatially localize interactions with self-supervision on a large corpus of videos with accompanying transcribed narrations. To achieve this goal, we propose a multilayer cross-modal attention network that enables effective optimization of a contrastive loss during training. We introduce a divided strategy that alternates between computing inter- and intra-modal attention across the visual and natural language modalities, which allows effective training via directly contrasting the two modalities' representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by self-training on the HowTo100M instructional video dataset and evaluating on a newly collected dataset of localized described interactions in the YouCook2 dataset. We show that our approach outperforms alternative baselines, including shallow co-attention and full cross-modal attention. We also apply our approach to grounding phrases in images with weak supervision on Flickr30K and show that stacking multiple attention layers is effective and, when combined with a word-to-region loss, achieves state of the art on recall-at-one and pointing hand accuracies.
originalAbstract: We introduce the task of spatially localizing narrated interactions in videos. Key to our approach is the ability to learn to spatially localize interactions with self-supervision on a large corpus of videos with accompanying transcribed narrations. To achieve this goal, we propose a multilayer cross-modal attention network that enables effective optimization of a contrastive loss during training. We introduce a divided strategy that alternates between computing inter- and intra-modal attention across the visual and natural language modalities, which allows effective training via directly contrasting the two modalities' representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by self-training on the HowTo100M instructional video dataset and evaluating on a newly collected dataset of localized described interactions in the YouCook2 dataset. We show that our approach outperforms alternative baselines, including shallow co-attention and full cross-modal attention. We also apply our approach to grounding phrases in images with weak supervision on Flickr30K and show that stacking multiple attention layers is effective and, when combined with a word-to-region loss, achieves state of the art on recall-at-one and pointing hand accuracies.

This divided arrangement supports training with a contrastive loss that directly compares their representations. title: Look at What I’m Doing: Self-Supervised Spatial Grounding of Narrations in Instructional Videos

abstract: Unlike standard prediction tasks, survival analysis requires modeling right censored data, which must be treated with care. While deep neural networks excel in traditional supervised learning, it remains unclear how to best utilize these models in survival analysis. A key question asks which data-generating assumptions of traditional survival models should be retained and which should be made more flexible via the function-approximating capabilities of neural networks. Rather than estimating the survival function targeted by most existing methods, we introduce a Deep Extended Hazard (DeepEH) model to provide a flexible and general framework for deep survival analysis. The extended hazard model includes the conventional Cox proportional hazards and accelerated failure time models as special cases, so DeepEH subsumes the popular Deep Cox proportional hazard (DeepSurv) and Deep Accelerated Failure Time (DeepAFT) models. We additionally provide theoretical support for the proposed DeepEH model by establishing consistency and convergence rate of the survival function estimator, which underscore the attractive feature that deep learning is able to detect low-dimensional structure of data in high-dimensional space. Numerical experiments also provide evidence that the proposed methods outperform existing statistical and deep learning approaches to survival analysis.

Their theory highlights the ability to detect low-dimensional structure within high-dimensional data. Numerical experiments also provide evidence of improvements over existing statistical and deep-learning survival methods, supporting the framework through both estimation theory and empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: DeepEH broadens deep survival modeling through an extended hazard framework that includes DeepSurv and DeepAFT and has theoretical estimation guarantees.

title: Deep Extended Hazard Models for Survival Analysis

abstract: Quantization is a technique used in deep neural networks (DNNs) to increase execution performance and hardware efficiency. Uniform post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are common, since they can be implemented efficiently in hardware and do not require extensive hardware resources or a training set. Mapping FP32 models to INT8 using uniform PTQ yields models with negligible accuracy degradation; however, reducing precision below 8 bits with PTQ is challenging, as accuracy degradation becomes noticeable, due to the increase in quantization noise. In this paper, we propose a sparsity-aware quantization (SPARQ) method, in which the unstructured and dynamic activation sparsity is leveraged in different representation granularities. 4-bit quantization, for example, is employed by dynamically examining the bits of 8-bit values and choosing a window of 4 bits, while first skipping zero-value bits. Moreover, instead of quantizing activation-by-activation to 4 bits, we focus on pairs of 8-bit activations and examine whether one of the two is equal to zero. If one is equal to zero, the second can opportunistically use the other's 4-bit budget; if both do not equal zero, then each is dynamically quantized to 4 bits, as described. SPARQ achieves minor accuracy degradation and a practical hardware implementation.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the precision of neural-network values to improve execution and hardware efficiency. Uniform post-training quantization works well when moving from 32-bit floating-point values to 8-bit integers, but lower precision introduces more noticeable errors. SPARQ addresses this difficulty by exploiting zeros and unused bits in activation values.

At the individual-value level, the method examines an 8-bit activation and dynamically selects a four-bit window while first skipping zero-valued bits. This adapts the representation to the value being encoded. It also examines pairs of activations, allowing the available bit budget to be allocated according to whether either member is zero.

If one activation in a pair is zero, the other can use its four-bit allocation as well. When both are nonzero, each receives a dynamically selected four-bit representation. The authors report minor accuracy degradation and a practical hardware implementation. The central idea is to use activation sparsity at multiple representation granularities so that limited precision can be spent where values need it.
summary.tldr: SPARQ uses activation zeros and dynamic bit selection to allocate low-precision representations more effectively after training.

title: Post-Training Sparsity-Aware Quantization

abstract: Many supervised learning problems involve high-dimensional data such as images, text, or graphs. In order to make efficient use of data, it is often useful to leverage certain geometric priors in the problem at hand, such as invariance to translations, permutation subgroups, or stability to small deformations. We study the sample complexity of learning problems where the target function presents such invariance and stability properties, by considering spherical harmonic decompositions of such functions on the sphere. We provide non-parametric rates of convergence for kernel methods, and show improvements in sample complexity by a factor equal to the size of the group when using an invariant kernel over the group, compared to the corresponding non-invariant kernel. These improvements are valid when the sample size is large enough, with an asymptotic behavior that depends on spectral properties of the group. Finally, these gains are extended beyond invariance groups to also cover geometric stability to small deformations, modeled here as subsets (not necessarily subgroups) of permutations.

paragraphs: Some prediction problems have useful geometric structure: a target may be unchanged by particular transformations or vary only slightly under small deformations. This paper studies how such properties affect the number of training examples needed. It analyzes target functions on the sphere using spherical harmonic decompositions.

The authors derive nonparametric convergence rates for kernel methods. When the target has the relevant invariance, using a kernel invariant under the transformation group improves sample complexity by a factor equal to the group's size compared with the corresponding non-invariant kernel. This quantifies a potential data-efficiency benefit from encoding known symmetry.

The improvement is qualified by sample size: it holds when enough samples are available, and its asymptotic behavior depends on the group's spectral properties. The analysis also extends beyond exact group invariance to stability under small deformations, represented as sets of permutations that need not form subgroups. The contribution therefore covers both exact symmetries and a broader form of geometric stability within the stated mathematical setting.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies how invariant kernels can reduce sample complexity at sufficiently large sample sizes and extends the analysis to geometric stability.

title: On the Sample Complexity of Learning under Geometric Stability

abstract: Probabilistic circuits (PCs) are a powerful modeling framework for representing tractable probability distributions over combinatorial spaces. In machine learning and probabilistic programming, one is often interested in understanding whether the distributions learned using PCs are close to the desired distribution. Thus, given two probabilistic circuits, a fundamental problem of interest is to determine whether their distributions are close to each other.The primary contribution of this paper is a closeness test for PCs with respect to the total variation distance metric. Our algorithm utilizes two common PC queries, counting and sampling. In particular, we provide a poly-time probabilistic algorithm to check the closeness of two PCs, when the PCs support tractable approximate counting and sampling. We demonstrate the practical efficiency of our algorithmic framework via a detailed experimental evaluation of a prototype implementation against a set of 375 PC benchmarks. We find that our test correctly decides the closeness of all 375 PCs within 3600 seconds.

paragraphs: Probabilistic circuits represent probability distributions over combinatorial spaces while supporting useful computations. A basic validation question is whether two such circuits describe similar distributions. This matters when comparing a learned distribution with a desired one: different circuit representations alone do not tell us how different their probability assignments are.

The paper develops a test for closeness in total variation distance, a measure of discrepancy between probability distributions. Its algorithm uses counting and sampling queries that are common in probabilistic circuits. The main guarantee is a polynomial-time probabilistic test when both circuits support tractable approximate counting and sampling. Those query capabilities are the stated condition enabling the efficiency result.

The authors evaluate a prototype on 375 probabilistic-circuit benchmarks and report correct closeness decisions for all of them within the stated 3,600-second limit. The experimental results demonstrate practical promise alongside the theoretical guarantee. The method turns an abstract comparison between distributions into a procedure built from operations the circuits can already provide, under the required counting and sampling assumptions.
summary.tldr: A randomized polynomial-time test compares probabilistic-circuit distributions when efficient approximate counting and sampling are available.

title: Testing Probabilistic Circuits

abstract: This paper introduces a method for the nonparametric Bayesian learning of nonlinear operators, through the use of the Volterra series with kernels represented using Gaussian processes (GPs), which we term the nonparametric Volterra kernels model (NVKM). When the input function to the operator is unobserved and has a GP prior, the NVKM constitutes a powerful method for both single and multiple output regression, and can be viewed as a nonlinear and nonparametric latent force model. When the input function is observed, the NVKM can be used to perform Bayesian system identification. We use recent advances in efficient sampling of explicit functions from GPs to map process realisations through the Volterra series without resorting to numerical integration, allowing scalability through doubly stochastic variational inference, and avoiding the need for Gaussian approximations of the output processes. We demonstrate the performance of the model for both multiple output regression and system identification using standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper develops a Bayesian method for learning nonlinear operators: mappings that transform input functions into output functions. Its nonparametric Volterra kernels model, or NVKM, uses a Volterra series and represents the series' kernels with Gaussian processes. This provides a flexible probabilistic representation of the operator.

The model supports two settings. When the input function is hidden and given a Gaussian-process prior, it can perform regression with one or several outputs and acts as a nonlinear, nonparametric latent force model. When the input is observed, it can instead identify the system that maps those inputs to outputs.

The computational method samples explicit functions from Gaussian processes and passes these realizations through the Volterra series without numerical integration. Doubly stochastic variational inference supports scalability, and the method avoids requiring Gaussian approximations for the output processes. Evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate applications to multiple-output regression and system identification. The contribution combines uncertainty-aware nonlinear operator learning with an inference strategy that addresses the computation needed to use it.
summary.tldr: NVKM combines Gaussian-process Volterra kernels with efficient sampling to learn nonlinear operators for regression and system identification.

title: Learning Nonparametric Volterra Kernels with Gaussian Processes

abstract: We study gradient descent-ascent learning dynamics with timescale separation ($\tau$-GDA) in unconstrained continuous action zero-sum games where the minimizing player faces a nonconvex optimization problem and the maximizing player optimizes a Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) or strongly-concave (SC) objective. In contrast to past work on gradient-based learning in nonconvex-PL/SC zero-sum games, we assess convergence in relation to natural game-theoretic equilibria instead of only notions of stationarity. In pursuit of this goal, we prove that the only locally stable points of the $\tau$-GDA continuous-time limiting system correspond to strict local minmax equilibria in each class of games. For these classes of games, we exploit timescale separation to construct a potential function that when combined with the stability characterization and an asymptotic saddle avoidance result gives a global asymptotic almost-sure convergence guarantee for the discrete-time gradient descent-ascent update to a set of the strict local minmax equilibrium. Moreover, we provide convergence rates for the gradient descent-ascent dynamics with timescale separation to approximate stationary points.

paragraphs: The paper studies two-player zero-sum games in which one player minimizes an objective and the other maximizes it. The minimizing problem may be nonconvex, while the maximizing objective must satisfy a Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition or strong concavity. Actions are continuous and unconstrained. The learning rule uses gradient descent and ascent operating on separated timescales.

Rather than asking only whether gradients become small, the authors examine whether learning reaches meaningful game-theoretic equilibria. They prove that every locally stable point of the corresponding continuous-time system is a strict local minmax equilibrium. This connects dynamical stability to a local equilibrium concept within the game classes studied.

Using timescale separation, a potential function, and a result about avoiding saddles asymptotically, the authors establish global asymptotic almost-sure convergence of the discrete updates to a set of strict local minmax equilibria. They also give rates for reaching approximate stationary points. Global convergence here concerns the learning process; the destination remains a local minmax equilibrium, not a claimed global optimum of an arbitrary game.
summary.tldr: For specified nonconvex zero-sum games, gradient descent-ascent with separated timescales converges almost surely and asymptotically to strict local minmax equilibria.

title: Global Convergence to Local Minmax Equilibrium in Classes of Nonconvex Zero-Sum Games

abstract: In this paper, we introduce RELLISUR, a novel dataset of real low-light low-resolution images paired with normal-light high-resolution reference image counterparts. With this dataset, we seek to fill the gap between low-light image enhancement and low-resolution image enhancement (Super-Resolution (SR)) which is currently only being addressed separately in the literature, even though the visibility of real-world images are often limited by both low-light and low-resolution. Part of the reason for this, is the lack of a large-scale dataset. To this end, we release a dataset with 12750 paired images of different resolutions and degrees of low-light illumination, to facilitate learning of deep-learning based models that can perform a direct mapping from degraded images with low visibility to sharp and detail rich images of high resolution. Additionally, we provide a benchmark of the existing methods for separate Low Light Enhancement (LLE) and SR on the proposed dataset along with experiments with joint LLE and SR. The latter shows that joint processing results in more accurate reconstructions with better perceptual quality compared to sequential processing of the images. With this, we confirm that the new RELLISUR dataset can be useful for future machine learning research aimed at solving simultaneous image LLE and SR.

paragraphs: RELLISUR addresses images that are difficult to see because they are both dark and low resolution. The authors observe that low-light enhancement and super-resolution have generally been studied separately, even though real images can suffer from both problems at once. They introduce paired data to support studying the combined restoration task.

The dataset contains 12,750 image pairs spanning different resolutions and low-light levels. Each degraded image is paired with a normally lit, high resolution reference. These pairs support training models to map directly from poor visibility to an image with greater sharpness and detail, bringing both enhancement goals into a single learning problem.

The paper benchmarks existing methods for the separate tasks and experiments with joint enhancement. In the reported experiments, joint processing yields more accurate reconstructions and better perceptual quality than processing the tasks sequentially. This finding supports investigating combined methods and establishes RELLISUR as a resource for comparing approaches to simultaneous lighting and resolution improvement.
summary.tldr: RELLISUR provides paired data for simultaneous low-light enhancement and super-resolution, with experiments favoring joint over sequential processing.

title: RELLISUR: A Real Low-Light Image Super-Resolution Dataset

abstract: This paper considers the problem of lossy neural image compression (NIC). Current state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods adopt uniform posterior to approximate quantization noise, and single-sample pathwise estimator to approximate the gradient of evidence lower bound (ELBO). In this paper, we propose to train NIC with multiple-sample importance weighted autoencoder (IWAE) target, which is tighter than ELBO and converges to log likelihood as sample size increases. First, we identify that the uniform posterior of NIC has special properties, which affect the variance and bias of pathwise and score function estimators of the IWAE target. Moreover, we provide insights on a commonly adopted trick in NIC from gradient variance perspective. Based on those analysis, we further propose multiple-sample NIC (MS-NIC), an enhanced IWAE target for NIC. Experimental results demonstrate that it improves SOTA NIC methods. Our MS-NIC is plug-and-play, and can be easily extended to neural video compression.

paragraphs: Lossy neural image compression trains models to represent images compactly while allowing reconstruction error. Existing methods approximate quantization noise with a uniform posterior and commonly estimate the training gradient from one sample. This paper investigates how using multiple samples can improve that training process.

The starting point is the importance-weighted autoencoder objective, which gives a tighter bound than the usual evidence lower bound and approaches log likelihood as the sample count grows. The authors analyze how the uniform posterior used in compression affects the bias and variance of different gradient estimators. They also explain a commonly used compression-training trick through its effect on gradient variance.

From this analysis, they develop MS-NIC, an enhanced multi-sample objective tailored to neural image compression. Experiments show improvements to state-of-the-art compression methods. The approach is described as plug-and-play and readily extendable to neural video compression. Its contribution lies in adapting the objective and gradient analysis to the particular noise model used in compression, rather than treating additional samples as an automatically sufficient improvement.
summary.tldr: MS-NIC uses a compression-specific multi-sample training objective to improve existing neural image compression methods.

title: Multi-Sample Training for Neural Image Compression

abstract: Dale’s principle implies that biological neural networks are composed of neurons that are either excitatory or inhibitory. While the number of possible architectures of such Daleian networks is exponentially smaller than the number of non-Daleian ones, the computational and functional implications of using Daleian networks by the brain are mostly unknown. Here, we use models of recurrent spiking neural networks and rate-based ones to show, surprisingly, that despite the structural limitations on Daleian networks, they can approximate the computation performed by non-Daleian networks to a very high degree of accuracy. Moreover, we find that Daleian networks are more functionally robust to synaptic noise. We then show that unlike non-Daleian networks, Daleian ones can learn efficiently by tuning of single neuron features, nearly as well as learning by tuning individual synaptic weights. Importantly, this suggests a simpler and more biologically plausible learning mechanisms. We therefore suggest that in addition to architectural simplicity, Dale's principle confers computational and learning benefits for biological networks, and offer new directions for constructing and training biologically-inspired artificial neural networks.

paragraphs: Dale's principle divides biological neurons into excitatory and inhibitory types. This restricts the possible architectures of a network, raising a question about what those restrictions mean for computation and learning. The paper investigates that question using recurrent spiking networks and rate-based network models.

The authors find that Daleian networks can closely approximate computations performed by networks without this restriction, despite having an exponentially smaller set of possible architectures. They also find greater functional robustness to noise in synaptic connections. Together, these results suggest that the structural constraint can coexist with strong computational capability and may confer a robustness benefit in the models studied.

The learning results concern what needs to be adjusted. Daleian networks can learn efficiently by tuning features of individual neurons, nearly matching learning that adjusts individual synaptic weights. The authors report that this does not hold similarly for non-Daleian networks. They interpret the finding as support for simpler, more biologically plausible learning mechanisms and as a direction for designing artificial networks.
summary.tldr: The studied Daleian networks closely reproduce unrestricted computations, show greater resistance to synaptic noise, and learn effectively through neuron-level adjustments.

title: The computational and learning benefits of Daleian neural networks

abstract: Traditionally convolutional neural network architectures have been designed by stacking layers on top of each other to form deeper hierarchical networks. The cortex in the brain however does not just stack layers as done in standard convolution neural networks, instead different regions are organized next to each other in a large single sheet of neurons. Biological neurons self organize to form topographic maps, where neurons encoding similar stimuli group together to form logical clusters. Here we propose new self-organization principles that allow for the formation of hierarchical cortical regions (i.e. layers) in a completely unsupervised manner without requiring any predefined architecture. Synaptic connections are dynamically grown and pruned, which allows us to actively constrain the number of incoming and outgoing connections. This way we can minimize the wiring cost by taking into account both the synaptic strength and the connection length. The proposed method uses purely local learning rules in the form of spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) with lateral excitation and inhibition. We show experimentally that these self-organization rules are sufficient for topographic maps and hierarchical layers to emerge. Our proposed Self-Organizing Neural Sheet (SONS) model can thus form traditional neural network layers in a completely unsupervised manner from just a single large pool of unstructured spiking neurons.

paragraphs: Conventional convolutional networks obtain their hierarchy from layers arranged by a designer. This paper investigates whether a hierarchy can instead emerge from a single unstructured population of spiking neurons. The inspiration is cortical organization, where neighboring regions form maps and neurons responding to similar stimuli cluster together.

The Self-Organizing Neural Sheet model uses local learning rules based on spike timing, together with lateral excitation and inhibition. Connections can grow and disappear dynamically, allowing the model to constrain incoming and outgoing connectivity. Both connection strength and connection length enter the wiring-cost considerations, linking the learned organization to the cost of maintaining connections.

Experiments show that these rules are sufficient for both topographic maps and hierarchical layers to emerge without a predefined architecture or supervision. This is a demonstration of one workable route to such organization, rather than a claim that these rules are uniquely required. The contribution is an architecture-forming learning process: a common pool of neurons can develop structured regions resembling traditional network layers.
summary.tldr: Local learning and dynamic connectivity let hierarchical layers and topographic maps emerge experimentally from an unstructured sheet of spiking neurons.

title: Emergence of Hierarchical Layers in a Single Sheet of Self-Organizing Spiking Neurons

abstract: Meta-learning approaches enable machine learning systems to adapt to new tasks given few examples by leveraging knowledge from related tasks. However, a large number of meta-training tasks are still required for generalization to unseen tasks during meta-testing, which introduces a critical bottleneck for real-world problems that come with only few tasks, due to various reasons including the difficulty and cost of constructing tasks. Recently, several task augmentation methods have been proposed to tackle this issue using domain-specific knowledge to design augmentation techniques to densify the meta-training task distribution. However, such reliance on domain-specific knowledge renders these methods inapplicable to other domains. While Manifold Mixup based task augmentation methods are domain-agnostic, we empirically find them ineffective on non-image domains. To tackle these limitations, we propose a novel domain-agnostic task augmentation method, Meta-Interpolation, which utilizes expressive neural set functions to densify the meta-training task distribution using bilevel optimization. We empirically validate the efficacy of Meta-Interpolation on eight datasets spanning across various domains such as image classification, molecule property prediction, text classification and speech recognition. Experimentally, we show that Meta-Interpolation consistently outperforms all the relevant baselines. Theoretically, we prove that task interpolation with the set function regularizes the meta-learner to improve generalization. We provide our source code in the supplementary material.

paragraphs: Meta-learning aims to adapt to new tasks from few examples, but training the meta-learner can itself require many tasks. This becomes a bottleneck when tasks are expensive or difficult to construct. The paper addresses that shortage by augmenting the distribution of available training tasks.

Existing augmentation methods can depend on domain-specific knowledge, making them difficult to transfer. The authors also find empirically that domain-agnostic Manifold Mixup approaches are ineffective in non-image domains. Their alternative, Meta-Interpolation, uses expressive neural set functions and bilevel optimization to construct interpolated tasks and make the training-task distribution denser.

Experiments cover eight datasets across image classification, molecular property prediction, text classification, and speech recognition. Meta-Interpolation consistently outperforms the relevant baselines in those evaluations. A theoretical result also shows that set-function task interpolation regularizes the meta-learner to improve generalization. The contribution combines a method designed to work across domains with empirical breadth and a theoretical explanation for why interpolating tasks can help when relatively few original tasks are available.
summary.tldr: Meta-Interpolation learns domain-agnostic task augmentations that improve few-task meta-learning across the evaluated domains.

title: Set-based Meta-Interpolation for Few-Task Meta-Learning

abstract: Recently, model-based agents have achieved better performance than model-free ones using the same computational budget and training time in single-agent environments. However, due to the complexity of multi-agent systems, it is tough to learn the model of the environment. The significant compounding error may hinder the learning process when model-based methods are applied to multi-agent tasks. This paper proposes an implicit model-based multi-agent reinforcement learning method based on value decomposition methods. Under this method, agents can interact with the learned virtual environment and evaluate the current state value according to imagined future states in the latent space, making agents have the foresight. Our approach can be applied to any multi-agent value decomposition method. The experimental results show that our method improves the sample efficiency in different partially observable Markov decision process domains.
