paragraphs: A learned environment model can help reinforcement learning agents reason about future outcomes before gathering more real experience. Extending this idea to cooperating agents is difficult because multi-agent environments are complex. Errors in a learned model can accumulate across imagined steps and interfere with learning, making straightforward model-based approaches challenging.

The paper proposes an implicit model-based method built around multi-agent value decomposition. Agents interact with a learned virtual environment and imagine future states in a latent representation. They then use those imagined states to evaluate the current state. This gives future-oriented information a direct role in assessing what the agents should do now.

The authors state that the approach can be applied to any multi-agent value-decomposition method. Experiments in different partially observable decision-process domains show improved sample efficiency, meaning learning makes better use of collected experience. The stated evidence supports latent imagination as a useful addition to cooperative learning in those settings, while the motivation emphasizes the difficulty of learning reliable environment models when several agents interact.
summary.tldr: The method adds latent-space imagination to multi-agent value decomposition and improves sample efficiency in tested partially observable domains.

title: Mingling Foresight with Imagination: Model-Based Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent developments in monocular multi-object tracking have been very successful in tracking visible objects and bridging short occlusion gaps, mainly relying on data-driven appearance models. While significant advancements have been made in short-term tracking performance, bridging longer occlusion gaps remains elusive: state-of-the-art object trackers only bridge less than 10% of occlusions longer than three seconds. We suggest that the missing key is reasoning about future trajectories over a longer time horizon. Intuitively, the longer the occlusion gap, the larger the search space for possible associations. In this paper, we show that even a small yet diverse set of trajectory predictions for moving agents will significantly reduce this search space and thus improve long-term tracking robustness. Our experiments suggest that the crucial components of our approach are reasoning in a bird's-eye view space and generating a small yet diverse set of forecasts while accounting for their localization uncertainty. This way, we can advance state-of-the-art trackers on the MOTChallenge dataset and significantly improve their long-term tracking performance. This paper's source code and experimental data are available at https://github.com/dendorferpatrick/QuoVadis.

paragraphs: Tracking objects in a single-camera video becomes difficult when they disappear behind obstacles for an extended period. Appearance-based trackers handle visible objects and short interruptions well, but the paper reports that state-of-the-art trackers bridge fewer than 10% of occlusions lasting over three seconds. Longer gaps create more possible ways to associate reappearing objects with earlier tracks.

Quo Vadis addresses this ambiguity by forecasting future movement. The authors show that even a small, diverse collection of predicted trajectories can substantially narrow the search for plausible associations. Instead of relying only on how an object looked before disappearing, tracking also uses predictions of where it could move.

Experiments suggest that three ingredients are crucial: reasoning from a bird's-eye perspective, maintaining a small but diverse set of forecasts, and accounting for uncertainty in localization. Applying this approach to state-of-the-art trackers improves their long-term tracking performance on MOTChallenge. The findings support trajectory forecasting as a useful component for reconnecting tracks across extended occlusions.
summary.tldr: A small, diverse set of trajectory forecasts improves long-term tracking by narrowing associations across extended occlusions.

title: Quo Vadis: Is Trajectory Forecasting the Key Towards Long-Term Multi-Object Tracking?

abstract: Pretraining on noisy, internet-scale datasets has been heavily studied as a technique for training models with broad, general capabilities for text, images, and other modalities. However, for many sequential decision domains such as robotics, video games, and computer use, publicly available data does not contain the labels required to train behavioral priors in the same way. We extend the internet-scale pretraining paradigm to sequential decision domains through semi-supervised imitation learning wherein agents learn to act by watching online unlabeled videos. Specifically, we show that with a small amount of labeled data we can train an inverse dynamics model accurate enough to label a huge unlabeled source of online data -- here, online videos of people playing Minecraft -- from which we can then train a general behavioral prior. Despite using the native human interface (mouse and keyboard at 20Hz), we show that this behavioral prior has nontrivial zero-shot capabilities and that it can be fine-tuned, with both imitation learning and reinforcement learning, to hard-exploration tasks that are impossible to learn from scratch via reinforcement learning. For many tasks our models exhibit human-level performance, and we are the first to report computer agents that can craft diamond tools, which can take proficient humans upwards of 20 minutes (24,000 environment actions) of gameplay to accomplish.

paragraphs: Online videos contain many demonstrations of sequential behavior but usually lack the action labels needed for imitation learning. Video PreTraining addresses this gap with a semi-supervised pipeline. A small labeled dataset trains an inverse dynamics model, which then supplies action labels for a much larger collection of online Minecraft videos.

The automatically labeled videos train a general behavioral prior using the native mouse-and-keyboard interface at 20 Hz. The resulting agent exhibits meaningful capabilities without task-specific fine-tuning. It can also be adapted through imitation learning or reinforcement learning to difficult exploration tasks that the authors report cannot be learned from scratch through reinforcement learning in their setting.

The models achieve human-level performance on many tasks, and the authors report the first computer agents able to craft diamond tools. They contextualize this achievement as a task that can require proficient humans more than 20 minutes, or 24,000 environment actions. The contribution demonstrates how limited action-labeled data can unlock much larger video collections for learning behavior and provide a useful starting point for demanding sequential tasks.
summary.tldr: VPT uses a small action-labeled dataset to label online Minecraft videos and train agents with useful transferable behavior.

title: Video PreTraining (VPT): Learning to Act by Watching Unlabeled Online Videos

abstract: Cascading bandits is a natural and popular model that frames the task of learning to rank from Bernoulli click feedback in a bandit setting. For the case of unstructured rewards, we prove matching upper and lower bounds for the problem-independent (i.e., gap-free) regret, both of which strictly improve the best known. A key observation is that the hard instances of this problem are those with small mean rewards, i.e., the small click-through rates that are most relevant in practice. Based on this, and the fact that small mean implies small variance for Bernoullis, our key technical result shows that variance-aware confidence sets derived from the Bernstein and Chernoff bounds lead to optimal algorithms (up to log terms), whereas Hoeffding-based algorithms suffer order-wise suboptimal regret. This sharply contrasts with the standard (non-cascading) bandit setting, where the variance-aware algorithms only improve constants. In light of this and as an additional contribution, we propose a variance-aware algorithm for the structured case of linear rewards and show its regret strictly improves the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Cascading bandits model learning to rank from binary click feedback. The paper studies regret, which measures the cost of learning instead of already knowing the best ranking choices. For unstructured rewards, it establishes matching problem-independent upper and lower bounds, improving the best previously known bounds without relying on reward-gap parameters.

The key observation is that difficult instances have small click probabilities. For Bernoulli outcomes, a small mean also implies small variance. Confidence sets based on Bernstein and Chernoff bounds exploit that relationship and yield optimal algorithms up to logarithmic terms. Hoeffding-based algorithms instead have regret that is worse in its order of growth.

This difference is stronger than in standard non-cascading bandits, where accounting for variance improves only constants. The authors also introduce a variance-aware algorithm for structured linear rewards and prove a strict improvement over the prior regret bound. The results identify variance sensitivity as a central ingredient in optimal cascading-bandit learning, especially in the low-click regime highlighted by the analysis.
summary.tldr: Variance-aware confidence bounds yield optimal cascading-bandit regret up to logarithmic terms, with further improvements for linear rewards.

title: Minimax Regret for Cascading Bandits

abstract: Understanding decision-making is a core goal in both neuroscience and psychology, and computational models have often been helpful in the pursuit of this goal. While many models have been developed for characterizing behavior in binary decision-making and bandit tasks, comparatively little work has focused on animal decision-making in more complex tasks, such as navigation through a maze. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) is a promising approach for understanding such behavior, as it aims to infer the unknown reward function of an agent from its observed trajectories through state space. However, IRL has yet to be widely applied in neuroscience. One potential reason for this is that existing IRL frameworks assume that an agent's reward function is fixed over time. To address this shortcoming, we introduce dynamic inverse reinforcement learning (DIRL), a novel IRL framework that allows for time-varying intrinsic rewards. Our method parametrizes the unknown reward function as a time-varying linear combination of spatial reward maps (which we refer to as "goal maps"). We develop an efficient inference method for recovering this dynamic reward function from behavioral data. We demonstrate DIRL in simulated experiments and then apply it to a dataset of mice exploring a labyrinth. Our method returns interpretable reward functions for two separate cohorts of mice, and provides a novel characterization of exploratory behavior. We expect DIRL to have broad applicability in neuroscience, and to facilitate the design of biologically-inspired reward functions for training artificial agents.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning tries to infer what an agent values from the paths it takes through an environment. This can help characterize animal decisions in complex settings such as mazes. However, existing approaches typically assume the underlying reward function stays fixed, which restricts their ability to describe motivations that change over time.

Dynamic inverse reinforcement learning, or DIRL, allows intrinsic rewards to vary. It represents the unknown reward function as a changing linear combination of spatial goal maps. The maps describe spatial reward patterns, while their changing contributions describe how the overall reward changes. The authors develop an efficient inference method to recover this dynamic description from observed behavior.

The paper first demonstrates DIRL in simulations and then applies it to mice exploring a labyrinth. It obtains interpretable reward functions for two separate cohorts and offers a characterization of exploratory behavior. These results illustrate how allowing changing rewards can enrich behavioral analysis. Broader neuroscience applications and biologically inspired rewards for artificial agents are proposed as potential uses of the framework.
summary.tldr: DIRL infers changing reward functions from animal trajectories, yielding interpretable descriptions of mice exploring a labyrinth.

title: Dynamic Inverse Reinforcement Learning for Characterizing Animal Behavior

abstract: Consider the task of learning a hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$ in the presence of an adversary that can replace up to an $\eta$ fraction of the examples in the training set with arbitrary adversarial examples. The adversary aims to fail the learner on a particular target test point $x$ which is \emph{known} to the adversary but not to the learner. In this work we aim to characterize the smallest achievable error $\epsilon=\epsilon(\eta)$ by the learner in the presence of such an adversary in both realizable and agnostic settings. We fully achieve this in the realizable setting, proving that $\epsilon=\Theta(\mathtt{VC}(\mathcal{H})\cdot \eta)$, where $\mathtt{VC}(\mathcal{H})$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{H}$. Remarkably, we show that the upper bound can be attained by a deterministic learner. In the agnostic setting we reveal a more elaborate landscape: we devise a deterministic learner with a multiplicative regret guarantee of $\epsilon \leq C\cdot\mathtt{OPT} + O(\mathtt{VC}(\mathcal{H})\cdot \eta)$, where $C > 1$ is a universal numerical constant. We complement this by showing that for any deterministic learner there is an attack which worsens its error to at least $2\cdot \mathtt{OPT}$. This implies that a multiplicative deterioration in the regret is unavoidable in this case. Finally, the algorithms we develop for achieving the optimal rates are inherently improper. Nevertheless, we show that for a variety of natural concept classes, such as linear classifiers, it is possible to retain the dependence $\epsilon=\Theta_{\mathcal{H}}(\eta)$ by a proper algorithm in the realizable setting. Here $\Theta_{\mathcal{H}}$ conceals a polynomial dependence on $\mathtt{VC}(\mathcal{H})$.

paragraphs: The paper studies an attacker who can replace an eta fraction of training examples to make a learner fail on a particular test point. The attacker knows that target, while the learner does not. The question is how small the learner's error can be despite this targeted poisoning.

In the realizable setting, where the hypothesis class can represent the correct labeling, the optimal error scales as VC dimension times eta, up to constant factors. A deterministic learner can attain the upper bound. In the agnostic setting, the authors obtain error bounded by a constant greater than one times the best achievable class error, plus a poisoning term proportional to VC dimension times eta.

The agnostic analysis also shows that every deterministic learner faces an attack forcing error to at least twice the best class error. Thus, multiplicative deterioration is unavoidable there. The optimal-rate algorithms may output hypotheses outside the original class. For several natural classes, including linear classifiers, proper learners retain linear dependence on eta in the realizable setting, with a polynomial dependence on VC dimension hidden in the constants.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal realizable learning error under targeted poisoning and proves an unavoidable multiplicative penalty for deterministic agnostic learners.

title: On Optimal Learning Under Targeted Data Poisoning

abstract: Neural architecture search tries to shift the manual design of neural network (NN) architectures to algorithmic design. In these cases, the NN architecture itself can be viewed as data and needs to be modeled. A better modeling could help explore novel architectures automatically and open the black box of automated architecture design. To this end, this work proposes a new encoding scheme for neural architectures, the Training-Analogous Graph-based ArchiTecture Encoding Scheme (TA-GATES). TA-GATES encodes an NN architecture in a way that is analogous to its training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the flexibility and discriminative power of TA-GATES lead to better modeling of NN architectures. We expect our methodology of explicitly modeling the NN training process to benefit broader automated deep learning systems. The code is available at https://github.com/walkerning/aw_nas.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search treats network design as an algorithmic task. To reason about candidate networks, the search system needs a representation of the architecture itself. This paper focuses on that representation problem: how to encode a network design so that an automated system can model it and distinguish it from other designs.

TA-GATES is a graph-based encoding scheme that represents an architecture through a process analogous to its training. The central methodological choice is to make the encoding reflect the training process explicitly. This connects the representation of a candidate architecture to the process that will ultimately determine how that candidate learns.

The authors report extensive experiments showing that TA-GATES offers flexibility and discriminative power that improve architecture modeling. Better modeling matters because it supports the broader effort to explore new network designs automatically and understand automated design decisions. The authors also expect explicit modeling of training to help wider automated deep learning systems; that broader benefit is presented as an expectation, beyond the stated experimental finding about architecture representations.
summary.tldr: TA-GATES improves neural architecture modeling with a graph-based encoding designed to mirror the network training process.

title: TA-GATES: An Encoding Scheme for Neural Network Architectures

abstract: We consider the bandit optimization problem with the reward function defined over graph-structured data. This problem has important applications in molecule design and drug discovery, where the reward is naturally invariant to graph permutations. The key challenges in this setting are scaling to large domains, and to graphs with many nodes. We resolve these challenges by embedding the permutation invariance into our model. In particular, we show that graph neural networks (GNNs) can be used to estimate the reward function, assuming it resides in the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space of a permutation-invariant additive kernel. By establishing a novel connection between such kernels and the graph neural tangent kernel (GNTK), we introduce the first GNN confidence bound and use it to design a phased-elimination algorithm with sublinear regret. Our regret bound depends on the GNTK's maximum information gain, which we also provide a bound for. Perhaps surprisingly, even though the reward function depends on all $N$ node features, our guarantees are independent of the number of graph nodes $N$. Empirically, our approach exhibits competitive performance and scales well on graph-structured domains.

paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making when candidate choices are graphs and their rewards are initially unknown. Molecule design motivates the setting: relabeling a graph's nodes should not change its reward. The authors incorporate this permutation invariance into a graph neural network model to address large search domains and graphs with many nodes.

Their theory assumes that the reward belongs to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space of a permutation-invariant additive kernel. They connect this kernel structure to the graph neural tangent kernel, derive a confidence bound for the network's reward estimates, and use that bound in a phased-elimination algorithm. The algorithm has sublinear regret, meaning its accumulated disadvantage grows more slowly than the number of decisions.

The regret guarantee depends on the kernel's maximum information gain, for which the authors also provide a bound. Notably, their guarantees do not depend on the number of nodes, even though reward uses all node features. Empirical results show competitive performance and good scaling, complementing the guarantees under the stated reward-function assumption.
summary.tldr: The paper builds graph neural network bandit algorithms with sublinear regret guarantees that are independent of node count under a stated kernel assumption.

title: Graph Neural Network Bandits

abstract: The ability to extrapolate from short problem instances to longer ones is an important form of out-of-distribution generalization in reasoning tasks, and is crucial when learning from datasets where longer problem instances are rare. These include theorem proving, solving quantitative mathematics problems, and reading/summarizing novels. In this paper, we run careful empirical studies exploring the length generalization capabilities of transformer-based language models. We first establish that naively finetuning transformers on length generalization tasks shows significant generalization deficiencies independent of model scale. We then show that combining pretrained large language models' in-context learning abilities with scratchpad prompting (asking the model to output solution steps before producing an answer) results in a dramatic improvement in length generalization. We run careful failure analyses on each of the learning modalities and identify common sources of mistakes that highlight opportunities in equipping language models with the ability to generalize to longer problems.

paragraphs: Length generalization is the ability to learn from shorter problems and handle longer ones. It matters when long training examples are scarce, as can happen in mathematical reasoning, theorem proving, and work with long texts. This paper empirically investigates how transformer language models perform when the length of a problem extends beyond their learning examples.

The authors first find substantial weaknesses when transformers are naively finetuned for length-generalization tasks. Increasing model scale does not remove these deficiencies in the studied setting. They then combine pretrained models’ ability to learn from examples in context with scratchpad prompting, which asks for intermediate solution steps before the final answer.

That combination produces a dramatic improvement in the reported length-generalization results. The paper also analyzes failures across the different learning approaches and identifies recurring sources of mistakes. These findings make the learning setup and prompting procedure central to the discussion: the study reports meaningful improvement through their combination, while its failure analysis shows that generalizing to longer problems still presents unresolved challenges.
summary.tldr: Combining in-context learning with scratchpad prompting substantially improves length generalization where naive transformer finetuning shows persistent weaknesses.

title: Exploring Length Generalization in Large Language Models

abstract: Finding correspondences between images is a fundamental problem in computer vision. In this paper, we show that correspondence emerges in image diffusion models without any explicit supervision. We propose a simple strategy to extract this implicit knowledge out of diffusion networks as image features, namely DIffusion FeaTures (DIFT), and use them to establish correspondences between real images. Without any additional fine-tuning or supervision on the task-specific data or annotations, DIFT is able to outperform both weakly-supervised methods and competitive off-the-shelf features in identifying semantic, geometric, and temporal correspondences. title: Emergent Correspondence from Image Diffusion

abstract: We aim to deepen the theoretical understanding of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) on large graphs, with a focus on their expressive power.Existing analyses relate this notion to the graph isomorphism problem, which is mostly relevant for graphs of small sizes, or studied graph classification or regression tasks, while prediction tasks on \emph{nodes} are far more relevant on large graphs. Recently, several works showed that, on very general random graphs models, GNNs converge to certains functions as the number of nodes grows.In this paper, we provide a more complete and intuitive description of the function space generated by equivariant GNNs for node-tasks, through general notions of convergence that encompass several previous examples. We emphasize the role of input node features, and study the impact of \emph{node Positional Encodings} (PEs), a recent line of work that has been shown to yield state-of-the-art results in practice. Through the study of several examples of PEs on large random graphs, we extend previously known universality results to significantly more general models. Our theoretical results hint at some normalization tricks, which is shown numerically to have a positive impact on GNN generalization on synthetic and real data. Our proofs contain new concentration inequalities of independent interest.

paragraphs: Understanding graph neural networks on large graphs requires studying what they can predict about individual nodes. This paper develops that perspective through random-graph models, examining the functions GNNs approach as graph size grows. Its focus complements expressivity analyses centered on graph isomorphism or whole-graph prediction.

The authors give a more complete description of the function space generated by equivariant GNNs for node-level tasks. Their convergence framework encompasses several earlier results and highlights the importance of input node features. They particularly examine positional encodings, which add information about a node's position in the graph, and study how those inputs affect what the network can compute.

By analyzing several positional encodings, the paper extends previously known universality results to substantially more general random-graph models. The theory also suggests normalization choices that improve generalization numerically on synthetic and real data. New concentration inequalities support the proofs. Together, these contributions connect large-graph expressivity with input representation choices and offer theoretically motivated adjustments whose benefits are demonstrated in experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes large-random-graph GNN expressivity and shows how positional encodings expand theoretical capabilities and motivate useful normalization choices.

title: What functions can Graph Neural Networks compute on random graphs? The role of Positional Encoding

abstract: Consider the setting of constrained optimization, with some parameters unknown at solving time and requiring prediction from relevant features. Predict+Optimize is a recent framework for end-to-end training supervised learning models for such predictions, incorporating information about the optimization problem in the training process in order to yield better predictions in terms of the quality of the predicted solution under the true parameters. Almost all prior works have focused on the special case where the unknowns appear only in the optimization objective and not the constraints. Hu et al. proposed the first adaptation of Predict+Optimize to handle unknowns appearing in constraints, but the framework has somewhat ad-hoc elements, and they provided a training algorithm only for covering and packing linear programs. In this work, we give a new simpler and more powerful framework called Two-Stage Predict+Optimize, which we believe should be the canonical framework for the Predict+Optimize setting. We also give a training algorithm usable for all mixed integer linear programs, vastly generalizing the applicability of the framework. Experimental results demonstrate the superior prediction performance of our training framework over all classical and state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Predict+Optimize trains a prediction model with the downstream optimization problem in mind. The goal is for predicted parameters to produce good decisions when judged using the true parameters. This paper addresses the case where unknown quantities appear in constraints, extending beyond the more commonly studied setting where uncertainty affects only the objective.

Earlier work had adapted the framework to uncertain constraints, but its training algorithm covered only covering and packing linear programs. The authors introduce Two-Stage Predict+Optimize as a simpler, more powerful framework and provide a training algorithm usable for all mixed integer linear programs. This substantially broadens the class of constrained decision problems that the approach can address.

Experimental results report superior prediction performance over the classical and state-of-the-art methods included in the evaluation. The paper’s central contribution is the expanded framework and algorithmic applicability: learning can account for downstream optimization even when predicted quantities enter constraints in mixed integer problems. The authors also propose their framework as a canonical formulation, which is a recommendation about how to organize this setting.
summary.tldr: Two-Stage Predict+Optimize extends decision-aware prediction to unknown constraint parameters with a training algorithm applicable to all mixed integer linear programs.

title: Two-Stage Predict+Optimize for MILPs with Unknown Parameters in Constraints

abstract: Collaborative learning techniques have significantly advanced in recent years, enabling private model training across multiple organizations. Despite this opportunity, firms face a dilemma when considering data sharing with competitors—while collaboration can improve a company’s machine learning model, it may also benefit competitors and hence reduce profits. In this work, we introduce a general framework for analyzing this data-sharing trade-off. The framework consists of three components, representing the firms’ production decisions, the effect of additional data on model quality, and the data-sharing negotiation process, respectively. We then study an instantiation of the framework, based on a conventional market model from economic theory, to identify key factors that affect collaboration incentives. Our findings indicate a profound impact of market conditions on the data-sharing incentives. In particular, we find that reduced competition, in terms of the similarities between the firms’ products, and harder learning tasks foster collaboration.

paragraphs: Collaborative learning can improve a firm’s model while allowing training across organizations privately. Yet a firm may still hesitate to collaborate with competitors: the same exchange can strengthen rival models and reduce its own profits. This paper studies that economic trade-off, treating technical learning gains as one part of the incentive to share.

The authors introduce a framework with three components: firms’ production decisions, the effect of extra data on model quality, and the process through which firms negotiate data sharing. They then analyze an instance based on a conventional economic market model. This connects improvements in prediction quality to competitive outcomes and negotiated collaboration.

The analysis finds that market conditions have a substantial effect on sharing incentives. In the studied setting, reduced competition associated with less similar products and harder learning tasks encourage collaboration. These findings show why better models alone do not determine whether firms will cooperate. The economic value of learning depends on how much competitors also gain and how their products compete.
summary.tldr: An economic framework shows how product competition and learning difficulty shape competing firms’ incentives to share data.

title: Strategic Data Sharing between Competitors

abstract: Despite a growing interest in diffusion-based language models, existing work has not shown that these models can attain nontrivial likelihoods on standard language modeling benchmarks. In this work, we take the first steps towards closing the likelihood gap between autoregressive and diffusion-based language models, with the goal of building and releasing a diffusion model which outperforms a small but widely-known autoregressive model. We pursue this goal through algorithmic improvements, scaling laws, and increased compute. On the algorithmic front, we introduce several methodological improvements for the maximum-likelihood training of diffusion language models. We then study scaling laws for our diffusion models and find compute-optimal training regimes which differ substantially from autoregressive models. Using our methods and scaling analysis, we train and release Plaid 1B, a large diffusion language model which outperforms GPT-2 124M in likelihood on benchmark datasets and generates fluent samples in unconditional and zero-shot control settings.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether diffusion language models can become competitive on likelihood, a measure of how well a model assigns probability to benchmark text. The authors frame their work as an initial step toward closing the gap with autoregressive language models. Their concrete target is to outperform a small, widely recognized autoregressive model.

The approach combines improvements to maximum-likelihood training, scaling analysis, and increased computation. The scaling study identifies compute-optimal training regimes that differ substantially from those of autoregressive models. The reported achievement concerns this specific comparison, rather than a general superiority claim over autoregressive language models.
summary.tldr: Improved training and diffusion-specific scaling analysis enable Plaid 1B to exceed GPT-2 124M on benchmark likelihood.

title: Likelihood-Based Diffusion Language Models

abstract: We present new upper and lower bounds on the number of learner mistakes in the `transductive' online learning setting of Ben-David, Kushilevitz and Mansour (1997). This setting is similar to standard online learning, except that the adversary fixes a sequence of instances $x_1,\dots,x_n$ to be labeled at the start of the game, and this sequence is known to the learner. Qualitatively, we prove a \emph{trichotomy}, stating that the minimal number of mistakes made by the learner as $n$ grows can take only one of precisely three possible values: $n$, $\Theta\left(\log (n)\right)$, or $\Theta(1)$. Furthermore, this behavior is determined by a combination of the VC dimension and the Littlestone dimension. Quantitatively, we show a variety of bounds relating the number of mistakes to well-known combinatorial dimensions. In particular, we improve the known lower bound on the constant in the $\Theta(1)$ case from $\Omega\left(\sqrt{\log(d)}\right)$ to $\Omega(\log(d))$ where $d$ is the Littlestone dimension. Finally, we extend our results to cover multiclass classification and the agnostic setting.

paragraphs: In transductive online learning, a learner knows the full sequence of inputs before making predictions, but must still predict their labels through an online interaction. The adversary fixes those inputs at the start. This paper asks how many mistakes a learner must make in this setting and how that number changes as the sequence becomes longer.

The main result establishes exactly three possible growth patterns for the optimal mistake count: n, logarithmic in n, or bounded by a constant as n grows. Which pattern occurs depends on a combination of VC dimension and Littlestone dimension. These mathematical measures therefore help determine whether advance knowledge of the inputs permits a bounded, slowly growing, or fully linear mistake count.

The paper also provides quantitative upper and lower bounds using combinatorial dimensions. In the constant-growth case, it strengthens a known lower bound from the square root of log d to log d, where d is the Littlestone dimension. Here, constant means independent of sequence length, not independent of the learning problem. Extensions cover multiclass classification and the agnostic setting.
summary.tldr: Optimal mistake counts in transductive online learning fall into exactly three growth regimes determined by combinatorial dimensions.

title: A Trichotomy for Transductive Online Learning

abstract: Learning rule-based systems plays a pivotal role in knowledge graph completion (KGC). Existing rule-based systems restrict the input of the system to structural knowledge only, which may omit some useful knowledge for reasoning, e.g., textual knowledge. In this paper, we propose a two-stage framework that imposes both structural and textual knowledge to learn rule-based systems. In the first stage, we compute a set of triples with confidence scores (called \emph{soft triples}) from a text corpus by distant supervision, where a textual entailment model with multi-instance learning is exploited to estimate whether a given triple is entailed by a set of sentences. In the second stage, these soft triples are used to learn a rule-based model for KGC. To mitigate the negative impact of noise from soft triples, we propose a new formalism for rules to be learnt, named \emph{text enhanced rules} or \emph{TE-rules} for short. To effectively learn TE-rules, we propose a neural model that simulates the inference of TE-rules. We theoretically show that any set of TE-rules can always be interpreted by a certain parameter assignment of the neural model. We introduce three new datasets to evaluate the effectiveness of our method. Experimental results demonstrate that the introduction of soft triples and TE-rules results in significant performance improvements in inductive link prediction.

paragraphs: Rule-based knowledge graph completion uses existing relationships to infer missing ones. Restricting this reasoning to graph structure can leave useful textual evidence unused. This paper introduces a two-stage framework that brings information from a text corpus into the process of learning rules for graph completion.

First, the method extracts candidate triples with confidence scores, called soft triples. A textual entailment model uses multiple sentences to estimate whether they support a proposed relationship, with distant supervision supplying the learning signal. Second, the system uses these soft triples to train a rule-based model. Because text-derived candidates can be noisy, the authors introduce text-enhanced rules designed to reduce their negative effects.

A neural model simulates inference with these rules. The authors prove that any set of text-enhanced rules can be represented by some parameter assignment of that model, establishing a representational guarantee. They also introduce three evaluation datasets and report significant improvements in inductive link prediction from combining soft triples with the proposed rules.
summary.tldr: A two-stage framework converts textual evidence into confidence-weighted triples and learns text-enhanced rules for inductive knowledge graph completion.

title: Learning from Both Structural and Textual Knowledge for Inductive Knowledge Graph Completion

abstract: We propose a causal interpretation of self-attention in the Transformer neural network architecture. We interpret self-attention as a mechanism that estimates a structural equation model for a given input sequence of symbols (tokens). The structural equation model can be interpreted, in turn, as a causal structure over the input symbols under the specific context of the input sequence. Importantly, this interpretation remains valid in the presence of latent confounders. Following this interpretation, we estimate conditional independence relations between input symbols by calculating partial correlations between their corresponding representations in the deepest attention layer. This enables learning the causal structure over an input sequence using existing constraint-based algorithms. In this sense, existing pre-trained Transformers can be utilized for zero-shot causal-discovery. We demonstrate this method by providing causal explanations for the outcomes of Transformers in two tasks: sentiment classification (NLP) and recommendation.

paragraphs: This paper proposes interpreting self-attention as estimating a structural equation model for the tokens in an input sequence. Such a model describes relationships among variables and can be interpreted as a causal structure. Here, that structure concerns the input symbols within the particular context supplied by their sequence.

The authors turn this interpretation into a procedure for extracting relationships. They calculate partial correlations between token representations in the deepest attention layer to estimate conditional independence: whether two symbols remain related after accounting for others. Existing algorithms that infer causal structure from independence constraints then use these estimates to construct a structure over the sequence.

The proposed interpretation accommodates latent confounders, meaning influences that are not directly represented as observed variables. Within this framework, an existing pretrained Transformer can support causal discovery without additional task-specific training. Demonstrations provide causal explanations for sentiment-classification and recommendation outcomes. The contribution is both an interpretation of attention and a way to use learned representations to produce context-specific explanations.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets self-attention through structural equations and uses pretrained representations for context-specific causal discovery.

title: Causal Interpretation of Self-Attention in Pre-Trained Transformers

abstract: There is currently a significant gap between the performance of fine-tuned models and prompting approaches using Large Language Models (LLMs) on the challenging task of text-to-SQL, as evaluated on datasets such as Spider. To improve the performance of LLMs in the reasoning process, we study how decomposing the task into smaller sub-tasks can be effective. In particular, we show that breaking down the generation problem into sub-problems and feeding the solutions of those sub-problems into LLMs can be an effective approach for significantly improving their performance. Our experiments with three LLMs show that this approach consistently improves their simple few-shot performance by roughly 10%, pushing the accuracy of LLMs towards SOTA or surpassing it. On the holdout test set of Spider, the SOTA, in terms of execution accuracy, was 79.9 and the new SOTA at the time of this writing using our approach is 85.3. Our approach with in-context learning beats many heavily fine-tuned models by at least 5%. Additionally, when evaluated on the BIRD benchmark, our approach achieved an execution accuracy of 55.9%, setting a new SOTA on its holdout test set.

paragraphs: Text-to-SQL requires translating a natural-language request into a database query. The paper starts from a performance gap between prompting large language models and models trained specifically for this task. It investigates whether organizing the reasoning process more carefully can improve results obtained through in-context learning.

The central approach breaks query generation into smaller subproblems and feeds their solutions back into the language model. This gives later generation stages intermediate results to work from. Across experiments with three language models, the authors report improvements of roughly 10% over simple few-shot prompting, with performance approaching or exceeding the leading results in their comparisons.

On Spider’s held-out test set, execution accuracy reaches 85.3, compared with the previous leading result of 79.9 cited by the authors. The approach also beats many heavily fine-tuned models by at least 5% and reaches 55.9% execution accuracy on BIRD’s held-out test set. Both benchmark records are claims made at the time of the paper. The findings show that decomposition can make prompting substantially more competitive for database query generation.
summary.tldr: DIN-SQL improves prompted text-to-SQL generation by solving smaller subproblems and supplying their results to the language model.

title: DIN-SQL: Decomposed In-Context Learning of Text-to-SQL with Self-Correction

abstract: Despite the growing use of transformer models in computer vision, a mechanistic understanding of these networks is still needed. This work introduces a method to reverse-engineer Vision Transformers trained to solve image classification tasks. Inspired by previous research in NLP, we demonstrate how the inner representations at any level of the hierarchy can be projected onto the learned class embedding space to uncover how these networks build categorical representations for their predictions. We use our framework to show how image tokens develop class-specific representations that depend on attention mechanisms and contextual information, and give insights on how self-attention and MLP layers differentially contribute to this categorical composition. We additionally demonstrate that this method (1) can be used to determine the parts of an image that would be important for detecting the class of interest, and (2) exhibits significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. Taken together, our results position our proposed framework as a powerful tool for mechanistic interpretability and explainability research.

paragraphs: A Vision Transformer produces an image classification through a sequence of internal representations, but the final label reveals little about how those representations develop. This paper introduces a method for examining that process in the model's learned class embedding space, where internal information can be interpreted in terms of the categories the network predicts.

The method projects representations from any level of the network into that space. This allows the authors to trace how image tokens acquire class-specific information and how that development depends on attention and surrounding context. The analysis also distinguishes the contributions of self-attention layers and multilayer perceptron layers to the construction of categorical representations.

The authors demonstrate that the framework can identify image regions important for detecting a chosen class. They also report significant advantages over traditional linear probing approaches. These findings support its usefulness for studying the mechanisms behind classification: it connects intermediate computations to class-related information and helps explain how different parts of the network contribute to predictions.
summary.tldr: Projecting internal Vision Transformer representations into class embedding space reveals how image tokens and network layers build classification information.

title: Analyzing Vision Transformers for Image Classification in Class Embedding Space

abstract: Social conflict is a survival mechanism yielding both normal and pathological behaviors. To understand its underlying principles, we collected behavioral and whole-brain neural data from mice advancing through stages of social conflict. We modeled the animals’ interactions as a normal-form game using Bayesian inference to account for the partial observability of animals’ strengths. We find that our behavioral and neural data are consistent with the first-level Theory of Mind (1-ToM) model where mice form “primary” beliefs about the strengths of all mice involved and “secondary” beliefs that estimate the beliefs of their opponents. Our model identifies the brain regions that carry the information about these beliefs and offers a framework for studies of social behaviors in partially observable settings.

We find that our behavioral and neural data are consistent with the first-level Theory of Mind (1-ToM) model where mice form “primary” beliefs about the strengths of all mice involved and “secondary” beliefs that estimate the beliefs of their opponents. paragraphs: Social conflict involves decisions made with incomplete knowledge of an opponent. This paper studies that uncertainty by collecting behavioral observations and whole-brain neural data from mice as their social conflicts progress. The researchers connect these measurements to a mathematical account of how animals might assess one another and choose their actions.

The account represents interactions as a normal-form game and uses Bayesian inference to handle strengths that cannot be observed directly. Its central distinction is between two kinds of belief: an animal’s estimates of the participants’ strengths, and its estimates of what its opponent believes about those strengths. The latter introduces a first level of reasoning about another animal’s perspective.

The behavioral and neural observations are consistent with this first-level Theory of Mind model. The model also identifies brain regions carrying information about the proposed beliefs. These findings support a framework for studying social behavior under partial observability; consistency with the model does not establish that mice necessarily perform its exact computations.
summary.tldr: Behavioral and brain measurements in mice are consistent with a model of social conflict that includes beliefs about opponents’ beliefs.

title: A normative theory of social conflict

abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in machine learning applications.Normalization techniques, such as Layer Normalization (LayerNorm, LN) and Root Mean Square Normalization (RMSNorm), play a critical role in accelerating and stabilizing the training of Transformers.While LayerNorm recenters and rescales input vectors, RMSNorm only rescales the vectors by their RMS value.Despite being more computationally efficient, RMSNorm may compromise the representation ability of Transformers.There is currently no consensus regarding the preferred normalization technique, as some models employ LayerNorm while others utilize RMSNorm, especially in recent large language models.It is challenging to convert Transformers with one normalization to the other type.While there is an ongoing disagreement between the two normalization types,we propose a solution to unify two mainstream Transformer architectures, Pre-LN and Pre-RMSNorm Transformers.By removing the inherent redundant mean information in the main branch of Pre-LN Transformers, we can reduce LayerNorm to RMSNorm, achieving higher efficiency.We further propose the Compressed RMSNorm (CRMSNorm) and Pre-CRMSNorm Transformer based on a lossless compression of the zero-mean vectors.We formally establish the equivalence of Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm Transformer variants in both training and inference.It implies that Pre-LN Transformers can be substituted with Pre-(C)RMSNorm counterparts at almost no cost, offering the same arithmetic functionality along with free efficiency improvement.Experiments demonstrate that we can reduce the training and inference time of Pre-LN Transformers by 1% - 10%.

paragraphs: Layer normalization recenters and rescales a vector, whereas RMS normalization only rescales it. Although RMS normalization costs less computation, changing normalization schemes can raise questions about a Transformer’s representational ability. This paper examines how particular Pre-LN and Pre-RMSNorm architectures can be made equivalent while reducing the work required for normalization.

The key observation concerns redundant mean information in the main branch of a Pre-LN Transformer. Removing that redundancy allows layer normalization to reduce to RMS normalization. The authors then introduce compressed RMS normalization, or CRMSNorm, using a lossless compression of zero-mean vectors to obtain an additional equivalent architecture.

The paper formally establishes equivalence among its Pre-LN, Pre-RMSNorm, and Pre-CRMSNorm variants during both training and inference. This supports substituting the corresponding architectures while retaining the same arithmetic functionality. Experiments report training and inference time reductions of 1–10%. The significance is that the efficiency improvement follows from removing redundant computation while preserving the established functionality of these variants.
summary.tldr: Removing redundant mean information yields equivalent Transformer normalization variants with reported training and inference savings of 1–10%.

title: Pre-RMSNorm and Pre-CRMSNorm Transformers: Equivalent and Efficient Pre-LN Transformers

abstract: Dosing models often use differential equations to model biological dynamics. Neural differential equations in particular can learn to predict the derivative of a process, which permits predictions at irregular points of time. However, this temporal flexibility often comes with a high sensitivity to noise, whereas medical problems often present high noise and limited data. Moreover, medical dosing models must generalize reliably over individual patients and changing treatment policies. To address these challenges, we introduce the Neural Eigen Stochastic Differential Equation algorithm (NESDE). NESDE provides individualized modeling (using a hypernetwork over patient-level parameters); generalization to new treatment policies (using decoupled control); tunable expressiveness according to the noise level (using piecewise linearity); and fast, continuous, closed-form prediction (using spectral representation). We demonstrate the robustness of NESDE in both synthetic and real medical problems, and use the learned dynamics to publish simulated medical gym environments.

paragraphs: Dosing models need to describe how biological processes evolve over time, often from noisy and limited observations. Neural differential equations can predict at irregular times by learning rates of change, but this flexibility can come with sensitivity to noise. The paper introduces NESDE to address that challenge while accounting for differences between patients and treatment policies.

NESDE combines several design choices with distinct roles. A hypernetwork uses patient-level parameters to individualize the dynamics. Decoupled control supports generalization when treatment policies change. Piecewise linearity lets the model's expressiveness be adjusted to the noise level, while a spectral representation enables fast, continuous predictions in closed form.

Together, these components aim to make flexible temporal modeling more suitable for the data conditions found in medical problems. The authors demonstrate robustness on synthetic and real medical problems and release simulated medical gym environments built from learned dynamics. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling algorithm and reusable simulation environments, with evidence focused on robust prediction of individualized dynamics.
summary.tldr: NESDE combines individualized dynamics, decoupled treatment control, and closed-form prediction to model noisy medical time series robustly.

title: Individualized Dosing Dynamics via Neural Eigen Decomposition

abstract: We study recovering fluid density and velocity from sparse multiview videos. Existing neural dynamic reconstruction methods predominantly rely on optical flows; therefore, they cannot accurately estimate the density and uncover the underlying velocity due to the inherent visual ambiguities of fluid velocity, as fluids are often shapeless and lack stable visual features. The challenge is further pronounced by the turbulent nature of fluid flows, which calls for properly designed fluid velocity representations. To address these challenges, we propose hybrid neural fluid fields (HyFluid), a neural approach to jointly infer fluid density and velocity fields. Specifically, to deal with visual ambiguities of fluid velocity, we introduce a set of physics-based losses that enforce inferring a physically plausible velocity field, which is divergence-free and drives the transport of density. To deal with the turbulent nature of fluid velocity, we design a hybrid neural velocity representation that includes a base neural velocity field that captures most irrotational energy and a vortex particle-based velocity that models residual turbulent velocity. We show that our method enables recovering vortical flow details. Our approach opens up possibilities for various learning and reconstruction applications centered around 3D incompressible flow, including fluid re-simulation and editing, future prediction, and neural dynamic scene composition. Project website: https://kovenyu.com/HyFluid/

paragraphs: HyFluid reconstructs fluid density and velocity from sparse videos taken from multiple viewpoints. Fluids often lack stable shapes or visible features, so apparent image motion can leave the underlying velocity ambiguous. Turbulence adds another difficulty: the representation must capture swirling motion as well as broader flow patterns.

The method jointly learns density and velocity while applying physics-based losses. These encourage a divergence-free velocity field that transports the inferred density, tying the reconstruction to the behavior of incompressible flow. Its hybrid velocity representation combines a base neural field, which captures most irrotational energy, with vortex particles that model the remaining turbulent velocity.

The authors show that this combination can recover vortical flow details. The significance is that visible appearance and physical motion are inferred together using a representation designed for different components of the flow. The paper identifies fluid re-simulation, editing, future prediction, and dynamic scene composition as possible applications of the approach. Those applications are presented as opportunities opened by the reconstruction method.
summary.tldr: HyFluid combines physical constraints, neural fields, and vortex particles to recover fluid density and detailed velocity from sparse multiview videos.

title: Inferring Hybrid Neural Fluid Fields from Videos

abstract: We introduce a suite of new particle-based algorithms for sampling in constrained domains which are entirely learning rate free. Our approach leverages coin betting ideas from convex optimisation, and the viewpoint of constrained sampling as a mirrored optimisation problem on the space of probability measures. Based on this viewpoint, we also introduce a unifying framework for several existing constrained sampling algorithms, including mirrored Langevin dynamics and mirrored Stein variational gradient descent. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithms on a range of numerical examples, including sampling from targets on the simplex, sampling with fairness constraints, and constrained sampling problems in post-selection inference. Our results indicate that our algorithms achieve competitive performance with existing constrained sampling methods, without the need to tune any hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Sampling in a constrained domain means generating samples while respecting restrictions on where those samples can lie. The paper introduces particle-based algorithms for this task that do not require a learning rate. This removes a tuning choice that otherwise affects how a sampling procedure progresses toward its target distribution.

The approach combines coin-betting ideas from convex optimization with a view of constrained sampling as mirrored optimization over probability measures. In that view, optimization operates on distributions while accounting for the domain's constraints. The authors also use this perspective to build a common framework for existing methods, including mirrored Langevin dynamics and mirrored Stein variational gradient descent.

Numerical examples cover targets on the simplex, fairness-constrained sampling, and constrained problems arising in post-selection inference. Across these examples, the results indicate performance competitive with existing constrained samplers without hyperparameter tuning. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and conceptual: it offers sampling methods that reduce tuning effort and a shared formulation that relates several approaches to the same underlying optimization viewpoint.
summary.tldr: Coin-betting-based particle samplers handle constrained domains without learning-rate tuning and show competitive numerical performance.

title: Learning Rate Free Sampling in Constrained Domains

abstract: For a sequence of classification tasks that arrive over time, it is common that tasks are evolving in the sense that consecutive tasks often have a higher similarity. The incremental learning of a growing sequence of tasks holds promise to enable accurate classification even with few samples per task by leveraging information from all the tasks in the sequence (forward and backward learning). However, existing techniques developed for continual learning and concept drift adaptation are either designed for tasks with time-independent similarities or only aim to learn the last task in the sequence. This paper presents incremental minimax risk classifiers (IMRCs) that effectively exploit forward and backward learning and account for evolving tasks. In addition, we analytically characterize the performance improvement provided by forward and backward learning in terms of the tasks’ expected quadratic change and the number of tasks. The experimental evaluation shows that IMRCs can result in a significant performance improvement, especially for reduced sample sizes.

paragraphs: Classification tasks arriving over time often evolve gradually, so neighboring tasks can be more similar than distant ones. This creates an opportunity to share information when each task has few examples. The paper considers learning across the whole sequence, including using earlier tasks to help later ones and later tasks to improve earlier ones.

The authors introduce incremental minimax risk classifiers, or IMRCs, that account for this evolving relationship while supporting both forward and backward learning. This addresses a gap in approaches designed around similarities that do not depend on time, as well as methods focused solely on the most recent task. The objective includes improving classification throughout the growing sequence.

The theoretical analysis characterizes performance gains in terms of the number of tasks and their expected quadratic change, a measure of how tasks evolve. Experiments show that IMRCs can substantially improve performance, particularly when sample sizes are small. Together, these results connect the value of information sharing to the amount of task evolution and show why revisiting earlier tasks can be useful.
summary.tldr: Incremental minimax classifiers exploit both earlier and later evolving tasks, with theoretical performance characterizations and strong small-sample results.

title: Minimax Forward and Backward Learning of Evolving Tasks with Performance Guarantees

abstract: A common explanation for the failure of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is that the model trained with empirical risk minimization (ERM) learns spurious features instead of invariant features. However, several recent studies challenged this explanation and found that deep networks may have already learned sufficiently good features for OOD generalization. Despite the contradictions at first glance, we theoretically show that ERM essentially learns both spurious and invariant features, while ERM tends to learn spurious features faster if the spurious correlation is stronger. Moreover, when fed the ERM learned features to the OOD objectives, the invariant feature learning quality significantly affects the final OOD performance, as OOD objectives rarely learn new features. Therefore, ERM feature learning can be a bottleneck to OOD generalization. To alleviate the reliance, we propose Feature Augmented Training (FeAT), to enforce the model to learn richer features ready for OOD generalization. FeAT iteratively augments the model to learn new features while retaining the already learned features. In each round, the retention and augmentation operations are performed on different subsets of the training data that capture distinct features. Extensive experiments show that FeAT effectively learns richer features thus boosting the performance of various OOD objectives.

paragraphs: One explanation for failure on unfamiliar distributions is that ordinary training learns misleading correlations instead of stable features. Other studies suggest useful features are already present. This paper reconciles those views theoretically: empirical risk minimization learns both kinds, but tends to learn spurious features faster when their correlation is stronger.

The authors also find that the quality of invariant features strongly affects the performance of later out-of-distribution objectives, which rarely learn new features themselves. This makes the earlier feature-learning stage a potential bottleneck. A later objective may have limited ability to compensate if the representation does not already contain sufficiently useful invariant information.

Feature Augmented Training, or FeAT, addresses that bottleneck through repeated rounds of feature retention and augmentation. Different subsets of training data support preserving existing features and learning additional ones. Extensive experiments show richer learned features and improved performance for several out-of-distribution objectives. The findings direct attention to expanding the available representation before expecting a downstream objective to generalize from it.
summary.tldr: FeAT expands learned features while preserving existing ones, improving the representations available to out-of-distribution training objectives.

title: Understanding and Improving Feature Learning for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: Image super-resolution (SR) aims to learn a mapping from low-resolution (LR) to high-resolution (HR) using paired HR-LR training images. Conventional SR methods typically gather the paired training data by synthesizing LR images from HR images using a predetermined degradation model, e.g., Bicubic down-sampling. However, the realistic degradation type of test images may mismatch with the training-time degradation type due to the dynamic changes of the real-world scenarios, resulting in inferior-quality SR images. To address this, existing methods attempt to estimate the degradation model and train an image-specific model, which, however, is quite time-consuming and impracticable to handle rapidly changing domain shifts. Moreover, these methods largely concentrate on the estimation of one degradation type (e.g., blur degradation), overlooking other degradation types like noise and JPEG in real-world test-time scenarios, thus limiting their practicality. To tackle these problems, we present an efficient test-time adaptation framework for SR, named SRTTA, which is able to quickly adapt SR models to test domains with different/unknown degradation types. Specifically, we design a second-order degradation scheme to construct paired data based on the degradation type of the test image, which is predicted by a pre-trained degradation classifier. Then, we adapt the SR model by implementing feature-level reconstruction learning from the initial test image to its second-order degraded counterparts, which helps the SR model generate plausible HR images. Extensive experiments are conducted on newly synthesized corrupted DIV2K datasets with 8 different degradations and several real-world datasets, demonstrating that our SRTTA framework achieves an impressive improvement over existing methods with satisfying speed. The source code is available at https://github.com/DengZeshuai/SRTTA.

SRTTA addresses this mismatch by adapting a super-resolution model at test time to different or unknown degradation types.

The authors report improved results over existing methods with satisfactory speed, supporting the framework's usefulness for the tested changes in image degradation.
summary.tldr: SRTTA adapts super-resolution models using further-degraded versions of each test image, improving results across tested corruptions with satisfactory speed.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation for Super-Resolution with Second-Order Degradation and Reconstruction

abstract: Time series forecasting has played a pivotal role across various industries, including finance, transportation, energy, healthcare, and climate. Due to the abundant seasonal information they contain, timestamps possess the potential to offer robust global guidance for forecasting techniques. However, existing works primarily focus on local observations, with timestamps being treated merely as an optional supplement that remains underutilized. When data gathered from the real world is polluted, the absence of global information will damage the robust prediction capability of these algorithms. To address these problems, we propose a novel framework named GLAFF. Within this framework, the timestamps are modeled individually to capture the global dependencies. Working as a plugin, GLAFF adaptively adjusts the combined weights for global and local information, enabling seamless collaboration with any time series forecasting backbone. Extensive experiments conducted on nine real-world datasets demonstrate that GLAFF significantly enhances the average performance of widely used mainstream forecasting models by 12.5\%, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art method by 5.5\%.

paragraphs: Forecasting models often emphasize recent observations while treating timestamps as optional supporting information. This paper argues that timestamps contain seasonal structure that can provide broader guidance. That guidance becomes especially valuable when observed data are polluted and relying on local measurements alone weakens prediction robustness.

GLAFF models timestamps separately to capture global dependencies. As a plugin, it combines that information with the local information used by a forecasting backbone. The combination is adaptive: the framework adjusts the relative weights assigned to the global and local sources, allowing them to contribute jointly to the prediction.

The authors present GLAFF as compatible with any time-series forecasting backbone and evaluate it on nine real-world datasets. They report an average performance improvement of 12.5% for widely used forecasting models and a 5.5% advantage over the previous state-of-the-art method. These findings support treating time information as an independently modeled source of predictive structure. The approach matters because it can enhance existing forecasting architectures through a plugin rather than requiring a wholly new backbone.
summary.tldr: GLAFF adaptively combines timestamp-based global structure with local observations, improving forecasting performance across nine real-world datasets.

title: Rethinking the Power of Timestamps for Robust Time Series Forecasting: A Global-Local Fusion Perspective

abstract: Natural behaviors, even stereotyped ones, exhibit variability. Despite its role in exploring and learning, the function and neural basis of this variability is still not well understood. Given the coupling between neural activity and behavior, we ask what type of neural variability does not compromise behavioral performance. While previous studies typically curtail variability to allow for high task performance in neural networks, our approach takes the reversed perspective. We investigate how to generate maximal neural variability while at the same time having high network performance. To do so, we extend to neural activity the maximum occupancy principle (MOP) developed for behavior, and refer to this new neural principle as NeuroMOP. NeuroMOP posits that the goal of the nervous system is to maximize future action-state entropy, a reward-free, intrinsic motivation that entails creating all possible activity patterns while avoiding terminal or dangerous ones.We show that this goal can be achieved through a neural network controller that injects currents (actions) into a recurrent neural network of fixed random weights to maximize future cumulative action-state entropy. High activity variability can be induced while adhering to an energy constraint or while avoiding terminal states defined by specific neurons' activities, also in a context-dependent manner. The network solves these tasks by flexibly switching between stochastic and deterministic modes as needed and projecting noise onto a null space. Based on future maximum entropy production, NeuroMOP contributes to a novel theory of neural variability that reconciles stochastic and deterministic behaviors within a single framework.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much neural activity can vary while behavior remains reliable. Its starting point reverses the usual strategy of suppressing variability to protect task performance. The authors instead seek maximal variability subject to successful operation, extending the maximum occupancy principle from behavior to neural activity.

Their proposed principle, NeuroMOP, treats maximizing future action-state entropy as an intrinsic objective without an external reward. A controller injects currents into a recurrent neural network with fixed random weights to pursue that objective. The network switches between stochastic and deterministic operation and projects noise into a null space. These demonstrations support NeuroMOP as a proposed account of how variable activity and reliable performance can coexist; they do not establish it as the nervous system's actual objective.
summary.tldr: NeuroMOP generates highly variable recurrent-network activity while maintaining specified energy or state-avoidance constraints.

title: Controlled maximal variability along with reliable performance in recurrent neural networks

abstract: Message-passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) have emerged as a powerful paradigm for graph-based machine learning. Despite their effectiveness, MPNNs face challenges such as under-reaching and over-squashing, where limited receptive fields and structural bottlenecks hinder information flow in the graph. While graph transformers hold promise in addressing these issues, their scalability is limited due to quadratic complexity regarding the number of nodes, rendering them impractical for larger graphs. Here, we propose implicitly rewired message-passing neural networks (IPR-MPNNs), a novel approach that integrates implicit probabilistic graph rewiring into MPNNs. By introducing a small number of virtual nodes, i.e., adding additional nodes to a given graph and connecting them to existing nodes, in a differentiable, end-to-end manner, IPR-MPNNs enable long-distance message propagation, circumventing quadratic complexity. Theoretically, we demonstrate that IPR-MPNNs surpass the expressiveness of traditional MPNNs. Empirically, we validate our approach by showcasing its ability to mitigate under-reaching and over-squashing effects, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple graph datasets. Notably, IPR-MPNNs outperform graph transformers while maintaining significantly faster computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Message-passing graph networks can struggle to move information across long distances or through narrow structural bottlenecks. Graph transformers offer another route, but their quadratic dependence on node count limits scalability. This paper proposes IPR-MPNNs to improve information flow while avoiding that quadratic cost.

The method adds a small number of virtual nodes and connects them to existing graph nodes through implicit probabilistic rewiring. These connections are learned differentiably as part of end-to-end training. The additional nodes provide routes for long-distance messages, allowing the network to change how information travels without requiring the costly interaction structure associated with graph transformers.

The authors prove that IPR-MPNNs are more expressive than traditional message-passing networks. Experiments show reduced under-reaching and over-squashing, alongside leading performance across multiple graph datasets. The evaluated models also outperform graph transformers while running substantially faster. Together, the theoretical and empirical results support learned virtual-node connectivity as a way to strengthen graph reasoning while retaining favorable computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: IPR-MPNNs learn virtual-node connections that improve long-range graph communication and expressiveness without quadratic computational complexity.

title: Probabilistic Graph Rewiring via Virtual Nodes

abstract: The challenge of discovering new molecules with desired properties is crucial in domains like drug discovery and material design. Recent advances in deep learning-based generative methods have shown promise but face the issue of sample efficiency due to the computational expense of evaluating the reward function. This paper proposes a novel algorithm for sample-efficient molecular optimization by distilling a powerful genetic algorithm into deep generative policy using GFlowNets training, the off-policy method for amortized inference. This approach enables the deep generative policy to learn from domain knowledge, which has been explicitly integrated into the genetic algorithm. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in the official molecular optimization benchmark, significantly outperforming previous methods. It also demonstrates effectiveness in designing inhibitors against SARS-CoV-2 with substantially fewer reward calls.
