The experiments also highlight the potential to attribute information flow between arbitrary Transformer components. This breadth matters because the same decomposition framework can support questions about input contributions and questions about internal processing. The stated contribution is a flexible attribution tool whose usefulness is supported across multiple experimental forms of analysis.
summary.tldr: DePass traces Transformer feature contributions through one decomposed forward pass without auxiliary training.

title: DePass: Unified Feature Attributing by Simple Decomposed Forward Pass

abstract: Layer pruning has emerged as a widely used technique for compressing large language models (LLMs). However, existing layer pruning approaches often incur substantial performance degradation. We identify the majority of this degradation to a single yet previously overlooked issue: \textit{the mismatch of activation magnitudes at the pruning interface}. The pre-interface activations exhibit significantly different scales from the post-interface ones, causing the distributional shift as it propagates through the remaining layers. To address this issue, we introduce \textsc{LinearPatch}, a lightweight and plug-and-play technique that fuses two operations into one matrix multiply at the pruning interface: (i) a Hadamard transformation that suppresses massive outliers at particular tokens and (ii) a channel-wise scaling that aligns activation statistics. On LLaMA-3-8B, \textsc{LinearPatch} preserves up to \textbf{94.15\%} of the original model's performance when pruning 5 out of 32 layers, outperforming the previous state of the art by \textbf{4\%}. The patch can be further refined with 5K unlabeled samples via memory-efficient offline distillation, pushing the retention to 95.16\% within only 30 minutes on a single GPU. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/chenxinrui-tsinghua/LinearPatch}.

This paper attributes most of that degradation to a mismatch in activation magnitudes where the remaining layers meet. The values arriving at this interface have different scales from those expected downstream, and the resulting distribution shift propagates through the rest of the model.

LinearPatch repairs this interface with two operations combined into one matrix multiplication. A Hadamard transformation suppresses unusually large values associated with particular tokens, while channel-wise scaling aligns activation statistics. The intervention therefore targets the flow of representations at the pruning boundary, providing a lightweight addition to an already pruned model.

Optional offline distillation using 5,000 unlabeled samples raises retention to 95.16% in 30 minutes on one GPU. These findings support activation-scale repair as a substantial recovery mechanism in the evaluated setting.
summary.tldr: LinearPatch recovers much of a layer-pruned language model’s performance by correcting activation scales at the pruning interface.

title: A Simple Linear Patch Revives Layer-Pruned Large Language Models

abstract: Inference in both brains and machines can be formalized by optimizing a shared objective: maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO) in machine learning, or minimizing variational free energy ($\mathcal{F}$) in neuroscience (ELBO = $-\mathcal{F}$). While this equivalence suggests a unifying framework, it leaves open how inference is implemented in neural systems. Here, we introduce FOND (*Free energy Online Natural-gradient Dynamics*), a framework that derives neural inference dynamics from three principles: (1) natural gradients on $\mathcal{F}$, (2) online belief updating, and (3) iterative refinement. We apply FOND to derive iP-VAE (*iterative Poisson variational autoencoder*), a recurrent spiking neural network that performs variational inference through membrane potential dynamics, replacing amortized encoders with iterative inference updates. Theoretically, iP-VAE yields several desirable features such as emergent normalization via lateral competition, and hardware-efficient integer spike count representations. Empirically, iP-VAE outperforms both standard VAEs and Gaussian-based predictive coding models in sparsity, reconstruction, and biological plausibility, and scales to complex color image datasets such as CelebA. iP-VAE also exhibits strong generalization to out-of-distribution inputs, exceeding hybrid iterative-amortized VAEs. These results demonstrate how deriving inference algorithms from first principles can yield concrete architectures that are simultaneously biologically plausible and empirically effective.

This paper develops a framework that connects the objective to explicit neural dynamics.

The model also handles complex color images and exceeds hybrid iterative-amortized VAEs on out-of-distribution inputs. These findings support deriving useful architectures from explicit inference principles while retaining features motivated by neural computation.
summary.tldr: FOND derives iterative neural inference dynamics that produce a spiking VAE with strong reconstruction and generalization results.

title: Brain-like Variational Inference

abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has become a powerful post-training paradigm for aligning large language models with human preferences. A core challenge in RLHF is constructing accurate reward signals, where the conventional Bradley-Terry reward models (BT RMs) often suffer from sensitivity to data size and coverage, as well as vulnerability to reward hacking. Generative reward models (GenRMs) offer a more robust alternative by generating chain-of-thought (CoT) rationales followed by a final verdict. However, existing GenRMs rely on shallow, vertically scaled reasoning, limiting their capacity to handle nuanced or complex tasks. Moreover, their pairwise preference outputs are incompatible with standard RLHF algorithms that require pointwise reward signals. In this work, we introduce Think-RM, a training framework that enables long-horizon reasoning in GenRMs by modeling an internal thinking process. Rather than producing structured, externally provided rationales, Think-RM generates flexible, self-guided reasoning traces that support advanced capabilities such as self-reflection, hypothetical reasoning, and divergent reasoning. To elicit these reasoning abilities, we first warm-up the models by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) over long CoT data. We then further improve the model's long-horizon abilities by rule-based reinforcement learning (RL). In addition, we propose a novel pairwise RLHF pipeline that directly optimizes policies from pairwise comparisons, eliminating the need for pointwise reward conversion. Experiments show that Think-RM outperforms baselines on both in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, with particularly strong gains on reasoning-heavy benchmarks: more than 10\% and 5\% on RewardBench's Chat Hard and Reasoning, and 12\% on RM-Bench's Math domain. When combined with our pairwise RLHF pipeline, it demonstrates superior end-policy performance compared to traditional approaches. This depth-oriented approach not only broadens the GenRM design space but also establishes a new paradigm for preference-based policy optimization in RLHF.

title: Think-RM: Enabling Long-Horizon Reasoning in Generative Reward Models

abstract: We study the problem of topic modeling in corpora whose documents are organized in a multi-level hierarchy. We explore a parametric approach to this problem, assuming that the number of topics is known or can be estimated by cross-validation. The models we consider can be viewed as special (finite-dimensional) instances of hierarchical Dirichlet processes (HDPs). For these models we show that there exists a simple variational approximation for probabilistic inference. The approximation relies on a previously unexploited inequality that handles the conditional dependence between Dirichlet latent variables in adjacent levels of the model’s hierarchy. We compare our approach to existing implementations of nonparametric HDPs. On several benchmarks we find that our approach is faster than Gibbs sampling and able to learn more predictive models than existing variational methods. Finally, we demonstrate the large-scale viability of our approach on two newly available corpora from researchers in computer security–one with 350,000 documents and over 6,000 internal subcategories, the other with a five-level deep hierarchy.

paragraphs: Documents often belong to categories nested inside larger categories. This paper develops topic-model inference for corpora with such multilevel organization. It takes a parametric approach, assuming that the number of topics is known or can be selected through cross-validation. The models are finite-dimensional special cases of hierarchical Dirichlet processes.

The central technical contribution is a simple variational approximation that handles dependence between latent Dirichlet variables at neighboring levels of the hierarchy. A previously unused inequality makes that approximation possible. This matters because inference must account for how adjacent levels relate, rather than treating the document hierarchy as merely an external organizational label.

On several benchmarks, the approach runs faster than Gibbs sampling and learns more predictive models than existing variational methods. The authors also demonstrate large-scale use on two computer-security corpora: one containing 350,000 documents and more than 6,000 internal subcategories, and another with five hierarchical levels. These results support both the inference method's practical efficiency and its applicability to substantial hierarchical collections.
summary.tldr: A new variational approximation enables efficient topic modeling of hierarchical document collections when the number of topics is fixed or selected in advance.

title: A Variational Approximation for Topic Modeling of Hierarchical Corpora

abstract: This paper presents a lower bound for optimizing a finite sum of n functions, where each function is L-smooth and the sum is μ-strongly convex. We show that no algorithm can reach an error εin minimizing all functions from this class in fewer than Ω(n + \sqrtn(κ-1)\log(1/ε)) iterations, where κ=L/μis a surrogate condition number. We then compare this lower bound to upper bounds for recently developed methods specializing to this setting. When the functions involved in this sum are not arbitrary, but based on i.i.d. random data, then we further contrast these complexity results with those for optimal first-order methods to directly optimize the sum. The conclusion we draw is that a lot of caution is necessary for an accurate comparison, and identify machine learning scenarios where the new methods help computationally.

paragraphs: The paper studies the computational difficulty of minimizing a finite sum of functions. Its setting assumes that each component is smooth and that the sum is strongly convex. Smoothness controls how rapidly gradients change, while strong convexity supplies curvature to the overall objective. The ratio of these quantities provides the condition-number parameter used in the analysis.

The authors establish a lower bound on the iterations needed to achieve a desired error across this function class. The bound relates the required computation to the number of component functions, the condition number, and the requested accuracy. It provides a benchmark for judging upper bounds from methods designed specifically to exploit finite-sum structure.

The paper also distinguishes arbitrary component functions from functions generated by independent, identically distributed data. In that statistical setting, it compares specialized finite-sum methods with optimal first-order methods that optimize the sum directly. The authors emphasize that careful comparisons are necessary and identify machine-learning scenarios where the specialized methods offer computational benefits. The result is a qualified account of when exploiting the sum structure helps.
summary.tldr: The paper derives a finite-sum optimization lower bound and examines when specialized methods offer computational advantages in machine learning.

title: A Lower Bound for the Optimization of Finite Sums

abstract: The Noisy Non-negative Matrix factorization (NMF) is: given a data matrix A (d x n), find non-negative matrices B;C (d x k, k x n respy.) so that A = BC +N, where N is a noise matrix. Existing polynomial time algorithms with proven error guarantees require EACH column N_⋅j to have l1 norm much smaller than ||(BC)_⋅j ||_1, which could be very restrictive. In important applications of NMF such as Topic Modeling as well as theoretical noise models (e.g. Gaussian with high sigma), almost EVERY column of N_.j violates this condition. We introduce the heavy noise model which only requires the average noise over large subsets of columns to be small. We initiate a study of Noisy NMF under the heavy noise model. We show that our noise model subsumes noise models of theoretical and practical interest (for e.g. Gaussian noise of maximum possible sigma). We then devise an algorithm TSVDNMF which under certain assumptions on B,C, solves the problem under heavy noise. Our error guarantees match those of previous algorithms. Our running time of O(k.(d+n)^2) is substantially better than the O(d.n^3) for the previous best. Our assumption on B is weaker than the “Separability” assumption made by all previous results. We provide empirical justification for our assumptions on C. We also provide the first proof of identifiability (uniqueness of B) for noisy NMF which is not based on separability and does not use hard to check geometric conditions. Our algorithm outperforms earlier polynomial time algorithms both in time and error, particularly in the presence of high noise.

paragraphs: Noisy non-negative matrix factorization seeks two non-negative matrices whose product explains an observed matrix up to noise. Earlier polynomial-time guarantees required every noise column to be small relative to its signal column. The paper argues that this condition is restrictive for topic modeling and high-noise models, where almost every column may violate it.

The authors introduce a heavy-noise model requiring small average noise over large subsets of columns. Their algorithm, TSVDNMF, solves the problem under stated assumptions on the factors. Its assumption on the first factor is weaker than separability, while the paper supplies empirical justification for assumptions on the second. The error guarantees match previous algorithms, with a better stated running time.

The paper also proves uniqueness of the first factor without relying on separability or difficult-to-check geometric conditions. Its noise model covers cases of theoretical and practical interest. Empirical comparisons show improvements in both runtime and error over earlier polynomial-time algorithms, especially under high noise, supporting the usefulness of relaxing column-by-column noise restrictions.
summary.tldr: TSVDNMF handles an aggregate heavy-noise condition with matching prior error guarantees and improved runtime under assumptions on the factors.

title: Non-negative Matrix Factorization under Heavy Noise

abstract: Conditional gradient algorithms (also often called Frank-Wolfe algorithms) are popular due to their simplicity of only requiring a linear optimization oracle and more recently they also gained significant traction for online learning. While simple in principle, in many cases the actual implementation of the linear optimization oracle is costly. We show a general method to lazify various conditional gradient algorithms, which in actual computations leads to several orders of magnitude of speedup in wall-clock time. This is achieved by using a faster separation oracle instead of a linear optimization oracle, relying only on few linear optimization oracle calls.

paragraphs: Conditional gradient methods, also called Frank-Wolfe methods, are attractive because they rely on a linear optimization oracle. This oracle is a subroutine that solves a linear optimization problem for the algorithm. The surrounding method can be simple even when implementing and repeatedly calling that subroutine is computationally expensive.

This paper proposes a general way to make several conditional gradient algorithms lazy. The method uses a faster separation oracle in place of most linear optimization calls, while retaining a small number of calls to the original oracle. The central change is therefore how the algorithm obtains the information needed to keep progressing.

In actual computations, the authors report wall-clock speedups of several orders of magnitude. The finding highlights a practical distinction between an algorithm's simple description and the cost of its underlying operations. When linear optimization is expensive, reducing dependence on that operation can deliver large runtime improvements. The contribution is a reusable modification for various conditional gradient methods, rather than a single application-specific optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: Replacing most costly linear optimization calls with a faster separation oracle substantially accelerates several conditional gradient methods.

title: Lazifying Conditional Gradient Algorithms

abstract: Even though active learning forms an important pillar of machine learning, deep learning tools are not prevalent within it. Deep learning poses several difficulties when used in an active learning setting. First, active learning (AL) methods generally rely on being able to learn and update models from small amounts of data. Recent advances in deep learning, on the other hand, are notorious for their dependence on large amounts of data. Second, many AL acquisition functions rely on model uncertainty, yet deep learning methods rarely represent such model uncertainty. In this paper we combine recent advances in Bayesian deep learning into the active learning framework in a practical way. We develop an active learning framework for high dimensional data, a task which has been extremely challenging so far, with very sparse existing literature. Taking advantage of specialised models such as Bayesian convolutional neural networks, we demonstrate our active learning techniques with image data, obtaining a significant improvement on existing active learning approaches. We demonstrate this on both the MNIST dataset, as well as for skin cancer diagnosis from lesion images (ISIC2016 task).

paragraphs: Active learning uses a model to help choose which examples should receive labels next. This creates two challenges for deep learning: the model must be useful when labeled data are scarce, and many selection rules need a meaningful estimate of model uncertainty. Conventional deep learning methods do not automatically meet either requirement.

The paper combines Bayesian deep learning with active learning in a practical framework for high-dimensional data. Specialized models, including Bayesian convolutional neural networks, provide the connection between image modeling and uncertainty-aware selection. The approach addresses the mismatch between methods that typically benefit from large datasets and a learning process designed to choose additional data from a small starting collection.

The authors demonstrate the framework on MNIST and on skin-lesion images in the ISIC2016 diagnosis task, reporting a significant improvement over existing active learning approaches. These results support the usefulness of Bayesian deep models for selecting informative image data. The contribution is an active learning framework and its demonstrated performance on those tasks, rather than a claim about clinical deployment.
summary.tldr: Bayesian deep learning enables uncertainty-aware active learning for images, improving on existing approaches in two demonstrated tasks.

title: Deep Bayesian Active Learning with Image Data

abstract: In this paper, we adapt the control theoretic concept of dissipativity theory to provide a natural understanding of Nesterov’s accelerated method. Our theory ties rigorous convergence rate analysis to the physically intuitive notion of energy dissipation. Moreover, dissipativity allows one to efficiently construct Lyapunov functions (either numerically or analytically) by solving a small semidefinite program. Using novel supply rate functions, we show how to recover known rate bounds for Nesterov’s method and we generalize the approach to certify both linear and sublinear rates in a variety of settings. Finally, we link the continuous-time version of dissipativity to recent works on algorithm analysis that use discretizations of ordinary differential equations.

Our theory ties rigorous convergence rate analysis to the physically intuitive notion of energy dissipation. Moreover, dissipativity allows one to efficiently construct Lyapunov functions (either numerically or analytically) by solving a small semidefinite program. Using novel supply rate functions, we show how to recover known rate bounds for Nesterov’s method and we generalize the approach to certify both linear and sublinear rates in a variety of settings. Finally, we link the continuous-time version of dissipativity to recent works on algorithm analysis that use discretizations of ordinary differential equations.

The guiding idea is to relate progress in an optimization algorithm to the dissipation of energy in a physical system. This provides an intuitive interpretation while supporting rigorous statements about how quickly the method converges.

A key practical benefit is a systematic way to construct Lyapunov functions, mathematical quantities used to certify progress. The authors show that dissipativity permits their numerical or analytical construction through a small semidefinite program. They introduce supply rate functions that allow the framework to recover known convergence-rate bounds for Nesterov's method.

The approach also certifies linear and sublinear convergence rates across a variety of settings. Its continuous-time formulation connects with research that analyzes optimization algorithms using discretized ordinary differential equations. The contribution is therefore both explanatory and methodological: it links acceleration to energy reasoning and supplies a tractable procedure for building convergence certificates, rather than presenting a new accelerated optimizer.
summary.tldr: Dissipativity theory explains Nesterov acceleration through energy dissipation and provides a systematic way to certify convergence rates.

title: Dissipativity Theory for Nesterov’s Accelerated Method

abstract: We present a model that, after learning on observations of (sequence, outcome) pairs, can be efficiently used to revise a new sequence in order to improve its associated outcome. Our framework requires neither example improvements, nor additional evaluation of outcomes for proposed revisions. To avoid combinatorial-search over sequence elements, we specify a generative model with continuous latent factors, which is learned via joint approximate inference using a recurrent variational autoencoder (VAE) and an outcome-predicting neural network module. Under this model, gradient methods can be used to efficiently optimize the continuous latent factors with respect to inferred outcomes. By appropriately constraining this optimization and using the VAE decoder to generate a revised sequence, we ensure the revision is fundamentally similar to the original sequence, is associated with better outcomes, and looks natural. These desiderata are proven to hold with high probability under our approach, which is empirically demonstrated for revising natural language sentences.

The guarantees belong to the proposed model and constrained procedure, preserving the distinction between inferred outcomes and newly measured evaluations.
summary.tldr: A sequence model revises inputs by optimizing continuous latent factors for predicted outcomes while constraining similarity and naturalness.

title: Sequence to Better Sequence: Continuous Revision of Combinatorial Structures

abstract: This paper first presents a theory for generative adversarial methods that does not rely on the traditional minimax formulation. It shows that with a strong discriminator, a good generator can be learned so that the KL divergence between the distributions of real data and generated data improves after each functional gradient step until it converges to zero. Based on the theory, we propose a new stable generative adversarial method. A theoretical insight into the original GAN from this new viewpoint is also provided. The experiments on image generation show the effectiveness of our new method.

Based on the theory, we propose a new stable generative adversarial method. A theoretical insight into the original GAN from this new viewpoint is also provided. The experiments on image generation show the effectiveness of our new method.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial learning aims to produce samples whose distribution matches that of real data. This paper develops a theoretical account of that process without relying on the traditional minimax formulation. Its focus is on how successive changes to the generator can improve the match between generated and real distributions.

The analysis uses functional gradient steps and measures progress with KL divergence, a measure of discrepancy between distributions. With a strong discriminator, the authors show that a good generator can be learned through steps that improve this divergence until it converges to zero. The discriminator condition is essential to the stated result: the convergence claim belongs to that theoretical setting.

The authors turn this perspective into a new generative adversarial method described as stable, and also use it to provide insight into the original GAN. Image-generation experiments demonstrate the new method's effectiveness. Together, the theory and experiments connect a distribution-level account of progress with a practical learning procedure, while serving different roles in supporting the contribution.
summary.tldr: A functional-gradient view yields a stable adversarial learning method and conditional guarantees that generated distributions approach the real-data distribution.

title: Composite Functional Gradient Learning of Generative Adversarial Models

abstract: Methods for reasoning under uncertainty are a key building block of accurate and reliable machine learning systems. Bayesian methods provide a general framework to quantify uncertainty. However, because of model misspecification and the use of approximate inference, Bayesian uncertainty estimates are often inaccurate {—} for example, a 90% credible interval may not contain the true outcome 90% of the time. Here, we propose a simple procedure for calibrating any regression algorithm; when applied to Bayesian and probabilistic models, it is guaranteed to produce calibrated uncertainty estimates given enough data. Our procedure is inspired by Platt scaling and extends previous work on classification. We evaluate this approach on Bayesian linear regression, feedforward, and recurrent neural networks, and find that it consistently outputs well-calibrated credible intervals while improving performance on time series forecasting and model-based reinforcement learning tasks.

Bayesian methods provide uncertainty estimates, but imperfect models and approximate inference can make those estimates misleading. For example, an interval labeled 90% may cover the true outcome less or more often than that label suggests.

The paper proposes a simple calibration procedure for regression algorithms. It extends an idea associated with Platt scaling in classification to predictions of numerical outcomes. Applied to Bayesian and other probabilistic models, the procedure has a guarantee of calibrated uncertainty when enough data are available. That data requirement is part of the claim, rather than an unconditional promise about every fitted model.

The authors evaluate the procedure with Bayesian linear regression and feedforward and recurrent neural networks. They report consistently well-calibrated credible intervals and improved performance in time series forecasting and model-based reinforcement learning. These findings connect better uncertainty estimates to practical prediction and decision tasks, beyond merely changing the confidence labels attached to predictions.
summary.tldr: A regression calibration procedure makes uncertainty estimates reliable given enough data and improves performance in the evaluated forecasting and reinforcement learning tasks.

title: Accurate Uncertainties for Deep Learning Using Calibrated Regression

abstract: Much recent work on large-scale visual recogni- tion aims to scale up learning to massive, noisily- annotated datasets. We address the problem of scaling-up the evaluation of such models to large- scale datasets with noisy labels. Current protocols for doing so require a human user to either vet (re-annotate) a small fraction of the testset and ignore the rest, or else correct errors in annotation as they are found through manual inspection of results. In this work, we re-formulate the problem as one of active testing, and examine strategies for efficiently querying a user so as to obtain an accurate performance estimate with minimal vet- ting. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed active testing framework on estimating two performance metrics, Precision@K and mean Average Precisions, for two popular Computer Vi- sion tasks, multilabel classification and instance segmentation, respectively. We further show that our approach is able to siginificantly save human annotation effort and more robust than alterna- tive evaluation protocols.

paragraphs: Large visual recognition datasets often contain incorrect labels, making model evaluation difficult as well as model training. A performance estimate depends on the reliability of the labels used to judge predictions. Existing evaluation practices described here either recheck a small part of the test set and discard the rest, or correct annotation mistakes as people encounter them.

The paper reframes evaluation as active testing. Instead of treating human checking as a fixed preliminary step, it examines how to choose which examples a person should verify to obtain an accurate performance estimate with little annotation work. The goal is efficient measurement of a model's performance on a noisy test set.

The authors demonstrate the framework for Precision@K in multilabel classification and mean Average Precision in instance segmentation. They report substantial savings in human annotation effort and greater robustness than alternative evaluation protocols. These findings suggest that choosing verification queries carefully can make large-scale evaluation more practical without requiring every test annotation to be manually corrected.
summary.tldr: Active testing selectively requests human label verification to estimate visual recognition performance accurately with less annotation effort.

title: Active Testing: An Efficient and Robust Framework for Estimating Accuracy

abstract: Residual Networks (ResNets) have become state-of-the-art models in deep learning and several theoretical studies have been devoted to understanding why ResNet works so well. One attractive viewpoint on ResNet is that it is optimizing the risk in a functional space by consisting of an ensemble of effective features. In this paper, we adopt this viewpoint to construct a new gradient boosting method, which is known to be very powerful in data analysis. To do so, we formalize the boosting perspective of ResNet mathematically using the notion of functional gradients and propose a new method called ResFGB for classification tasks by leveraging ResNet perception. Two types of generalization guarantees are provided from the optimization perspective: one is the margin bound and the other is the expected risk bound by the sample-splitting technique. Experimental results show superior performance of the proposed method over state-of-the-art methods such as LightGBM.

In that interpretation, a ResNet acts as an ensemble of useful features and improves its predictive risk within a space of functions. The authors use this perspective to connect residual network ideas with gradient boosting, which builds a predictor through successive improvements.

They formalize the connection using functional gradients and introduce ResFGB. A functional gradient describes an improvement direction at the level of the prediction function, providing a mathematical basis for the boosting interpretation. The contribution is therefore both an account of how to view residual networks and a new algorithm built from that account.

These address how the learned classifier can perform beyond its training data. Experiments report better performance than strong existing methods, including LightGBM. The stated results combine theoretical support for the method with empirical evidence for its usefulness in classification.
summary.tldr: ResFGB turns a functional-gradient interpretation of residual networks into a boosting classifier with generalization guarantees and favorable experimental results.

title: Functional Gradient Boosting based on Residual Network Perception

abstract: Depth is one of the keys that make neural networks succeed in the task of large-scale image recognition. The state-of-the-art network architectures usually increase the depths by cascading convolutional layers or building blocks. In this paper, we present an alternative method to increase the depth. Our method is by introducing computation orderings to the channels within convolutional layers or blocks, based on which we gradually compute the outputs in a channel-wise manner. The added orderings not only increase the depths and the learning capacities of the networks without any additional computation costs, but also eliminate the overlap singularities so that the networks are able to converge faster and perform better. Experiments show that the networks based on our method achieve the state-of-the-art performances on CIFAR and ImageNet datasets.

paragraphs: Increasing network depth is a major route to stronger image recognition, usually accomplished by stacking more convolutional layers or blocks. This paper introduces another way to deepen computation: placing an order on the channels inside an existing layer or block and computing their outputs gradually.

The ordering adds structure within the computation already present in the network. According to the authors, it increases depth and learning capacity without adding computational cost. They also report that the ordering removes overlap singularities, connecting this architectural change with faster convergence and better performance. The proposed benefit therefore involves both representational capacity and training behavior.

Networks built with this gradual channel-wise computation achieve reported state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR and ImageNet. These experiments support computation order as an architectural design choice for large-scale recognition. The key contribution is showing that increased depth can come from reorganizing how channels are computed, broadening the usual strategy of adding successive layers or blocks.
summary.tldr: Ordering channel computations increases network depth and capacity without additional computation, with reported state-of-the-art image-recognition results.

title: Gradually Updated Neural Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition

abstract: In transfer learning, what and how to transfer are two primary issues to be addressed, as different transfer learning algorithms applied between a source and a target domain result in different knowledge transferred and thereby the performance improvement in the target domain. Determining the optimal one that maximizes the performance improvement requires either exhaustive exploration or considerable expertise. Meanwhile, it is widely accepted in educational psychology that human beings improve transfer learning skills of deciding what to transfer through meta-cognitive reflection on inductive transfer learning practices. Motivated by this, we propose a novel transfer learning framework known as Learning to Transfer (L2T) to automatically determine what and how to transfer are the best by leveraging previous transfer learning experiences. We establish the L2T framework in two stages: 1) we learn a reflection function encrypting transfer learning skills from experiences; and 2) we infer what and how to transfer are the best for a future pair of domains by optimizing the reflection function. We also theoretically analyse the algorithmic stability and generalization bound of L2T, and empirically demonstrate its superiority over several state-of-the-art transfer learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Transfer learning requires deciding what knowledge to reuse and how to move it from a source domain to a target domain. Different choices can produce different improvements, and choosing among them may require extensive search or expertise. Learning to Transfer addresses this selection problem by learning from previous experiences of transferring knowledge.

The framework has two stages. First, it learns a reflection function that encodes transfer-learning skills from those experiences. Then, for a new pair of domains, it optimizes that function to determine what and how to transfer. Past transfer attempts thus become evidence for choosing a future transfer strategy.

The authors analyze the framework’s algorithmic stability and generalization bound and report empirical superiority over several state-of-the-art transfer-learning algorithms. These results support treating transfer selection itself as something that can be learned. The contribution moves the decision process beyond manually choosing a fixed transfer method, using accumulated experience to guide choices for new source-target pairs.
summary.tldr: Learning to Transfer uses past transfer experiences to choose what knowledge to transfer and how to transfer it.

title: Transfer Learning via Learning to Transfer

abstract: This paper studies the problem of estimating the graphon function – a generative mechanism for a class of random graphs that are useful approximations to real networks. Specifically, a graph of $n$ vertices is generated such that each pair of two vertices $i$ and $j$ are connected independently with probability $\rho_n \times f(x_i,x_j)$, where $x_i$ is the unknown $d$-dimensional label of vertex $i$, $f$ is an unknown symmetric function, and $\rho_n$, assumed to be $\Omega(\log n/n)$, is a scaling parameter characterizing the graph sparsity. The task is to estimate graphon $f$ given the graph. Recent studies have identified the minimax optimal estimation error rate for $d=1$. However, there exists a wide gap between the known error rates of polynomial-time estimators and the minimax optimal error rate. We improve on the previously known error rates of polynomial-time estimators, by analyzing a spectral method, namely universal singular value thresholding (USVT) algorithm. When $f$ belongs to either Hölder or Sobolev space with smoothness index $\alpha$, we show the error rates of USVT are at most $(n\rho)^{ -2 \alpha / (2\alpha+d)}$. These error rates approach the minimax optimal error rate $\log (n\rho)/(n\rho)$ proved in prior work for $d=1$, as $\alpha$ increases, i.e., $f$ becomes smoother. Furthermore, when $f$ is analytic with infinitely many times differentiability, we show the error rate of USVT is at most $\log^d (n\rho)/(n\rho)$. When $f$ is a step function which corresponds to the stochastic block model with $k$ blocks for some $k$, the error rate of USVT is at most $k/(n\rho)$, which is larger than the minimax optimal error rate by at most a multiplicative factor $k/\log k$. This coincides with the computational gap observed in community detection. A key ingredient of our analysis is to derive the eigenvalue decaying rate of the edge probability matrix using piecewise polynomial approximations of the graphon function $f$.

These results narrow known gaps between computationally efficient estimation and statistical limits, with the resulting rates depending on smoothness, dimension, sparsity, or block structure.
summary.tldr: Sharper analysis of spectral graphon estimation links achievable error to graph smoothness, sparsity, hidden dimension, and block structure.

title: Rates of Convergence of Spectral Methods for Graphon Estimation

abstract: The apparent contradiction in the title is a wordplay on the different meanings attributed to the word reproducible across different scientific fields. What we imply is that unreproducible findings can be built upon reproducible methods. Without denying the importance of facilitating the reproduction of methods, we deem important to reassert that reproduction of findings is a fundamental step of the scientific inquiry. We argue that the commendable quest towards easy deterministic reproducibility of methods and numerical results should not have us forget the even more important necessity of ensuring the reproducibility of empirical findings and conclusions by properly accounting for essential sources of variations. We provide experiments to exemplify the brittleness of current common practice in the evaluation of models in the field of deep learning, showing that even if the results could be reproduced, a slightly different experiment would not support the findings. We hope to help clarify the distinction between exploratory and empirical research in the field of deep learning and believe more energy should be devoted to proper empirical research in our community. This work is an attempt to promote the use of more rigorous and diversified methodologies. It is not an attempt to impose a new methodology and it is not a critique on the nature of exploratory research.

paragraphs: This paper distinguishes reproducing a computational procedure from reproducing the scientific conclusion drawn from it. A method may reliably generate the same numerical result, while the broader finding fails when relevant aspects of the experiment vary. The title highlights this difference: reproducible methods can still support conclusions that do not hold up across experiments.

The authors provide deep-learning experiments in which results can be reproduced, yet a slightly different experiment no longer supports the original finding. They argue that evaluation should account for essential sources of variation, rather than treating deterministic reruns as sufficient evidence. The concern is whether the empirical conclusion survives meaningful changes, not simply whether the original computation can be repeated.

The paper advocates more rigorous and varied empirical methodologies while recognizing the value of making methods easy to reproduce. It also seeks to clarify the distinction between exploratory work and empirical research. Its position is explicitly pluralistic: it promotes stronger support for conclusions without prescribing one new methodology or criticizing the role of exploration in deep-learning research.
summary.tldr: Repeatable numerical results can support fragile conclusions, so reproducibility also requires testing empirical findings across essential sources of variation.

title: Unreproducible Research is Reproducible

abstract: Abstractive summarization has been studied using neural sequence transduction methods with datasets of large, paired document-summary examples. However, such datasets are rare and the models trained from them do not generalize to other domains. Recently, some progress has been made in learning sequence-to-sequence mappings with only unpaired examples. In our work, we consider the setting where there are only documents (product or business reviews) with no summaries provided, and propose an end-to-end, neural model architecture to perform unsupervised abstractive summarization. Our proposed model consists of an auto-encoder where the mean of the representations of the input reviews decodes to a reasonable summary-review. We consider variants of the proposed architecture and perform an ablation study to show the importance of specific components. We show through metrics and human evaluation that the generated summaries are highly abstractive, fluent, relevant, and representative of the average sentiment of the input reviews. Finally, we collect a ground-truth evaluation dataset and show that our model outperforms a strong extractive baseline.

paragraphs: Training a neural summarizer usually requires documents paired with example summaries, but such datasets are scarce and can transfer poorly between domains. MeanSum tackles a setting containing only product or business reviews, with no summaries supplied for training. Its aim is to generate a new summary from several reviews rather than simply select passages from them.

The model uses an autoencoder and averages the representations of the input reviews. That mean representation is decoded into a summary-review. This makes averaging in the representation space the central mechanism for combining documents within an end-to-end neural architecture. The authors investigate architectural variants and use an ablation study to assess the importance of individual components.

Metrics and human evaluations indicate that the generated summaries are fluent, relevant, highly abstractive, and representative of the reviews' average sentiment. The authors also collect a reference evaluation dataset and report outperforming a strong extractive baseline. These findings support learning multi-review summarization from documents alone, with evaluation summaries used to assess the resulting system.
summary.tldr: MeanSum generates review summaries without training summaries by decoding the average of input-review representations.

title: MeanSum: A Neural Model for Unsupervised Multi-Document Abstractive Summarization

abstract: A central capability of intelligent systems is the ability to continuously build upon previous experiences to speed up and enhance learning of new tasks. Two distinct research paradigms have studied this question. Meta-learning views this problem as learning a prior over model parameters that is amenable for fast adaptation on a new task, but typically assumes the tasks are available together as a batch. In contrast, online (regret based) learning considers a setting where tasks are revealed one after the other, but conventionally trains a single model without task-specific adaptation. This work introduces an online meta-learning setting, which merges ideas from both paradigms to better capture the spirit and practice of continual lifelong learning. We propose the follow the meta leader (FTML) algorithm which extends the MAML algorithm to this setting. Theoretically, this work provides an O(log T) regret guarantee with one additional higher order smoothness assumption (in comparison to the standard online setting). Our experimental evaluation on three different large-scale problems suggest that the proposed algorithm significantly outperforms alternatives based on traditional online learning approaches.

Online learning handles tasks arriving sequentially, but conventionally updates one model without task-specific adaptation. This paper combines the two settings to study how experience can accumulate while preserving the ability to adapt separately to each new task.

The proposed algorithm, follow the meta leader, extends MAML to this sequential setting. Its purpose is to use earlier tasks to improve the basis from which adaptation begins on later tasks. This makes fast adaptation part of the online learning objective, capturing an aspect of continual learning that either paradigm alone can miss.

The theoretical result is an O(log T) regret guarantee, requiring an additional higher-order smoothness assumption compared with the standard online setting. That assumption is part of the guarantee's scope. Experiments on three large-scale problems suggest substantial improvements over alternatives based on traditional online learning, supporting the practical value of combining sequential experience with task-specific adaptation.
summary.tldr: Follow the meta leader combines sequential task learning with rapid adaptation and obtains logarithmic regret under an additional smoothness assumption.

title: Online Meta-Learning

abstract: Recent work has documented the susceptibility of deep learning systems to adversarial examples, but most such attacks directly manipulate the digital input to a classifier. Although a smaller line of work considers physical adversarial attacks, in all cases these involve manipulating the object of interest, e.g., putting a physical sticker on an object to misclassify it, or manufacturing an object specifically intended to be misclassified. In this work, we consider an alternative question: is it possible to fool deep classifiers, over all perceived objects of a certain type, by physically manipulating the camera itself? We show that by placing a carefully crafted and mainly-translucent sticker over the lens of a camera, one can create universal perturbations of the observed images that are inconspicuous, yet misclassify target objects as a different (targeted) class. To accomplish this, we propose an iterative procedure for both updating the attack perturbation (to make it adversarial for a given classifier), and the threat model itself (to ensure it is physically realizable). For example, we show that we can achieve physically-realizable attacks that fool ImageNet classifiers in a targeted fashion 49.6% of the time. This presents a new class of physically-realizable threat models to consider in the context of adversarially robust machine learning. Our demo video can be viewed at: https://youtu.be/wUVmL33Fx54

The question is whether one camera modification can cause objects of a chosen type to be classified as a different, attacker-selected class.

The sticker is mostly translucent and produces inconspicuous changes across the observed images. Designing it requires accounting for both the classifier and physical feasibility. The authors use an iterative procedure that updates the adversarial perturbation alongside the threat model, adjusting the description of allowable changes so the resulting attack can actually be realized.

The authors demonstrate physically realizable targeted attacks against ImageNet classifiers, reporting success in 49.6% of cases. The shared camera modification makes the perturbation universal across observations, but the reported success rate does not imply that every image is fooled. The contribution expands the physical attack surface considered in robust machine learning to include manipulation of the imaging device.
summary.tldr: A mostly translucent camera-lens sticker can produce reusable physical perturbations that make classifiers assign attacker-chosen labels.

title: Adversarial camera stickers: A physical camera-based attack on deep learning systems

abstract: In this paper, we introduce the Preselection Bandit problem, in which the learner preselects a subset of arms (choice alternatives) for a user, which then chooses the final arm from this subset. The learner is not aware of the user’s preferences, but can learn them from observed choices. In our concrete setting, we allow these choices to be stochastic and model the user’s actions by means of the Plackett-Luce model. The learner’s main task is to preselect subsets that eventually lead to highly preferred choices. To formalize this goal, we introduce a reasonable notion of regret and derive lower bounds on the expected regret. Moreover, we propose algorithms for which the upper bound on expected regret matches the lower bound up to a logarithmic term of the time horizon.

paragraphs: The Preselection Bandit problem separates a system's decision from a user's final choice. The learner selects a subset of available alternatives, and the user then chooses one option from that subset. The learner initially does not know the user's preferences, so it must infer them from the choices it observes over time.

The paper models those choices as stochastic using the Plackett-Luce model. Its objective is to learn which subsets lead to highly preferred final selections. This makes the composition of the offered subset central to learning: the learner controls what is available, while the user's choice determines which alternative is ultimately selected.

The authors introduce a regret measure for this setting and derive lower bounds on expected regret. They then propose algorithms whose upper bounds match those lower bounds up to a logarithmic factor in the time horizon. These results provide both a formal model for learning through preselection and evidence that the proposed algorithms approach the achievable performance limits under the stated choice model.
summary.tldr: Preselection bandits learn which subsets to offer a stochastic user, with regret bounds matching lower bounds up to a logarithmic factor.

title: Preselection Bandits

abstract: Recent convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have led to impressive performance but often suffer from poor calibration. They tend to be overconfident, with the model confidence not always reflecting the underlying true ambiguity and hardness. In this paper, we propose angular visual hardness (AVH), a score given by the normalized angular distance between the sample feature embedding and the target classifier to measure sample hardness. We validate this score with an in-depth and extensive scientific study, and observe that CNN models with the highest accuracy also have the best AVH scores. This agrees with an earlier finding that state-of-art models improve on the classification of harder examples. We observe that the training dynamics of AVH is vastly different compared to the training loss. Specifically, AVH quickly reaches a plateau for all samples even though the training loss keeps improving. This suggests the need for designing better loss functions that can target harder examples more effectively. We also find that AVH has a statistically significant correlation with human visual hardness. Finally, we demonstrate the benefit of AVH to a variety of applications such as self-training for domain adaptation and domain generalization.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence can be a poor guide to how difficult an image really is. Convolutional networks may be highly confident even when an example is ambiguous. This paper proposes angular visual hardness, or AVH, to assess difficulty using the normalized angle between an example’s feature representation and its target classifier.

The study finds that networks with the highest classification accuracy also have the best AVH scores, consistent with earlier evidence that stronger models improve on difficult examples. The authors interpret this difference as motivation for losses that address harder examples more effectively.

This supports its relevance as a measure of hardness, without making it interchangeable with human perception. The paper also demonstrates benefits in self-training for domain adaptation and in domain generalization, connecting the proposed score to practical learning applications.
summary.tldr: Angular visual hardness measures image difficulty through feature angles and reveals behavior that training loss and model confidence can miss.

title: Angular Visual Hardness

abstract: Deep semi-supervised learning (SSL) has been recently shown very effectively. However, its performance is seriously decreased when the class distribution is mismatched, among which a common situation is that unlabeled data contains some classes not seen in the labeled data. Efforts on this issue remain to be limited. This paper proposes a simple and effective safe deep SSL method to alleviate the harm caused by it. In theory, the result learned from the new method is never worse than learning from merely labeled data, and it is theoretically guaranteed that its generalization approaches the optimal in the order $O(\sqrt{d\ln(n)/n})$, even faster than the convergence rate in supervised learning associated with massive parameters. In the experiment of benchmark data, unlike the existing deep SSL methods which are no longer as good as supervised learning in 40% of unseen-class unlabeled data, the new method can still achieve performance gain in more than 60% of unseen-class unlabeled data. Moreover, the proposal is suitable for many deep SSL algorithms and can be easily extended to handle other cases of class distribution mismatch.

This paper proposes a method intended to make deep semi-supervised learning safer under that mismatch. Its goal is to preserve the benefit of unlabeled data while alleviating harm from unseen classes.

The theoretical result states that learning with the method is never worse than learning from the labeled data alone. The authors also establish a generalization rate approaching the optimum on the order of O(sqrt(d ln(n)/n)). They describe this rate as faster than the associated supervised-learning rate involving massive parameter counts. These are theoretical claims about the proposed method.

In benchmark experiments, existing methods lose their advantage over supervised learning when unseen classes account for 40% of unlabeled data, while the proposal still yields gains when that proportion exceeds 60%. The authors also state that the approach suits many deep semi-supervised algorithms and can extend to other class-distribution mismatches.
summary.tldr: The method provides a theoretical safeguard against harmful unlabeled data and retains empirical gains even with substantial unseen-class contamination.

title: Safe Deep Semi-Supervised Learning for Unseen-Class Unlabeled Data

abstract: We propose two novel conditional gradient-based methods for solving structured stochastic convex optimization problems with a large number of linear constraints. Instances of this template naturally arise from SDP-relaxations of combinatorial problems, which involve a number of constraints that is polynomial in the problem dimension. The most important feature of our framework is that only a subset of the constraints is processed at each iteration, thus gaining a computational advantage over prior works that require full passes. Our algorithms rely on variance reduction and smoothing used in conjunction with conditional gradient steps, and are accompanied by rigorous convergence guarantees. Preliminary numerical experiments are provided for illustrating the practical performance of the methods.

paragraphs: This paper addresses structured stochastic convex optimization problems with many linear constraints. Such problems arise when combinatorial optimization tasks are converted into semidefinite programming relaxations. Even when the constraint count grows polynomially with problem dimension, repeatedly processing every constraint can make each optimization step expensive.

The authors propose two methods based on conditional gradients. Their defining feature is that an iteration processes only a subset of the constraints, avoiding the full passes required by the prior approaches discussed in the abstract. Both methods combine conditional gradient steps with variance reduction and smoothing. These ingredients support an optimization procedure that uses partial constraint information while still admitting a rigorous convergence analysis.

The paper provides convergence guarantees for the algorithms and preliminary numerical experiments illustrating their practical behavior. The main result is a framework that reduces constraint-processing work per iteration without abandoning theoretical analysis. The experiments offer an initial practical demonstration; the abstract presents them as preliminary evidence rather than an extensive evaluation across applications.
summary.tldr: Two conditional gradient methods process only subsets of linear constraints while retaining rigorous convergence guarantees.

title: Conditional gradient methods for stochastically constrained convex minimization

abstract: To deal with complicated constraints via locally light computations in distributed online learning, a recent study has presented a projection-free algorithm called distributed online conditional gradient (D-OCG), and achieved an $O(T^{3/4})$ regret bound, where $T$ is the number of prediction rounds. However, in each round, the local learners of D-OCG need to communicate with their neighbors to share the local gradients, which results in a high communication complexity of $O(T)$. In this paper, we first propose an improved variant of D-OCG, namely D-BOCG, which enjoys an $O(T^{3/4})$ regret bound with only $O(\sqrt{T})$ communication complexity. The key idea is to divide the total prediction rounds into $\sqrt{T}$ equally-sized blocks, and only update the local learners at the beginning of each block by performing iterative linear optimization steps. Furthermore, to handle the more challenging bandit setting, in which only the loss value is available, we incorporate the classical one-point gradient estimator into D-BOCG, and obtain similar theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: Distributed online learning involves local learners making predictions and exchanging information with neighbors. The paper starts from a projection-free conditional gradient method that handles complicated constraints with light local computation. Its drawback is communication: sharing gradients every prediction round requires O(T) communication over T rounds, despite an O(T^(3/4)) regret guarantee.

The proposed D-BOCG method groups the prediction rounds into sqrt(T) blocks of equal size. Learners update only at the start of each block, using iterative linear optimization steps. This arrangement retains the O(T^(3/4)) regret bound while reducing communication complexity to O(sqrt(T)). The central gain is therefore less frequent communication with the same stated order of regret.

The authors also extend the approach to bandit feedback, where a learner receives only a loss value rather than a gradient. They incorporate a classical one-point gradient estimator and obtain similar theoretical guarantees. The work shows how organizing updates into blocks can improve the communication requirements of constrained distributed learning, including under a more restricted feedback model.
summary.tldr: D-BOCG preserves an O(T^(3/4)) regret bound while reducing distributed communication from O(T) to O(sqrt(T)).

title: Projection-free Distributed Online Convex Optimization with $O(\sqrtT)$ Communication Complexity

abstract: We design decentralized algorithms for regret minimization in the two sided matching market with one-sided bandit feedback that significantly improves upon the prior works (Liu et al.\,2020a, Sankararaman et al.\,2020, Liu et al.\,2020b). First, for general markets, for any $\varepsilon > 0$, we design an algorithm that achieves a $O(\log^{1+\varepsilon}(T))$ regret to the agent-optimal stable matching, with unknown time horizon $T$, improving upon the $O(\log^{2}(T))$ regret achieved in (Liu et al.\,2020b). Second, we provide the optimal $\Theta(\log(T))$ agent-optimal regret for markets satisfying {\em uniqueness consistency} – markets where leaving participants don’t alter the original stable matching. Previously, $\Theta(\log(T))$ regret was achievable (Sankararaman et al.\,2020, Liu et al.\,2020b) in the much restricted {\em serial dictatorship} setting, when all arms have the same preference over the agents. We propose a phase based algorithm, where in each phase, besides deleting the globally communicated dominated arms the agents locally delete arms with which they collide often. This \emph{local deletion} is pivotal in breaking deadlocks arising from rank heterogeneity of agents across arms. We further demonstrate superiority of our algorithm over existing works through simulations.

paragraphs: This paper studies decentralized learning in matching markets where two sides must be paired, but only one side receives bandit feedback. The objective is to reduce regret relative to the agent-optimal stable matching. For general markets, the authors obtain O(log^(1+ε)(T)) regret for any positive ε, improving the previous squared-logarithmic rate without requiring advance knowledge of the time horizon.

A stronger result applies to markets satisfying uniqueness consistency, where departing participants do not change the original stable matching. Under this condition, the algorithm achieves the optimal Θ(log(T)) rate. Earlier logarithmic guarantees required the more restrictive serial-dictatorship setting, in which all arms rank the agents in the same order.

The algorithm proceeds in phases and combines globally communicated removal of dominated arms with local removal of arms that produce frequent collisions. These local decisions help resolve deadlocks caused by different arms ranking agents differently. Simulations also show advantages over existing methods, complementing the theoretical improvements for both general and structured markets.
summary.tldr: Decentralized matching algorithms improve regret rates, with optimal logarithmic regret under a stated consistency condition.

title: Beyond $log^2(T)$ regret for decentralized bandits in matching markets

abstract: The threat of adversarial examples has motivated work on training certifiably robust neural networks to facilitate efficient verification of local robustness at inference time. We formalize a notion of global robustness, which captures the operational properties of on-line local robustness certification while yielding a natural learning objective for robust training. We show that widely-used architectures can be easily adapted to this objective by incorporating efficient global Lipschitz bounds into the network, yielding certifiably-robust models by construction that achieve state-of-the-art verifiable accuracy. Notably, this approach requires significantly less time and memory than recent certifiable training methods, and leads to negligible costs when certifying points on-line; for example, our evaluation shows that it is possible to train a large robust Tiny-Imagenet model in a matter of hours. Our models effectively leverage inexpensive global Lipschitz bounds for real-time certification, despite prior suggestions that tighter local bounds are needed for good performance; we posit this is possible because our models are specifically trained to achieve tighter global bounds. Namely, we prove that the maximum achievable verifiable accuracy for a given dataset is not improved by using a local bound.

paragraphs: Certifying robustness means verifying that a model's prediction withstands specified input changes. This paper formalizes global robustness in a way that supports local certification when individual inputs arrive. The same formulation supplies a learning objective, connecting how the network is trained with how its predictions will later be certified.

The method adapts widely used architectures by incorporating efficient global Lipschitz bounds, which control how much outputs can change as inputs change. The resulting models are certifiably robust by construction and achieve state-of-the-art verifiable accuracy in the reported evaluation. Training requires substantially less time and memory than recent certifiable training methods, while certification at inference adds negligible cost.

The authors suggest that inexpensive global bounds work well because the networks are specifically trained to make those bounds tighter. They also prove that using a local bound does not improve the maximum achievable verifiable accuracy for a given dataset. Together, the theoretical result and experiments support training models around global bounds as a practical route to efficient robustness certification.
summary.tldr: Training networks with efficient global Lipschitz bounds enables strong verifiable accuracy and inexpensive online robustness certification.

title: Globally-Robust Neural Networks

abstract: Temporal difference learning with linear function approximation is a popular method to obtain a low-dimensional approximation of the value function of a policy in a Markov Decision Process. We provide an interpretation of this method in terms of a splitting of the gradient of an appropriately chosen function. As a consequence of this interpretation, convergence proofs for gradient descent can be applied almost verbatim to temporal difference learning. Beyond giving a fuller explanation of why temporal difference works, this interpretation also yields improved convergence times. We consider the setting with $1/\sqrt{T}$ step-size, where previous comparable finite-time convergence time bounds for temporal difference learning had the multiplicative factor $1/(1-\gamma)$ in front of the bound, with $\gamma$ being the discount factor. We show that a minor variation on TD learning which estimates the mean of the value function separately has a convergence time where $1/(1-\gamma)$ only multiplies an asymptotically negligible term.

paragraphs: Temporal difference learning estimates a policy’s value function, and linear function approximation represents that function with a lower-dimensional model. This paper interprets the method as a splitting of the gradient of a suitably chosen function. The interpretation creates a direct connection between temporal difference updates and familiar gradient-descent analysis.

That connection allows convergence proofs for gradient descent to transfer almost unchanged to temporal difference learning. Beyond explaining why the updates work, it leads to improved convergence-time bounds. The authors study a step size of 1/√T, where T is the time parameter used in the bound, and examine how the discount factor γ affects the guarantee.

Earlier comparable finite-time bounds carried a multiplicative factor of 1/(1−γ) across the bound. The proposed minor variation estimates the mean of the value function separately, leaving that factor attached only to an asymptotically negligible term. This reduces the factor’s role in the long-run guarantee without claiming it disappears entirely. The result shows how a new interpretation can motivate a small algorithmic adjustment with a sharper theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: Viewing temporal difference learning as gradient splitting yields transferable convergence proofs and a sharper discount-factor dependence.

title: Temporal Difference Learning as Gradient Splitting

abstract: Variational autoencoders with deep hierarchies of stochastic layers have been known to suffer from the problem of posterior collapse, where the top layers fall back to the prior and become independent of input. We suggest that the hierarchical VAE objective explicitly includes the variance of the function parameterizing the mean and variance of the latent Gaussian distribution which itself is often a high variance function. Building on this we generalize VAE neural networks by incorporating a smoothing parameter motivated by Gaussian analysis to reduce higher frequency components and consequently the variance in parameterizing functions and show that this can help to solve the problem of posterior collapse. We further show that under such smoothing the VAE loss exhibits a phase transition, where the top layer KL divergence sharply drops to zero at a critical value of the smoothing parameter that is similar for the same model across datasets. We validate the phenomenon across model configurations and datasets.

paragraphs: Hierarchical variational autoencoders can suffer posterior collapse: their upper stochastic layers revert to the prior distribution and stop carrying information about the input. This paper connects that problem to the functions that specify the means and variances of latent Gaussian distributions. The authors suggest that these functions' own variance appears explicitly in the hierarchical training objective.

They introduce a smoothing parameter motivated by Gaussian analysis. Smoothing suppresses higher-frequency components of the parameterizing functions and thereby reduces their variance. The authors show that this modification can help address posterior collapse, giving the network a controllable property associated with the behavior of its latent layers.

Varying the smoothing parameter also reveals a sharp transition. At a critical value, the top layer's KL divergence falls to zero, marking collapse at that layer. For the same model, the critical value is similar across datasets, and the phenomenon is validated across model configurations and datasets. The results show both a potential intervention and an abrupt boundary in latent-layer behavior under smoothing.
summary.tldr: Smoothing latent-distribution parameter functions can help address posterior collapse and reveals a sharp transition in hierarchical VAE behavior.

title: Spectral Smoothing Unveils Phase Transitions in Hierarchical Variational Autoencoders

abstract: Despite their widespread success, the application of deep neural networks to functional data remains scarce today. The infinite dimensionality of functional data means standard learning algorithms can be applied only after appropriate dimension reduction, typically achieved via basis expansions. Currently, these bases are chosen a priori without the information for the task at hand and thus may not be effective for the designated task. We instead propose to adaptively learn these bases in an end-to-end fashion. We introduce neural networks that employ a new Basis Layer whose hidden units are each basis functions themselves implemented as a micro neural network. Our architecture learns to apply parsimonious dimension reduction to functional inputs that focuses only on information relevant to the target rather than irrelevant variation in the input function. Across numerous classification/regression tasks with functional data, our method empirically outperforms other types of neural networks, and we prove that our approach is statistically consistent with low generalization error.

paragraphs: Functional data consist of inputs treated as functions, creating an infinite-dimensional learning problem. Standard methods typically first reduce these inputs to a finite representation using a chosen set of basis functions. The paper questions choosing that basis before considering the prediction task, because it may preserve variation that contributes little to the desired output.

The proposed network learns its basis functions together with the rest of the predictor. A new Basis Layer contains hidden units that are themselves basis functions, each implemented by a small neural network. Training therefore adapts the dimension-reduction step to the target, seeking a compact representation that emphasizes relevant information in the input function.

Across multiple classification and regression tasks with functional inputs, the method empirically outperforms other neural-network approaches. The authors also prove statistical consistency and low generalization error for their approach. Together, these results support treating the basis as a learnable part of the prediction system: the representation is shaped by what the task needs, instead of being fixed independently of it.
summary.tldr: Adaptive Basis Layers learn task-relevant representations of functional inputs jointly with a neural predictor.

title: Deep Learning for Functional Data Analysis with Adaptive Basis Layers

abstract: Learning the principal eigenfunctions of an integral operator defined by a kernel and a data distribution is at the core of many machine learning problems. Traditional nonparametric solutions based on the Nystrom formula suffer from scalability issues. Recent work has resorted to a parametric approach, i.e., training neural networks to approximate the eigenfunctions. However, the existing method relies on an expensive orthogonalization step and is difficult to implement. We show that these problems can be fixed by using a new series of objective functions that generalizes the EigenGame to function space. We test our method on a variety of supervised and unsupervised learning problems and show it provides accurate approximations to the eigenfunctions of polynomial, radial basis, neural network Gaussian process, and neural tangent kernels. Finally, we demonstrate our method can scale up linearised Laplace approximation of deep neural networks to modern image classification datasets through approximating the Gauss-Newton matrix. Code is available at https://github.com/thudzj/neuraleigenfunction.

paragraphs: Many machine-learning problems require the principal eigenfunctions of an operator defined by a kernel and a data distribution. NeuralEF learns neural-network approximations to these functions. It addresses scalability problems in traditional Nyström-based solutions and the expensive orthogonalization step used by an existing neural approach.

The method introduces a sequence of objectives that extends EigenGame into function space. These objectives resolve the orthogonalization and implementation difficulties identified in the earlier parametric method. The central change is therefore in how the eigenfunctions are learned, making neural approximation a more practical way to work with the kernel's principal functions.

Tests on supervised and unsupervised problems show accurate approximations for polynomial, radial-basis, neural-network Gaussian-process, and neural tangent kernels. The authors also approximate the Gauss-Newton matrix to scale linearised Laplace approximation of deep networks to modern image-classification datasets. This application demonstrates how learning kernel eigenfunctions can support a larger inference procedure, beyond evaluating the approximation quality of the functions themselves.
summary.tldr: NeuralEF learns kernel eigenfunctions with new objectives that remove an expensive orthogonalization bottleneck.

title: NeuralEF: Deconstructing Kernels by Deep Neural Networks

abstract: Gradient-free/zeroth-order methods for black-box convex optimization have been extensively studied in the last decade with the main focus on oracle calls complexity. In this paper, besides the oracle complexity, we focus also on iteration complexity, and propose a generic approach that, based on optimal first-order methods, allows to obtain in a black-box fashion new zeroth-order algorithms for non-smooth convex optimization problems. Our approach not only leads to optimal oracle complexity, but also allows to obtain iteration complexity similar to first-order methods, which, in turn, allows to exploit parallel computations to accelerate the convergence of our algorithms. We also elaborate on extensions for stochastic optimization problems, saddle-point problems, and distributed optimization.
