paragraphs: Black-box optimization uses objective evaluations when gradients are unavailable. For nonsmooth convex problems, much previous work has focused on the total number of oracle calls. This paper also emphasizes iteration complexity: the number of successive optimization steps. The distinction matters because work performed within a step may be parallelized, whereas successive steps impose dependencies.

The authors propose a generic approach that builds zeroth-order algorithms from optimal first-order methods. It allows techniques developed for gradient-based optimization to be used as components in a black-box procedure for nonsmooth convex objectives. The resulting algorithms achieve optimal oracle complexity while retaining iteration complexity similar to first-order methods.

These two guarantees address different computational concerns: total evaluation effort and the number of sequential rounds. The iteration result makes it possible to exploit parallel computation to accelerate convergence. The paper also discusses extensions to stochastic optimization, saddle-point problems, and distributed optimization, showing how the approach connects to several related optimization settings.
summary.tldr: A generic conversion of first-order methods yields black-box nonsmooth convex algorithms with optimal oracle complexity and favorable parallelizable iteration complexity.

title: The power of first-order smooth optimization for black-box non-smooth problems

abstract: Creating reinforcement learning (RL) agents that are capable of accepting and leveraging task-specific knowledge from humans has been long identified as a possible strategy for developing scalable approaches for solving long-horizon problems. While previous works have looked at the possibility of using symbolic models along with RL approaches, they tend to assume that the high-level action models are executable at low level and the fluents can exclusively characterize all desirable MDP states. Symbolic models of real world tasks are however often incomplete. To this end, we introduce Approximate Symbolic-Model Guided Reinforcement Learning, wherein we will formalize the relationship between the symbolic model and the underlying MDP that will allow us to characterize the incompleteness of the symbolic model. We will use these models to extract high-level landmarks that will be used to decompose the task. At the low level, we learn a set of diverse policies for each possible task subgoal identified by the landmark, which are then stitched together. We evaluate our system by testing on three different benchmark domains and show how even with incomplete symbolic model information, our approach is able to discover the task structure and efficiently guide the RL agent towards the goal.

paragraphs: Human-provided symbolic descriptions can help reinforcement learning agents organize long tasks, but those descriptions are often incomplete. Earlier approaches commonly assume that symbolic actions can be executed at the lower level and that symbolic state descriptions cover all desirable states. This paper develops an approach that explicitly accommodates incomplete symbolic knowledge.

The authors formalize the relationship between a symbolic model and the underlying Markov decision process, making the model's incompleteness something the framework can characterize. They extract high-level landmarks from the symbolic description to divide the task into subgoals. For each subgoal, the agent learns a collection of diverse low-level policies, which are subsequently combined.

Evaluations across three benchmark domains show that the approach can discover task structure and efficiently guide an agent toward its goal despite incomplete symbolic information. The contribution connects approximate high-level guidance with diversity in learned skills, allowing a task description to provide useful organization without requiring it to specify every detail of successful execution.
summary.tldr: Incomplete symbolic models guide task decomposition, while diverse learned skills help reinforcement learning agents reach the resulting subgoals.

title: Leveraging Approximate Symbolic Models for Reinforcement Learning via Skill Diversity

abstract: In the area of physical simulations, nearly all neural-network-based methods directly predict future states from the input states. However, many traditional simulation engines instead model the constraints of the system and select the state which satisfies them. Here we present a framework for constraint-based learned simulation, where a scalar constraint function is implemented as a graph neural network, and future predictions are computed by solving the optimization problem defined by the learned constraint. Our model achieves comparable or better accuracy to top learned simulators on a variety of challenging physical domains, and offers several unique advantages. We can improve the simulation accuracy on a larger system by applying more solver iterations at test time. We also can incorporate novel hand-designed constraints at test time and simulate new dynamics which were not present in the training data. Our constraint-based framework shows how key techniques from traditional simulation and numerical methods can be leveraged as inductive biases in machine learning simulators.

paragraphs: Most neural simulators predict a future physical state directly from the current state. This paper instead learns a constraint function and obtains the next state by solving an optimization problem defined by that function. The approach draws on traditional simulation engines, which construct states by satisfying constraints.

A graph neural network implements the scalar constraint function. Separating the learned description of the system from the procedure used to find its next state creates useful flexibility at inference time. The authors show that applying more solver iterations can improve accuracy when simulating a larger system, allowing additional computation to refine the prediction.

The framework also accepts new hand-designed constraints at test time, enabling simulations of dynamics absent from the training data. Across a variety of challenging physical domains, it achieves accuracy comparable to or better than leading learned simulators. These results show how constraint solving can provide a useful inductive bias while making a learned simulator adaptable through both its solver and its constraints.
summary.tldr: A graph network learns physical constraints, letting an optimization solver produce accurate simulations and incorporate new constraints at test time.

title: Constraint-based graph network simulator

abstract: Artificial neural nets can represent and classify many types of high-dimensional data but are often tailored to particular applications – e.g., for “fair” or “hierarchical” classification. Once an architecture has been selected, it is often difficult for humans to adjust models for a new task; for example, a hierarchical classifier cannot be easily transformed into a fair classifier that shields a protected field. Our contribution in this work is a new neural network architecture, the concept subspace network (CSN), which generalizes existing specialized classifiers to produce a unified model capable of learning a spectrum of multi-concept relationships. We demonstrate that CSNs reproduce state-of-the-art results in fair classification when enforcing concept independence, may be transformed into hierarchical classifiers, or may even reconcile fairness and hierarchy within a single classifier. The CSN is inspired by and matches the performance of existing prototype-based classifiers that promote interpretability.

paragraphs: Neural classifiers are often designed around one particular relationship between concepts. A hierarchical classifier organizes concepts through a hierarchy, while a fairness-oriented classifier may seek to shield a protected field. Once a specialized architecture is chosen, changing the kind of relationship it should express can be difficult. This paper proposes a shared architecture for a broader range of relationships.

The concept subspace network, or CSN, generalizes existing specialized classifiers into a model that can learn multiple kinds of concept relationships. Its design draws on prototype-based classifiers that promote interpretability. The goal is to make the organization of concepts adjustable within one modeling framework, rather than tying the architecture to a single classification objective.

The authors demonstrate state-of-the-art fairness results when concept independence is enforced. They also show that CSNs can be transformed into hierarchical classifiers and can reconcile fairness and hierarchy within one classifier. Performance matches that of the prototype-based models inspiring the design. These findings support a unified approach to classification tasks whose concept relationships would otherwise motivate separate specialized architectures.
summary.tldr: Concept subspace networks unify prototype-based classification across fairness, hierarchy, and combinations of those concept relationships.

title: Prototype Based Classification from Hierarchy to Fairness

abstract: Due to the representation limitation of the joint Q value function, multi-agent reinforcement learning methods with linear value decomposition (LVD) or monotonic value decomposition (MVD) suffer from relative overgeneralization. As a result, they can not ensure optimal consistency (i.e., the correspondence between individual greedy actions and the best team performance). In this paper, we derive the expression of the joint Q value function of LVD and MVD. According to the expression, we draw a transition diagram, where each self-transition node (STN) is a possible convergence. To ensure the optimal consistency, the optimal node is required to be the unique STN. Therefore, we propose the greedy-based value representation (GVR), which turns the optimal node into an STN via inferior target shaping and eliminates the non-optimal STNs via superior experience replay. Theoretical proofs and empirical results demonstrate that given the true Q values, GVR ensures the optimal consistency under sufficient exploration. Besides, in tasks where the true Q values are unavailable, GVR achieves an adaptive trade-off between optimality and stability. Our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in experiments on various benchmarks.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent learning, agents may choose their individually highest-valued actions while still failing to achieve the best team outcome. The paper traces this problem to restrictions in linear and monotonic decompositions of the joint action-value function. These representations can suffer from relative overgeneralization and fail to align individual greedy choices with optimal coordination.

The authors derive expressions for these joint value functions and use a transition diagram to identify possible convergence points. Their proposed greedy-based value representation changes this structure in two ways. Inferior target shaping makes the optimal node a self-transition node, while superior experience replay removes non-optimal self-transition nodes, leaving the desired coordination outcome as the target.

The guarantee is conditional: with true Q values and sufficient exploration, GVR ensures correspondence between individual greedy actions and optimal team performance. When true values are unavailable, the method instead achieves an adaptive balance between optimality and stability. Experiments across several benchmarks report improvements over leading baselines, complementing the theoretical account of when optimal coordination is ensured.
summary.tldr: GVR reshapes value learning to support optimal team coordination, with a guarantee requiring true Q values and sufficient exploration.

title: Greedy based Value Representation for Optimal Coordination in Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We show that the input correlation matrix of typical classification datasets has an eigenspectrum where, after a sharp initial drop, a large number of small eigenvalues are distributed uniformly over an exponentially large range. This structure is mirrored in a network trained on this data: we show that the Hessian and the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) have eigenvalues that are spread uniformly over exponentially large ranges. We call such eigenspectra “sloppy” because sets of weights corresponding to small eigenvalues can be changed by large magnitudes without affecting the loss. Networks trained on atypical datasets with non-sloppy inputs do not share these traits and deep networks trained on such datasets generalize poorly. Inspired by this, we study the hypothesis that sloppiness of inputs aids generalization in deep networks. We show that if the Hessian is sloppy, we can compute non-vacuous PAC-Bayes generalization bounds analytically. By exploiting our empirical observation that training predominantly takes place in the non-sloppy subspace of the FIM, we develop data-distribution dependent PAC-Bayes priors that lead to accurate generalization bounds using numerical optimization.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether the structure of training data helps explain why deep networks generalize. In typical classification datasets, the authors find an input correlation spectrum with a sharp initial drop followed by many small eigenvalues spanning an exponentially large range. Similar patterns appear in the trained network’s Hessian and Fisher information matrix.

They call these spectra sloppy because weight changes associated with small eigenvalues can be large without materially changing the loss. Networks trained on atypical inputs without this spectral structure lack the same traits and generalize poorly in the reported observations. These findings motivate the hypothesis that input sloppiness aids generalization; the observations themselves are not presented as a universal causal proof.

The authors then connect this hypothesis to formal generalization analysis. If the Hessian is sloppy, they can analytically obtain non-vacuous PAC-Bayes bounds. They also use the empirical observation that training mainly occurs in the Fisher matrix’s non-sloppy subspace to construct data-dependent priors. Numerical optimization with those priors yields accurate generalization bounds.
summary.tldr: Observed spectral structure in data and trained networks motivates a generalization hypothesis and enables informative PAC-Bayes bounds under stated conditions.

title: Does the Data Induce Capacity Control in Deep Learning?

abstract: Most existing methods in vision language pre-training rely on object-centric features extracted through object detection and make fine-grained alignments between the extracted features and texts. It is challenging for these methods to learn relations among multiple objects. To this end, we propose a new method called X-VLM to perform ‘multi-grained vision language pre-training.’ The key to learning multi-grained alignments is to locate visual concepts in the image given the associated texts, and in the meantime align the texts with the visual concepts, where the alignments are in multi-granularity. Experimental results show that X-VLM effectively leverages the learned multi-grained alignments to many downstream vision language tasks and consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Vision-language pretraining teaches a model to connect text with image content. Many existing methods use features extracted by object detectors and align those features with text. The paper identifies a difficulty with this object-centered approach: learning relationships involving multiple objects can be challenging when the representation is organized around individual detected objects.

X-VLM addresses this through alignments at multiple levels of granularity. Given associated text, the model learns to locate the corresponding visual concepts in an image while also aligning those concepts with the text. Localization and alignment therefore work together, giving pretraining a way to connect language with visual content at more than one level.

Experiments show that the learned alignments transfer effectively to multiple downstream vision-language tasks. X-VLM consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluation. The findings support multi-grained alignment as a useful pretraining strategy: matching text to visual concepts at different granularities provides representations that can serve several subsequent tasks, rather than being useful only for the pretraining exercise.
summary.tldr: X-VLM jointly learns to locate visual concepts and align them with text at multiple granularities, improving downstream vision-language performance.

title: Multi-Grained Vision Language Pre-Training: Aligning Texts with Visual Concepts

abstract: End-to-end (E2E) speech-to-text translation (ST) often depends on pretraining its encoder and/or decoder using source transcripts via speech recognition or text translation tasks, without which translation performance drops substantially. However, transcripts are not always available, and how significant such pretraining is for E2E ST has rarely been studied in the literature. In this paper, we revisit this question and explore the extent to which the quality of E2E ST trained on speech-translation pairs alone can be improved. We reexamine several techniques proven beneficial to ST previously, and offer a set of best practices that biases a Transformer-based E2E ST system toward training from scratch. Besides, we propose parameterized distance penalty to facilitate the modeling of locality in the self-attention model for speech. On four benchmarks covering 23 languages, our experiments show that, without using any transcripts or pretraining, the proposed system reaches and even outperforms previous studies adopting pretraining, although the gap remains in (extremely) low-resource settings. Finally, we discuss neural acoustic feature modeling, where a neural model is designed to extract acoustic features from raw speech signals directly, with the goal to simplify inductive biases and add freedom to the model in describing speech. For the first time, we demonstrate its feasibility and show encouraging results on ST tasks.

paragraphs: End-to-end speech translation often relies on pretraining with source-language transcripts, but those transcripts are not always available. This paper investigates how well a system can learn directly from paired speech and translations. It revisits previously useful techniques and assembles practices that favor training a Transformer-based translation system from scratch.

The authors also introduce a parameterized distance penalty to help speech self-attention model local relationships. This supplies an adjustable preference for locality within the attention mechanism. Alongside the training practices, it forms a system designed to learn without transcript-based speech-recognition or text-translation pretraining.

Across four benchmarks covering 23 languages, the system matches or exceeds previous pretrained approaches without using transcripts or pretraining. A gap remains in extremely low-resource settings, so the results do not eliminate the value of pretraining under all data conditions. The paper additionally demonstrates the feasibility of learning acoustic features directly from raw speech with a neural model, reporting encouraging translation results from that direction.
summary.tldr: Training practices and a learned locality penalty enable competitive speech translation from paired speech and translations alone, though very low-resource gaps remain.

title: Revisiting End-to-End Speech-to-Text Translation From Scratch

abstract: Despite the success of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in approximating partial differential equations (PDEs), PINNs can sometimes fail to converge to the correct solution in problems involving complicated PDEs. This is reflected in several recent studies on characterizing the "failure modes" of PINNs, although a thorough understanding of the connection between PINN failure modes and sampling strategies is missing. In this paper, we provide a novel perspective of failure modes of PINNs by hypothesizing that training PINNs relies on successful "propagation" of solution from initial and/or boundary condition points to interior points. We show that PINNs with poor sampling strategies can get stuck at trivial solutions if there are propagation failures, characterized by highly imbalanced PDE residual fields. To mitigate propagation failures, we propose a novel Retain-Resample-Release sampling (R3) algorithm that can incrementally accumulate collocation points in regions of high PDE residuals with little to no computational overhead. We provide an extension of R3 sampling to respect the principle of causality while solving time-dependent PDEs. We theoretically analyze the behavior of R3 sampling and empirically demonstrate its efficacy and efficiency in comparison with baselines on a variety of PDE problems.

paragraphs: Physics-informed neural networks approximate solutions to partial differential equations, but they can converge to incorrect, trivial solutions. This paper examines how the points sampled during training contribute to such failures. The authors hypothesize that successful learning depends on propagating solution information from initial or boundary conditions into the interior of the domain.

They show that poor sampling can accompany propagation failures characterized by strongly imbalanced equation residuals, which measure how much the predicted solution violates the equation. Their Retain-Resample-Release algorithm, or R3, incrementally accumulates collocation points in regions with high residuals. This directs training attention toward regions where satisfying the equation remains difficult, with little or no computational overhead.

The paper also extends R3 to respect causality in time-dependent equations. The authors theoretically analyze its behavior and compare its effectiveness and efficiency with baselines across several PDE problems. The contribution links a proposed explanation of training failure to an actionable sampling strategy, with both analysis and empirical evidence supporting the strategy’s ability to mitigate those failures.
summary.tldr: R3 sampling concentrates training points in high-residual regions to mitigate propagation failures in physics-informed neural networks.

title: Mitigating Propagation Failures in Physics-informed Neural Networks using Retain-Resample-Release (R3) Sampling

abstract: Deep Q-learning based algorithms have been applied successfully in many decision making problems, while their theoretical foundations are not as well understood. In this paper, we study a Fitted Q-Iteration with two-layer ReLU neural network parameterization, and find the sample complexity guarantees for the algorithm. Our approach estimates the Q-function in each iteration using a convex optimization problem. We show that this approach achieves a sample complexity of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(1/\epsilon^{2})$, which is order-optimal. This result holds for a countable state-spaces and does not require any assumptions such as a linear or low rank structure on the MDP.

paragraphs: Deep Q-learning methods have succeeded in decision-making applications, but their theoretical behavior is less well understood. This paper studies fitted Q-iteration with a two-layer ReLU neural network representing the Q-function. The Q-function describes the value of taking an action in a state, so learning it is central to choosing useful actions.

The proposed approach estimates that function at each iteration through a convex optimization problem. The authors analyze how many samples the resulting algorithm needs to reach a desired accuracy. They obtain a sample complexity proportional to the inverse square of the error tolerance, up to logarithmic factors, and establish that this rate is order-optimal.

The stated result applies to countable state spaces and does not require a linear or low-rank structure for the underlying Markov decision process. That scope matters because the guarantee does not depend on imposing either of those structural simplifications. The contribution is a sample-efficiency guarantee for the particular fitted Q-iteration approach studied, connecting neural function representation with a convex estimation procedure.
summary.tldr: A convex-estimation version of fitted Q-iteration with two-layer ReLU networks achieves an order-optimal sample-complexity guarantee.

title: On the Global Convergence of Fitted Q-Iteration with Two-layer Neural Network Parametrization

abstract: Dirichlet Process mixture models (DPMM) in combination with Gaussian kernels have been an important modeling tool for numerous data domains arising from biological, physical, and social sciences. However, this versatility in applications does not extend to strong theoretical guarantees for the underlying parameter estimates, for which only a logarithmic rate is achieved. In this work, we (re)introduce and investigate a metric, named Orlicz-Wasserstein distance, in the study of the Bayesian contraction behavior for the parameters. We show that despite the overall slow convergence guarantees for all the parameters, posterior contraction for parameters happens at almost polynomial rates in outlier regions of the parameter space. Our theoretical results provide new insight in understanding the convergence behavior of parameters arising from various settings of hierarchical Bayesian nonparametric models. In addition, we provide an algorithm to compute the metric by leveraging Sinkhorn divergences and validate our findings through a simulation study.

We show that despite the overall slow convergence guarantees for all the parameters, posterior contraction for parameters happens at almost polynomial rates in outlier regions of the parameter space. Our theoretical results provide new insight in understanding the convergence behavior of parameters arising from various settings of hierarchical Bayesian nonparametric models. In addition, we provide an algorithm to compute the metric by leveraging Sinkhorn divergences and validate our findings through a simulation study.

paragraphs: Gaussian Dirichlet process mixture models are widely useful, but theoretical guarantees for estimating their underlying parameters can converge only at a logarithmic rate. This paper examines whether that slow overall guarantee hides more favorable behavior in particular regions of parameter space. The focus is on how the posterior concentrates around parameter values as information accumulates.

The authors investigate this behavior using Orlicz-Wasserstein distance, a metric they reintroduce into the analysis of Bayesian parameter contraction. They show that posterior contraction in outlier regions can occur at almost polynomial rates, despite the slow guarantee covering all parameters together. The result therefore distinguishes regional behavior from the aggregate convergence picture.

This distinction provides insight into parameter estimation in hierarchical Bayesian nonparametric models: a weak global rate need not describe every part of the parameter space equally well. The paper also develops an algorithm for computing the metric using Sinkhorn divergences and validates its findings in simulations. Its contribution combines a more revealing theoretical measurement of convergence with a way to calculate that measurement.
summary.tldr: Orlicz-Wasserstein analysis reveals almost polynomial posterior contraction in outlier regions despite slow overall parameter-convergence guarantees.

title: On Excess Mass Behavior in Gaussian Mixture Models with Orlicz-Wasserstein Distances

abstract: Antibody design is an essential yet challenging task in various domains like therapeutics and biology. There are two major defects in current learning-based methods: 1) tackling only a certain subtask of the whole antibody design pipeline, making them suboptimal or resource-intensive. 2) omitting either the framework regions or side chains, thus incapable of capturing the full-atom geometry. To address these pitfalls, we propose dynamic Multi-channel Equivariant grAph Network (dyMEAN), an end-to-end full-atom model for E(3)-equivariant antibody design given the epitope and the incomplete sequence of the antibody. Specifically, we first explore structural initialization as a knowledgeable guess of the antibody structure and then propose shadow paratope to bridge the epitope-antibody connections. Both 1D sequences and 3D structures are updated via an adaptive multi-channel equivariant encoder that is able to process protein residues of variable sizes when considering full atoms. Finally, the updated antibody is docked to the epitope via the alignment of the shadow paratope. Experiments on epitope-binding CDR-H3 design, complex structure prediction, and affinity optimization demonstrate the superiority of our end-to-end framework and full-atom modeling.

title: End-to-End Full-Atom Antibody Design

abstract: Federated learning has exhibited vulnerabilities to Byzantine attacks, where the Byzantine attackers can send arbitrary gradients to a central server to destroy the convergence and performance of the global model. A wealth of robust AGgregation Rules (AGRs) have been proposed to defend against Byzantine attacks. However, Byzantine clients can still circumvent robust AGRs when data is non-Identically and Independently Distributed (non-IID). In this paper, we first reveal the root causes of performance degradation of current robust AGRs in non-IID settings: the curse of dimensionality and gradient heterogeneity. In order to address this issue, we propose GAS, a GrAdient Splitting approach that can successfully adapt existing robust AGRs to non-IID settings. We also provide a detailed convergence analysis when the existing robust AGRs are combined with GAS. Experiments on various real-world datasets verify the efficacy of our proposed GAS. The implementation code is provided in https://github.com/YuchenLiu-a/byzantine-gas.

paragraphs: Federated learning combines model updates from multiple clients at a central server. Byzantine attackers can submit arbitrary gradients to disrupt this process. Robust aggregation rules attempt to defend against those updates, but the paper examines why these defenses can still fail when clients hold differently distributed data.

The authors identify two causes of degraded performance in this heterogeneous setting: high dimensionality and variation among client gradients. This matters because the server must aggregate updates in a setting where legitimate clients already produce different signals. The proposed GAS method uses gradient splitting to adapt existing robust aggregation rules to these non-IID conditions, extending the usefulness of defenses that are already available.

The paper provides a convergence analysis for combinations of GAS and existing robust aggregation rules. Experiments on several real-world datasets also support the method’s effectiveness. Together, the analysis and experiments address both the behavior of the resulting learning process and whether the adaptation helps in evaluated heterogeneous-data settings.
summary.tldr: GAS uses gradient splitting to adapt existing Byzantine-robust aggregation rules to clients with heterogeneous data.

title: Byzantine-Robust Learning on Heterogeneous Data via Gradient Splitting

abstract: We present a representation-driven framework for reinforcement learning. By representing policies as estimates of their expected values, we leverage techniques from contextual bandits to guide exploration and exploitation. Particularly, embedding a policy network into a linear feature space allows us to reframe the exploration-exploitation problem as a representation-exploitation problem, where good policy representations enable optimal exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through its application to evolutionary and policy gradient-based approaches, leading to significantly improved performance compared to traditional methods. Our framework provides a new perspective on reinforcement learning, highlighting the importance of policy representation in determining optimal exploration-exploitation strategies.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through its application to evolutionary and policy gradient-based approaches, leading to significantly improved performance compared to traditional methods. Our framework provides a new perspective on reinforcement learning, highlighting the importance of policy representation in determining optimal exploration-exploitation strategies.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning must balance trying uncertain policies with using policies already expected to perform well. This paper approaches that choice through how policies are represented. It represents policies in terms of estimates of their expected values, making techniques from contextual bandits available for guiding exploration and exploitation.

The framework embeds a policy network in a linear feature space. This shifts the emphasis toward learning a representation that makes policy value useful for choosing what to try next. In the paper’s formulation, good policy representations enable optimal exploration, so representation quality becomes central to the exploration strategy rather than merely a supporting modeling decision.

The authors apply the framework to both evolutionary methods and policy-gradient approaches. They report significantly improved performance compared with traditional methods, supporting its usefulness across these two kinds of optimization. The stated findings suggest that improving how candidate policies are described and valued can improve the decisions made during learning. The framework’s broader contribution is to make policy representation an explicit part of the exploration-exploitation problem.
summary.tldr: The framework uses value-oriented policy representations and contextual-bandit techniques to improve exploration in evolutionary and policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

title: Representation-Driven Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite the great interest in the bandit problem, designing efficient algorithms for complex models remains challenging, as there is typically no analytical way to quantify uncertainty. In this paper, we propose Multiplier Bootstrap-based Exploration (MBE), a novel exploration strategy that is applicable to any reward model amenable to weighted loss minimization. We prove both instance-dependent and instance-independent rate-optimal regret bounds for MBE in sub-Gaussian multi-armed bandits. With extensive simulation and real-data experiments, we show the generality and adaptivity of MBE.

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms must decide when to choose an apparently rewarding option and when to gather more information. For complex reward models, that exploration decision is difficult because uncertainty often has no convenient analytical expression. This paper introduces Multiplier Bootstrap-based Exploration, or MBE, as a broadly applicable exploration strategy.

Its stated requirement is that the reward model can be trained by minimizing a weighted loss. That gives the method a concrete compatibility criterion and avoids tying its applicability to a particular analytical uncertainty formula. The contribution is therefore relevant to models for which fitting is available even when a direct uncertainty calculation is difficult.

The authors prove rate-optimal regret bounds for sub-Gaussian multi-armed bandits, both for bounds that depend on the particular problem instance and for bounds that do not. These theoretical guarantees apply to that specified bandit setting. Extensive simulations and real-data experiments additionally demonstrate the method’s generality and adaptivity. The paper combines a flexible interface for reward modeling with optimal-rate theory in a defined setting and broader empirical evidence.
summary.tldr: MBE supports exploration with reward models trained by weighted loss minimization and achieves optimal regret rates in sub-Gaussian multi-armed bandits.

title: Multiplier Bootstrap-based Exploration

abstract: Spurious correlations that degrade model generalization or lead the model to be right for the wrong reasons are one of the main robustness concerns for real-world deployments. However, mitigating these correlations during pre-training for large-scale models can be costly and impractical, particularly for those without access to high-performance computing resources. This paper proposes a novel approach to address spurious correlations during fine-tuning for a given domain of interest. With a focus on multi-modal models (e.g., CLIP), the proposed method leverages different modalities in these models to detect and explicitly set apart spurious attributes from the affected class, achieved through a multi-modal contrastive loss function that expresses spurious relationships through language. Our experimental results and in-depth visualizations on CLIP show that such an intervention can effectively i) improve the model’s accuracy when spurious attributes are not present, and ii) directs the model’s activation maps towards the actual class rather than the spurious attribute when present. In particular, on the Waterbirds dataset, our algorithm achieved a worst-group accuracy 23% higher than ERM on CLIP with a ResNet-50 backbone, and 32% higher on CLIP with a ViT backbone, while maintaining the same average accuracy as ERM.

These spurious relationships can undermine generalization. This paper addresses them during domain-specific fine-tuning, avoiding the cost and practical difficulty of intervening during large-scale pre-training.

The method uses the model's different modalities to detect spurious attributes and explicitly separate them from the affected class. A multimodal contrastive loss expresses the problematic relationships through language. These findings show that fine-tuning can improve performance for poorly served groups without reducing average performance in this evaluation.
summary.tldr: Language-guided contrastive fine-tuning reduces CLIP's reliance on spurious attributes and improves worst-group accuracy in the reported evaluation.

title: Mitigating Spurious Correlations in Multi-modal Models during Fine-tuning

abstract: The mission of active learning is to identify the most valuable data samples, thus attaining decent performance with much fewer samples. The data augmentation techniques seem straightforward yet promising to enhance active learning by extending the exploration of the input space, which helps locate more valuable samples. In this work, we thoroughly study the coupling of data augmentation and active learning, thereby proposing Controllable Augmentation ManiPulator for Active Learning. In contrast to the few prior works that touched on this line, CAMPAL emphasizes a purposeful, tighten, and better-controlled integration of data augmentation into active learning in three folds: (i)-carefully designed augmentation policies applied separately on labeled and unlabeled data pools; (ii)-controlled and quantifiably optimizable augmentation strengths; (iii)-full and flexible coverage for most (if not all) active learning schemes. Theories are proposed and associated with the development of key components in CAMPAL. Through extensive empirical experiments, we bring the performance of active learning methods to a new level: an absolute performance boost of 16.99% on CIFAR-10 and 12.25 on SVHN with 1,000 annotated samples. Codes are available at https://github.com/jnzju/CAMPAL.

paragraphs: Active learning seeks the most valuable examples to label so that a model can learn effectively from fewer annotations. Data augmentation can broaden exploration of the input space and help identify useful examples. This paper studies how to combine the two through a controlled framework called CAMPAL.

CAMPAL separates augmentation policies for the labeled and unlabeled data pools, making their treatment purposeful rather than uniform. It also provides controlled augmentation strengths that can be quantitatively optimized. The framework is designed to accommodate a broad range of active-learning schemes, and theoretical developments inform its key components. Together, these choices make augmentation an adjustable part of the selection process.

Extensive experiments report improved performance for active-learning methods, including an absolute boost of 16.99% on CIFAR-10 with 1,000 annotated samples and additional gains on SVHN. The findings support careful coordination between augmentation and active learning: choosing where and how strongly to augment can improve the value extracted from a limited annotation budget.
summary.tldr: CAMPAL improves active learning through separate augmentation policies and optimizable augmentation strengths for labeled and unlabeled data.

title: Towards Controlled Data Augmentations for Active Learning

abstract: Dense contrastive learning (DCL) has been recently explored for learning localized information for dense prediction tasks (e.g., detection and segmentation). It still suffers the difficulty of mining pixels/patches correspondence between two views. A simple way is inputting the same view twice and aligning the pixel/patch representation. However, it would reduce the variance of inputs, and hurts the performance. We propose a plug-in method PQCL (Positional Query for patch-level Contrastive Learning), which allows performing patch-level contrasts between two views with exact patch correspondence. Besides, by using positional queries, PQCL increases the variance of inputs, to enhance training. We apply PQCL to popular transformer-based CL frameworks (DINO and iBOT, and evaluate them on classification, detection and segmentation tasks, where our method obtains stable improvements, especially for dense tasks. It achieves new state-of-the-art in most settings. Code is available at https://github.com/Sherrylone/Query_Contrastive.

paragraphs: Dense visual tasks such as detection and segmentation need representations that preserve localized information. Contrastive learning at the pixel or patch level can support this, but matching corresponding locations across two views is difficult. Feeding the same view twice simplifies alignment, yet reduces input variation and can hurt learning performance.

The paper proposes Positional Query for patch-level Contrastive Learning, or PQCL, as a plug-in method. Positional queries enable patch-level comparisons between two views with exact correspondence. They also increase input variation to strengthen training. The method therefore addresses both the matching problem and the reduced diversity associated with simply repeating an identical view.

The authors apply PQCL to the transformer-based DINO and iBOT frameworks and evaluate classification, detection, and segmentation. They report consistent improvements, particularly for dense prediction, and state-of-the-art results in most evaluated settings. These findings support the value of combining reliable patch correspondence with varied inputs when pretraining visual representations, especially when later tasks depend on understanding specific parts of an image.
summary.tldr: PQCL uses positional queries to combine exact patch correspondence with varied inputs, improving visual pretraining in the reported evaluations.

title: Patch-level Contrastive Learning via Positional Query for Visual Pre-training

abstract: Exploration is a major challenge in reinforcement learning, especially for high-dimensional domains that require function approximation. We propose exploration objectives—policy optimization objectives that enable downstream maximization of any reward function—as a conceptual framework to systematize the study of exploration. We introduce a new objective, L1-Coverage, which generalizes previous exploration schemes and supports three fundamental desiderata: 1. Intrinsic complexity control. L1-Coverage is associated with a structural parameter, L1-Coverability, which reflects the intrinsic statistical difficulty of the underlying MDP, subsuming Block and Low-Rank MDPs. 2. Efficient planning. For a known MDP, L1-Coverage efficiently reduces to standard policy optimization, allowing flexible integration with off-the-shelf methods such as policy gradient and Q-learning approaches. 3. Efficient exploration. L1-Coverage enables the first computationally efficient model-based and model-free algorithms for online (reward-free or reward-driven) reinforcement learning in MDPs with low coverability. Empirically, we find that L1-Coverage effectively drives off-the-shelf policy optimization algorithms to explore the state space.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult in reinforcement learning when high-dimensional environments require function approximation. The paper proposes studying exploration through policy objectives designed to support later maximization of any reward function. Its new objective, L1-Coverage, provides a common framework for several previous exploration schemes.

The objective is associated with L1-Coverability, a structural quantity that captures intrinsic statistical difficulty in the underlying Markov decision process. The framework encompasses Block and Low-Rank MDPs. When the environment model is known, optimizing coverage efficiently reduces to standard policy optimization, allowing the use of established tools such as policy gradients and Q-learning.

For MDPs with low coverability, the authors obtain computationally efficient model-based and model-free online learning algorithms, covering both reward-free and reward-driven exploration. Experiments also find that L1-Coverage encourages existing policy optimization methods to explore the state space effectively. The contribution links an exploration objective, a structural measure of problem difficulty, and usable optimization machinery, with the efficiency results tied to the stated coverability condition.
summary.tldr: L1-Coverage connects exploration to standard policy optimization and enables efficient online reinforcement learning in environments with low coverability.

title: Scalable Online Exploration via Coverability

abstract: We initiate the study of the submodular cover problem in a dynamic setting where the elements of the ground set are inserted and deleted. In the classical submodular cover problem, we are given a monotone submodular function $f : 2^{V} \to \mathbb{R}^{\ge 0}$ and the goal is to obtain a set $S \subseteq V$ that minimizes the cost subject to the constraint $f(S) = f(V)$. This is a classical problem in computer science and generalizes the Set Cover problem, 2-Set Cover, and dominating set problem among others. We consider this problem in a dynamic setting where there are updates to our set $V$, in the form of insertions and deletions of elements from a ground set $\mathcal{V}$, and the goal is to maintain an approximately optimal solution with low query complexity per update. For this problem, we propose a randomized algorithm that, in expectation, obtains a $(1-O(\epsilon), O(\epsilon^{-1}))$-bicriteria approximation using polylogarithmic query complexity per update.

This is a classical problem in computer science and generalizes the Set Cover problem, 2-Set Cover, and dominating set problem among others. We consider this problem in a dynamic setting where there are updates to our set $V$, in the form of insertions and deletions of elements from a ground set $\mathcal{V}$, and the goal is to maintain an approximately optimal solution with low query complexity per update. paragraphs: The paper studies how to maintain a low-cost covering solution when available elements keep changing. In the classical problem, a monotone submodular function measures what a chosen set achieves, and the goal is to match the value of the entire available set at minimum cost. This formulation includes familiar problems such as set cover and dominating set.

The dynamic version allows elements to enter or leave the available set. An algorithm must therefore adjust its solution as the target and available choices change. The authors propose a randomized algorithm designed to maintain an approximately optimal solution while making relatively few queries after each update.

Its guarantee trades off coverage and cost: in expectation, it achieves a 1−O(ε) fraction of the target value with an O(1/ε) cost approximation. The number of queries per update is polylogarithmic. Thus, the contribution is an efficient maintenance guarantee that permits a controlled coverage shortfall, rather than requiring exact full coverage after every change.
summary.tldr: A randomized algorithm maintains approximately optimal submodular covers under insertions and deletions with polylogarithmic query complexity per update.

title: A Dynamic Algorithm for Weighted Submodular Cover Problem

abstract: We study $L_2$ mean estimation under central differential privacy and communication constraints, and address two key challenges: firstly, existing mean estimation schemes that simultaneously handle both constraints are usually optimized for $L_\infty$ geometry and rely on random rotation or Kashin’s representation to adapt to $L_2$ geometry, resulting in suboptimal leading constants in mean square errors (MSEs); secondly, schemes achieving order-optimal communication-privacy trade-offs do not extend seamlessly to streaming differential privacy (DP) settings (e.g., tree aggregation or matrix factorization), rendering them incompatible with DP-FTRL type optimizers. In this work, we tackle these issues by introducing a novel privacy accounting method for the sparsified Gaussian mechanism that incorporates the randomness inherent in sparsification into the DP noise. Unlike previous approaches, our accounting algorithm directly operates in $L_2$ geometry, yielding MSEs that fast converge to those of the uncompressed Gaussian mechanism. Additionally, we extend the sparsification scheme to the matrix factorization framework under streaming DP and provide a precise accountant tailored for DP-FTRL type optimizers. Empirically, our method demonstrates at least a 100x improvement of compression for DP-SGD across various FL tasks.

paragraphs: Estimating an average privately becomes harder when communication must also be compressed. Existing approaches often start from a different geometric setting and adapt to L2 geometry, which can worsen the leading constants in mean squared error. Methods with favorable communication-privacy trade-offs can also be difficult to use in streaming privacy systems.

The paper introduces privacy accounting for a sparsified Gaussian mechanism that incorporates randomness from sparsification into the privacy noise calculation. It works directly in L2 geometry, with errors that rapidly approach those of the uncompressed Gaussian mechanism. This ties the privacy analysis to the compression procedure rather than treating compression randomness as irrelevant to privacy.

The authors extend the scheme to matrix-factorization methods for streaming differential privacy and provide an accountant for DP-FTRL optimizers. Empirically, they report at least a hundredfold improvement in compression for DP-SGD across several federated learning tasks. The work therefore addresses both estimation accuracy under communication constraints and compatibility with privacy mechanisms that accumulate information over time.
summary.tldr: A new privacy accountant incorporates sparsification randomness to improve compressed private mean estimation and support streaming privacy optimizers.

title: Improved Communication-Privacy Trade-offs in $L_2$ Mean Estimation under Streaming Differential Privacy

abstract: Deep neural networks are over-parameterized and easily overfit to and memorize the datasets that they train on. In the extreme case, it has been shown that networks can memorize a randomly labeled dataset. In this paper, we propose using the curvature of the loss function around each training sample, averaged over training epochs, as a measure of memorization of a sample. We show that this curvature metric effectively captures memorization statistics, both qualitatively and quantitatively in popular image datasets. We provide quantitative validation of the proposed metric against memorization scores released by Feldman & Zhang (2020). Further, experiments on mislabeled data detection show that corrupted samples are learned with high curvature and using curvature for identifying mislabelled examples outperforms existing approaches. Qualitatively, we find that high curvature samples correspond to long-tailed, mislabeled, or conflicting instances, indicating a likelihood of memorization. Notably, this analysis helps us find, to the best of our knowledge, a novel failure mode on the CIFAR100 and ImageNet datasets: that of duplicated images with differing labels.

Notably, this analysis helps us find, to the best of our knowledge, a novel failure mode on the CIFAR100 and ImageNet datasets: that of duplicated images with differing labels.

paragraphs: Neural networks can memorize training examples, including datasets with random labels. This paper proposes measuring memorization at the level of individual samples using the curvature of the loss function around each example. Averaging that curvature over training epochs produces a score that reflects the sample's behavior throughout learning.

The authors test whether this score captures known memorization patterns on popular image datasets. They report both qualitative and quantitative agreement, including validation against previously released memorization scores. This connects a property of the local loss geometry to an independently measured tendency to memorize particular examples.

Experiments also show that corrupted labels are learned with high curvature, and curvature-based detection outperforms existing approaches for finding mislabeled examples. Qualitative inspection associates high-curvature samples with rare, mislabeled, or conflicting instances, indicating a likelihood of memorization rather than making every such sample a definitive case. The analysis additionally uncovers duplicated images carrying different labels in CIFAR100 and ImageNet, linking the proposed measure to a concrete dataset problem.
summary.tldr: Average loss curvature around training samples provides an empirical signal of memorization and helps identify mislabeled or conflicting images.

title: Memorization Through the Lens of Curvature of Loss Function Around Samples

abstract: Training large transformers is slow, but recent innovations on GPU architecture give us an advantage. NVIDIA Ampere GPUs can execute a fine-grained 2:4 sparse matrix multiplication twice as fast as its dense equivalent. In the light of this property, we comprehensively investigate the feasibility of accelerating feed-forward networks (FFNs) of transformers in pre-training. First, we define a “flip rate” to monitor the stability of a 2:4 training process. Utilizing this metric, we propose three techniques to preserve accuracy: to modify the sparse-refined straight-through estimator by applying the masked decay term on gradients, to determine a feasible decay factor in warm-up stage, and to enhance the model’s quality by a dense fine-tuning procedure near the end of pre-training. Besides, we devise two techniques to practically accelerate training: to calculate transposable 2:4 masks by convolution, and to accelerate gated activation functions by reducing GPU L2 cache miss. Experiments show that our 2:4 sparse training algorithm achieves similar convergence to dense training algorithms on several transformer pre-training tasks, while actual acceleration can be observed on different shapes of transformer block apparently. Our toolkit is available at https://github.com/huyz2023/2by4-pretrain.

title: Accelerating Transformer Pre-training with 2:4 Sparsity

abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) aims to transfer knowledge from larger (teacher) to smaller (student) networks. Previous studies focus on point-to-point or pairwise relationships in embedding features as knowledge and struggle to efficiently transfer relationships of complex latent spaces. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel KD method called TopKD, which considers the global topology of the latent spaces. We define global topology knowledge using the persistence diagram (PD) that captures comprehensive geometric structures such as shape of distribution, multiscale structure and connectivity, and the topology distillation loss for teaching this knowledge. To make the PD transferable within reasonable computational time, we employ approximated persistence images of PDs. Through experiments, we support the benefits of using global topology as knowledge and demonstrate the potential of TopKD. Code is available at https://github.com/jekim5418/TopKD

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a larger teacher network to a smaller student. Many approaches match individual feature representations or relationships between pairs of them. TopKD asks whether the broader organization of a network’s latent space also provides useful knowledge, particularly when that space has complex structure.

The method describes this global organization using persistence diagrams. These capture geometric characteristics such as distribution shape, connectivity, and structure at multiple scales. TopKD introduces a topology distillation loss to teach the student this information. The intended transfer therefore includes how representations are organized collectively, beyond the individual points or pairs emphasized by earlier methods.

Computing and transferring this information must also be practical. The authors use approximated persistence images of the diagrams to keep the transfer within reasonable computational time. Their experiments support the benefits of global topology as a source of knowledge and demonstrate the potential of TopKD. The findings make an empirical case for including broader latent-space structure in distillation, without claiming that topology is always the best information to transfer.
summary.tldr: TopKD transfers global latent-space structure from teacher to student using a topology-based loss and computationally practical approximations.

title: Do Topological Characteristics Help in Knowledge Distillation?

abstract: Inner product-based decoders are among the most influential frameworks used to extract meaningful data from latent embeddings. However, such decoders have shown limitations in representation capacity in numerous works within the literature, which have been particularly notable in graph reconstruction problems. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical elucidation of this pervasive phenomenon in graph data, and suggest straightforward modifications to circumvent this issue without deviating from the inner product framework.

paragraphs: Graph reconstruction requires turning latent embeddings into information about a graph. Inner-product decoders are a widely used framework for this step, but previous work has repeatedly observed limits in what they can represent. This paper focuses on explaining those limits theoretically, with sign rank providing the perspective identified in its title.

The central contribution is a theoretical account of a phenomenon that had already appeared across the literature. A representation-capacity question concerns which graph information the decoder can express through its chosen form. Establishing a mathematical explanation makes the decoder's structure a concrete part of understanding why graph reconstruction can be limited.

The authors also suggest straightforward modifications intended to circumvent the identified issue while retaining the inner-product framework. This gives the work both an explanatory and a design-oriented role: it connects observed reconstruction limitations to theory and points toward changes within the same broad family of decoders. The stated contribution concerns graph representation capacity and modifications to the decoding framework.
summary.tldr: The paper theoretically explains representation limits of inner-product graph decoders and proposes modifications that retain the inner-product framework.

title: Sign Rank Limitations for Inner Product Graph Decoders

abstract: Understanding and explaining the predictions of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), is crucial for enhancing their safety and trustworthiness. Subgraph-level explanations are gaining attention for their intuitive appeal. However, most existing subgraph-level explainers face efficiency challenges in explaining GNNs due to complex search processes. The key challenge is to find a balance between intuitiveness and efficiency while ensuring transparency. Additionally, these explainers usually induce subgraphs by nodes, which may introduce less-intuitive disconnected nodes in the subgraph-level explanations or omit many important subgraph structures. In this paper, we reveal that inducing subgraph explanations by edges is more comprehensive than other subgraph inducing techniques. We also emphasize the need of determining the subgraph explanation size for each data instance, as different data instances may involve different important substructures. Building upon these considerations, we introduce a training-free approach, named EiG-Search. We employ an efficient linear-time search algorithm over the edge-induced subgraphs, where the edges are ranked by an enhanced gradient-based importance. We conduct extensive experiments on a total of seven datasets, demonstrating its superior performance and efficiency both quantitatively and qualitatively over the leading baselines.

paragraphs: Explaining a graph neural network often involves identifying a smaller subgraph that helps account for its prediction. Searching for that subgraph can be expensive, and the way it is constructed affects which explanations are possible. This paper argues that selecting nodes can produce unintuitive disconnected nodes or miss important structures that a different construction would capture.

EiG-Search instead constructs explanations through selected edges. The authors find this approach more comprehensive than other subgraph-inducing techniques. They also emphasize choosing the explanation size separately for each instance, because different graphs can depend on important structures of different sizes. This avoids making a single explanation size the organizing principle for every prediction.

The method requires no explainer training. It ranks edges using an enhanced gradient-based importance measure and searches the edge-induced subgraphs in linear time. Experiments across seven datasets report stronger performance and efficiency than leading baselines, supported by quantitative and qualitative comparisons. The contribution combines a broader choice of explanatory structures with an efficient way to search for them.
summary.tldr: EiG-Search produces instance-specific graph explanations through a training-free, linear-time search over edge-induced subgraphs.

title: EiG-Search: Generating Edge-Induced Subgraphs for GNN Explanation in Linear Time

abstract: We present NeWRF, a novel deep-learning-based framework for predicting wireless channels. Wireless channel prediction is a long-standing problem in the wireless community and is a key technology for improving the coverage of wireless network deployments. Today, a wireless deployment is evaluated by a site survey which is a cumbersome process requiring an experienced engineer to perform extensive channel measurements. To reduce the cost of site surveys, we develop NeWRF, which is based on recent advances in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF). NeWRF trains a neural network model with a sparse set of channel measurements, and predicts the wireless channel accurately at any location in the site. We introduce a series of techniques that integrate wireless propagation properties into the NeRF framework to account for the fundamental differences between the behavior of light and wireless signals. We conduct extensive evaluations of our framework and show that our approach can accurately predict channels at unvisited locations with significantly lower measurement density than prior state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: NeWRF aims to reduce the measurement work needed to understand wireless coverage at a site. Conventional site surveys require an experienced engineer to collect extensive channel measurements. The paper instead trains a neural model from a sparse set of measurements and uses it to predict wireless channels at locations that have not been visited.

The framework builds on Neural Radiance Fields, an approach originally associated with modeling light. Transferring that idea to wireless prediction requires accounting for differences between optical and wireless propagation. NeWRF introduces techniques that incorporate wireless propagation properties into the framework, making those physical differences part of the model design.

The authors report that extensive evaluations show accurate channel prediction at unmeasured locations with substantially lower measurement density than prior state-of-the-art approaches. This makes the main practical contribution a reduction in the observations needed to reconstruct a site’s wireless field. The results support the potential to make site assessment less costly while retaining useful predictions for locations beyond the measurement set.
summary.tldr: NeWRF adapts neural field modeling to wireless propagation, predicting unmeasured channels from sparse site measurements.

title: NeWRF: A Deep Learning Framework for Wireless Radiation Field Reconstruction and Channel Prediction

abstract: In the rapidly changing healthcare landscape, the implementation of offline reinforcement learning (RL) in dynamic treatment regimes (DTRs) presents a mix of unprecedented opportunities and challenges. This position paper offers a critical examination of the current status of offline RL in the context of DTRs. We argue for a reassessment of applying RL in DTRs, citing concerns such as inconsistent and potentially inconclusive evaluation metrics, the absence of naive and supervised learning baselines, and the diverse choice of RL formulation in existing research. Through a case study with more than 17,000 evaluation experiments using a publicly available Sepsis dataset, we demonstrate that the performance of RL algorithms can significantly vary with changes in evaluation metrics and Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulations. Surprisingly, it is observed that in some instances, RL algorithms can be surpassed by random baselines subjected to policy evaluation methods and reward design. This calls for more careful policy evaluation and algorithm development in future DTR works. Additionally, we discussed potential enhancements toward more reliable development of RL-based dynamic treatment regimes and invited further discussion within the community. Code is available at https://github.com/GilesLuo/ReassessDTR.

paragraphs: This position paper questions how offline reinforcement learning is currently assessed for dynamic treatment regimes, where treatment decisions unfold over time. The authors identify inconsistent evaluation metrics, missing naive and supervised-learning baselines, and variation in how researchers formulate the decision problem. These choices can complicate claims about an algorithm's quality.

A case study on a public sepsis dataset includes more than 17,000 evaluation experiments. It shows that reported reinforcement learning performance can change substantially with the evaluation metric and Markov decision process formulation. In some cases, random baselines receive better evaluations than reinforcement learning algorithms under the chosen policy-evaluation methods and reward design.

These findings concern the reliability of the evaluation setup; they do not establish that random treatment decisions produce better patient outcomes. The authors call for more careful policy evaluation and algorithm development and discuss possible improvements. Their central argument is that progress in this application requires examining how conclusions depend on the definitions, comparisons, and evaluation procedures used to produce them.
summary.tldr: A large sepsis evaluation study shows that conclusions about treatment-policy reinforcement learning can depend strongly on metrics and problem formulation.

title: Position: Reinforcement Learning in Dynamic Treatment Regimes Needs Critical Reexamination

abstract: Abstract visual reasoning is a characteristically human ability, allowing the identification of relational patterns that are abstracted away from object features, and the systematic generalization of those patterns to unseen problems. Recent work has demonstrated strong systematic generalization in visual reasoning tasks involving multi-object inputs, through the integration of slot-based methods used for extracting object-centric representations coupled with strong inductive biases for relational abstraction. However, this approach was limited to problems containing a single rule, and was not scalable to visual reasoning problems containing a large number of objects. Other recent work proposed Abstractors, an extension of Transformers that incorporates strong relational inductive biases, thereby inheriting the Transformer’s scalability and multi-head architecture, but it has yet to be demonstrated how this approach might be applied to multi-object visual inputs. Here we combine the strengths of the above approaches and propose Slot Abstractors, an approach to abstract visual reasoning that can be scaled to problems involving a large number of objects and multiple relations among them. The approach displays state-of-the-art performance across four abstract visual reasoning tasks, as well as an abstract reasoning task involving real-world images.

paragraphs: Abstract visual reasoning requires identifying relationships that hold beyond the particular appearance of objects. Prior methods combined object-centered representations with architectural biases for learning relations, achieving strong systematic generalization. However, the approach described in the abstract was limited to single-rule problems and did not scale well to many objects.

A separate line of work introduced Abstractors, Transformer extensions designed to favor relational reasoning while retaining scalability and a multi-head architecture. Their application to visual scenes containing multiple objects had not yet been demonstrated. Slot Abstractors combine this approach with slot-based representations, bringing object extraction and relational abstraction into one method.

The resulting architecture scales to problems involving many objects and multiple relations among them. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across four abstract visual reasoning tasks and an additional reasoning task using real-world images. These findings support the value of combining explicit object-centered representations with a scalable mechanism for reasoning about relationships, addressing the object-count and relation-count restrictions described for earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: Slot Abstractors combine object-centered representations with scalable relational reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results on the evaluated abstract visual reasoning tasks.

title: Slot Abstractors: Toward Scalable Abstract Visual Reasoning

abstract: Multimodal survival methods combining gigapixel histology whole-slide images (WSIs) and transcriptomic profiles are particularly promising for patient prognostication and stratification. Current approaches involve tokenizing the WSIs into smaller patches ($>10^4$ patches) and transcriptomics into gene groups, which are then integrated using a Transformer for predicting outcomes. However, this process generates many tokens, which leads to high memory requirements for computing attention and complicates post-hoc interpretability analyses. Instead, we hypothesize that we can: (1) effectively summarize the morphological content of a WSI by condensing its constituting tokens using morphological prototypes, achieving more than $300\times$ compression; and (2) accurately characterize cellular functions by encoding the transcriptomic profile with biological pathway prototypes, all in an unsupervised fashion. The resulting multimodal tokens are then processed by a fusion network, either with a Transformer or an optimal transport cross-alignment, which now operates with a small and fixed number of tokens without approximations. Extensive evaluation on six cancer types shows that our framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods with much less computation while unlocking new interpretability analyses. The code is available at https://github.com/mahmoodlab/MMP.

paragraphs: Combining tissue-slide images with gene-expression profiles can support cancer survival prediction, but the inputs create a substantial computational burden. A slide may contribute more than ten thousand patch tokens, alongside tokens representing gene groups. Processing all of them with attention requires considerable memory and makes later interpretation more complicated.

The paper proposes summarizing these inputs through prototypes learned without supervision. Morphological prototypes condense the visual content of a slide, while biological pathway prototypes encode the transcriptomic profile in terms of cellular functions. The proposed image summary targets more than 300-fold compression. A fusion network then combines a small, fixed set of multimodal tokens using either a Transformer or optimal transport cross-alignment, without approximations at that fusion stage.

Evaluation across six cancer types shows better performance than state-of-the-art methods with substantially less computation. The compact representation also enables new interpretability analyses. The approach matters because its summaries address both the cost of combining large biological inputs and the difficulty of examining how those inputs contribute to survival predictions.
summary.tldr: Unsupervised morphological and pathway prototypes compactly combine tissue images and gene expression, improving survival prediction and computational efficiency across six cancer types.

title: Multimodal Prototyping for cancer survival prediction

abstract: Deep learning for time series forecasting has traditionally operated within a one-model-per-dataset framework, limiting its potential to leverage the game-changing impact of large pre-trained models. The concept of universal forecasting, emerging from pre-training on a vast collection of time series datasets, envisions a single Large Time Series Model capable of addressing diverse downstream forecasting tasks. However, constructing such a model poses unique challenges specific to time series data: (i) cross-frequency learning, (ii) accommodating an arbitrary number of variates for multivariate time series, and (iii) addressing the varying distributional properties inherent in large-scale data. To address these challenges, we present novel enhancements to the conventional time series Transformer architecture, resulting in our proposed Masked Encoder-based Universal Time Series Forecasting Transformer (Moirai). Trained on our newly introduced Large-scale Open Time Series Archive (LOTSA) featuring over 27B observations across nine domains, Moirai achieves competitive or superior performance as a zero-shot forecaster when compared to full-shot models. Code, data, and model weights can be found at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/uni2ts.

paragraphs: Moirai addresses universal time-series forecasting: training one model across a broad collection of datasets so it can handle diverse forecasting tasks. This ambition introduces specific difficulties. Series can have different sampling frequencies, different numbers of variables, and different distributional properties, all of which a shared forecasting model must accommodate.

The authors introduce architectural enhancements to a time-series Transformer to address these challenges, producing a masked-encoder-based model. They also introduce LOTSA, a training archive containing more than 27 billion observations across nine domains. The architecture and archive together provide the basis for learning across heterogeneous time-series data within a unified training approach.

In the reported evaluations, Moirai delivers competitive or better zero-shot forecasting performance compared with full-shot models. This supports the possibility of useful forecasts from a broadly pretrained model without task-specific training in the evaluated setting. The contribution combines a model designed for variation across forecasting problems with a large training collection, demonstrating progress toward a shared model for diverse downstream forecasting tasks.
summary.tldr: Moirai trains across heterogeneous time series and achieves competitive or superior zero-shot forecasting against the evaluated full-shot models.

title: Unified Training of Universal Time Series Forecasting Transformers

abstract: Recent research works demonstrate that one of the significant factors for the model Out-of-Distirbution detection performance is the scale of the OOD feature representation field. Consequently, model ensemble emerges as a trending method to expand this feature representation field leveraging expected model diversity. However, by proposing novel qualitative and quantitative model ensemble evaluation methods (i.e., Loss Basin/Barrier Visualization and Self-Coupling Index), we reveal that the previous ensemble methods incorporate affine-transformable weights with limited variability and fail to provide desired feature representation diversity. Therefore, we escalate the traditional model ensemble dimensions (different weight initialization, data holdout, etc.) into distinct supervision tasks, which we name as Multi-Comprehension (MC) Ensemble. MC Ensemble leverages various training tasks to form different comprehensions of the data and labels, resulting in the extension of the feature representation field. In experiments, we demonstrate the superior performance of the MC Ensemble strategy in the OOD detection task compared to both the naive Deep Ensemble method and the standalone model of comparable size.
