paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection depends partly on the range of features a model represents. Combining models could broaden that range, but only if their representations differ meaningfully. This paper questions whether conventional ensemble diversity, created through different initializations or held-out data, actually delivers the needed variety.

The authors introduce qualitative and quantitative evaluation tools called Loss Basin/Barrier Visualization and Self-Coupling Index. Their analysis finds limited variability in earlier ensembles, including weights related through affine transformations. They propose Multi-Comprehension Ensemble, which creates diversity through distinct supervision tasks. Different tasks encourage different interpretations of the same data and labels, expanding the feature representation field.

Experiments show better out-of-distribution detection than both a naive deep ensemble and a standalone model of comparable size. The contribution is therefore about how to produce useful ensemble diversity, rather than simply increasing the number of models. The reported results support varying supervision as an effective way to broaden representations for the evaluated detection tasks.
summary.tldr: Multi-Comprehension Ensemble improves out-of-distribution detection by training ensemble members on distinct supervision tasks.

title: Out-of-Distribution Detection via Deep Multi-Comprehension Ensemble

abstract: The growing use of machine learning (ML) has raised concerns that an ML model may reveal private information about an individual who has contributed to the training dataset. To prevent leakage of sensitive data, we consider using differentially- private (DP), synthetic training data instead of real training data to train an ML model. A key desirable property of synthetic data is its ability to preserve the low-order marginals of the original distribution. Our main contribution comprises novel upper and lower bounds on the excess empirical risk of linear models trained on such synthetic data, for continuous and Lipschitz loss functions. We perform extensive experimentation alongside our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper examines the learning cost of replacing real training records with differentially private synthetic data. The motivation is that models trained on sensitive records may reveal information about contributors. Synthetic training data offers a way to support model development while applying a formal privacy protection to the data-generation process.

The authors focus on synthetic data that preserves low-order marginals: distributional information involving small subsets of variables. Preserving these statistics is a desirable form of fidelity, but the central learning question is how well a model trained on the resulting data can perform. The paper studies this question specifically for linear models and considers continuous and Lipschitz loss functions.

Its main results are upper and lower bounds on excess empirical risk, quantifying the additional training-objective error associated with using this kind of synthetic data. Upper bounds constrain how large that error can be within the analyzed setting, while lower bounds characterize limits on achievable performance. Experiments accompany the theory. The contribution makes the connection between marginal preservation and downstream learning quality more explicit.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the extra empirical error of linear models trained on private synthetic data that preserves low-order marginals.

title: Bounding the Excess Risk for Linear Models Trained on Marginal-Preserving, Differentially-Private, Synthetic Data

abstract: Modeling the evolution of high-dimensional systems from limited snapshot observations at irregular time points poses a significant challenge in quantitative biology and related fields. Traditional approaches often rely on dimensionality reduction techniques, which can oversimplify the dynamics and fail to capture critical transient behaviors in non-equilibrium systems. We present Multi-Marginal Stochastic Flow Matching (MMSFM), a novel extension of simulation-free score and flow matching methods to the multi-marginal setting, enabling the alignment of high-dimensional data measured at non-equidistant time points without reducing dimensionality. The use of measure-valued splines enhances robustness to irregular snapshot timing, and score matching prevents overfitting in high-dimensional spaces. We validate our framework on several synthetic and benchmark datasets, including gene expression data collected at uneven time points and an image progression task, demonstrating the method’s versatility.

Multi-Marginal Stochastic Flow Matching extends simulation-free score and flow matching to align data distributions at multiple observation times. These examples demonstrate its versatility across different kinds of high-dimensional data. The contribution is a way to combine multiple irregularly spaced observations within a single modeling framework while avoiding the dimensionality reduction that can simplify away important parts of the system's evolution.
summary.tldr: MMSFM models evolving high-dimensional distributions from irregularly timed snapshots without reducing dimensionality.

title: Multi-Marginal Stochastic Flow Matching for High-Dimensional Snapshot Data at Irregular Time Points

abstract: How much information about training samples can be leaked through synthetic data generated by Large Language Models (LLMs)? Overlooking the subtleties of information flow in synthetic data generation pipelines can lead to a false sense of privacy. In this paper, we assume an adversary has access to some synthetic data generated by a LLM. We design membership inference attacks (MIAs) that target the training data used to fine-tune the LLM that is then used to synthesize data. The significant performance of our MIA shows that synthetic data leak information about the training data. Further, we find that canaries crafted for model-based MIAs are sub-optimal for privacy auditing when only synthetic data is released. Such out-of-distribution canaries have limited influence on the model’s output when prompted to generate useful, in-distribution synthetic data, which drastically reduces their effectiveness. To tackle this problem, we leverage the mechanics of auto-regressive models to design canaries with an in-distribution prefix and a high-perplexity suffix that leave detectable traces in synthetic data. This enhances the power of data-based MIAs and provides a better assessment of the privacy risks of releasing synthetic data generated by LLMs.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether released synthetic text can reveal information about the data used to fine-tune its generating language model. It assumes an adversary has access to some generated data and constructs membership inference attacks targeting the fine-tuning records. It strengthens membership inference based on released data and improves privacy auditing for this release scenario. The findings show why an audit must account for the generation pipeline and the information an adversary actually receives.
summary.tldr: Synthetic text can expose fine-tuning membership, and canaries tailored to the generation process improve detection of that privacy leakage.

title: The Canary’s Echo: Auditing Privacy Risks of LLM-Generated Synthetic Text

abstract: Dual-target molecule generation, which focuses on discovering compounds capable of interacting with two target proteins, has garnered significant attention due to its potential for improving therapeutic efficiency, safety and resistance mitigation. Existing approaches face two critical challenges. First, by simplifying the complex dual-target optimization problem to scalarized combinations of individual objectives, they fail to capture important trade-offs between target engagement and molecular properties. Second, they typically do not integrate synthetic planning into the generative process. This highlights a need for more appropriate objective function design and synthesis-aware methodologies tailored to the dual-target molecule generation task. In this work, we propose CombiMOTS, a Pareto Monte Carlo Tree Search (PMCTS) framework that generates dual-target molecules. CombiMOTS is designed to explore a synthesizable fragment space while employing vectorized optimization constraints to encapsulate target affinity and physicochemical properties. Extensive experiments on real-world databases demonstrate that CombiMOTS produces novel dual-target molecules with high docking scores, enhanced diversity, and balanced pharmacological characteristics, showcasing its potential as a powerful tool for dual-target drug discovery. The code and data is accessible through https://github.com/Tibogoss/CombiMOTS.

paragraphs: Designing a molecule to interact with two proteins requires balancing several goals, including affinity for each target and desirable molecular properties. CombiMOTS addresses both issues through Pareto Monte Carlo Tree Search. It explores a space of synthesizable molecular fragments while keeping target affinity and physicochemical requirements as a vector of objectives. This allows the search to represent competing goals explicitly, rather than reducing every comparison to a single combined score. Synthesis considerations are incorporated into the search space itself.

Experiments using real-world databases produce novel candidate molecules with high docking scores, greater diversity, and balanced pharmacological characteristics. These findings support the framework's potential for dual-target discovery. The reported evidence concerns generated candidates and their evaluated properties; the therapeutic efficiency, safety, and resistance benefits discussed in the motivation remain potential advantages of dual-target molecules.
summary.tldr: CombiMOTS searches synthesizable molecular fragments while explicitly balancing affinity for two protein targets and other molecular properties.

title: CombiMOTS: Combinatorial Multi-Objective Tree Search for Dual-Target Molecule Generation

abstract: Multiphysics simulation, which models the interactions between multiple physical processes, and multi-component simulation of complex structures are critical in fields like nuclear and aerospace engineering. Previous studies use numerical solvers or ML-based surrogate models for these simulations. However, multiphysics simulations typically require integrating multiple specialized solvers-each for a specific physical process-into a coupled program, which introduces significant development challenges. Furthermore, existing numerical algorithms struggle with highly complex large-scale structures in multi-component simulations. Here we propose compositional Multiphysics and Multi-component PDE Simulation with Diffusion models (M2PDE) to overcome these challenges. During diffusion-based training, M2PDE learns energy functions modeling the conditional probability of one physical process/component conditioned on other processes/components. In inference, M2PDE generates coupled multiphysics and multi-component solutions by sampling from the joint probability distribution. We evaluate M2PDE on two multiphysics tasks-reaction-diffusion and nuclear thermal coupling–where it achieves more accurate predictions than surrogate models in challenging scenarios. We then apply it to a multi-component prismatic fuel element problem, demonstrating that M2PDE scales from single-component training to a 64-component structure and outperforms existing domain-decomposition and graph-based approaches. The code is available at github.com/AI4Science-WestlakeU/M2PDE.

paragraphs: Simulating interacting physical processes often requires coupling several specialized solvers into one program. Large structures made of many components introduce further computational difficulties. M2PDE approaches both problems by learning how individual processes or components depend on one another, then composing them into a coupled simulation.

During diffusion-based training, the method learns energy functions representing the conditional probability of a process or component given the others. During inference, it samples from a joint probability distribution to generate a coupled solution. The key distinction is between learning conditional relationships locally and using them together when producing the overall physical state.

In a prismatic fuel element problem, it scales from training on a single component to a structure with 64 components and outperforms domain-decomposition and graph-based approaches. These results support compositional simulation in the tested settings, especially the possibility of building larger coupled predictions from training at a smaller component scale.
summary.tldr: M2PDE learns conditional physical relationships with diffusion models and composes them into coupled simulations, including a demonstrated 64-component structure.

title: M2PDE: Compositional Generative Multiphysics and Multi-component PDE Simulation

abstract: We challenge the dominant focus on neural scaling laws and advocate for a paradigm shift toward downscaling in the development of large language models (LLMs). While scaling laws have provided critical insights into performance improvements through increasing model and dataset size, we emphasize the significant limitations of this approach, particularly in terms of computational inefficiency, environmental impact, and deployment constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a holistic framework for downscaling LLMs that seeks to maintain performance while drastically reducing resource demands. This paper outlines practical strategies for transitioning away from traditional scaling paradigms, advocating for a more sustainable, efficient, and accessible approach to LLM development.

To address these challenges, we propose a holistic framework for downscaling LLMs that seeks to maintain performance while drastically reducing resource demands. paragraphs: This position paper challenges the emphasis on improving language models by increasing their size and the amount of training data. The authors acknowledge that scaling laws have helped explain performance gains. Their concern is that organizing development around continued growth also brings substantial computing costs, environmental consequences, and constraints on where models can be deployed.

The proposed alternative is a broad framework for downscaling. Its goal is to preserve model performance while sharply lowering resource requirements. That framing makes resource use part of the central development objective: progress would include making useful capabilities less demanding to train or deploy, alongside attention to the quality of the model’s outputs.

The paper outlines practical strategies for moving toward this objective and argues that efficiency, sustainability, and accessibility should guide language-model development. The key contribution is a change in research priorities and an organizing framework for pursuing it. Maintaining performance while greatly reducing resource demands is the framework’s stated ambition, rather than a result the abstract establishes for a particular model.
summary.tldr: The paper advocates downscaling language models to preserve useful performance while substantially reducing resource demands.

title: Position: Enough of Scaling LLMs! Lets Focus on Downscaling

abstract: Tokenizers provide the fundamental basis through which text is represented and processed by language models (LMs). Despite the importance of tokenization, its role in LM performance and behavior is poorly understood due to the challenge of measuring the impact of tokenization in isolation. To address this need, we present TokSuite, a collection of models and a benchmark that supports research into tokenization’s influence on LMs. Specifically, we release fourteen pre-trained models that use different off-the-shelf tokenizers but are otherwise identical, using the same architecture, dataset, training budget, and initialization. We also release a multilingual robustness benchmark that measures model performance under real-world perturbations in English, Chinese, Farsi, Italian, and Turkish, curated by native annotators. Together, TokSuite allows robust decoupling of the influence of a model’s tokenizer, supporting a series of novel findings that elucidate the respective benefits and shortcomings of a wide range of popular tokenizers.

paragraphs: Tokenizers determine the units through which language models represent and process text. Their effect is difficult to isolate when models also differ in architecture, training data, or training budget. TokSuite provides a controlled collection of models and a benchmark designed to make tokenizer choice a more directly measurable source of behavioral differences.

The collection contains fourteen pretrained models using different off-the-shelf tokenizers. Architecture, dataset, training budget, and initialization are held constant across the models. This shared setup supports comparisons in which differences are attributable more directly to tokenization than comparisons among independently developed language models would allow.

TokSuite also includes a multilingual robustness benchmark covering English, Chinese, Farsi, Italian, and Turkish. Native annotators curate real-world text perturbations to assess how model performance responds to changes in input. Together, the controlled models and benchmark support findings about the benefits and shortcomings of popular tokenizers. The contribution is an experimental resource for studying tokenization's influence on both performance and robustness across multiple languages.
summary.tldr: TokSuite isolates tokenizer effects with fourteen otherwise matched language models and a five-language robustness benchmark.

title: TokSuite: Measuring the Impact of Tokenizer Choice on Language Model Behavior

abstract: Most causal discovery methods recover a completed partially directed acyclic graph (CPDAG) representing a Markov equivalence class from observational data. Recent work has extended these methods to federated settings to address data decentralization and privacy constraints, but often under idealized assumptions that all clients share the same causal model. Such assumptions are unrealistic in practice, as client-specific policies, for instance, across hospitals, naturally induce heterogeneous and unknown interventions. In this work, we address federated causal discovery under unknown client-level interventions. We propose I-PERI, a novel federated algorithm that first recovers the CPDAG common to all clients and then orients additional edges by exploiting structural differences induced by interventions across clients. This yields a tighter equivalence class, which we call the $\mathbf{\Phi}$-Markov Equivalence Class, represented by an augmented version of the CPDAG, namely, a $\mathbf{\Phi}$-CPDAG. We provide theoretical guarantees on the convergence of I-PERI, as well as on its privacy-preserving properties, and present empirical evaluations demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

paragraphs: Observational data often identify a family of compatible causal graphs rather than one fully directed graph. Federated causal discovery must also work across clients that keep data decentralized. This paper addresses a complication: different client policies can act as unknown interventions, so assuming every client follows exactly the same causal model can be unrealistic.

The proposed I-PERI algorithm first recovers the partially directed graph common to all clients. It then uses structural differences created by client-level interventions to orient additional edges. Those differences become useful evidence for reducing causal ambiguity. The result is a tighter family of compatible graphs, called the Φ-Markov equivalence class, represented by an augmented partially directed graph called a Φ-CPDAG.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees for I-PERI’s convergence and privacy-preserving properties, together with empirical evaluations showing effectiveness. The intended gain is more informative causal structure under unknown interventions across clients. The output remains an equivalence-class representation, so additional edge orientations narrow the possibilities without implying that every causal direction is necessarily resolved.
summary.tldr: I-PERI uses differences induced by unknown client interventions to refine causal graphs in federated learning, with convergence and privacy guarantees.

title: Regret-Based Federated Causal Discovery with Unknown Interventions

abstract: In this paper, we propose a general theory of ambiguity-averse MDPs, which treats the uncertain transition probabilities as random variables and evaluates a policy via a risk measure applied to its random return. This ambiguity-averse MDP framework unifies several models of MDPs with epistemic uncertainty for specific choices of risk measures. We extend the concepts of value functions and Bellman operators to our setting. Based on these objects, we establish the consequences of dynamic programming principles in this framework (existence of stationary policies, value and policy iteration algorithms), and we completely characterize law-invariant risk measures compatible with dynamic programming. Our work draws connections among several variants of MDP models and fully delineates what is possible under the dynamic programming paradigm and which risk measures require leaving it.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a general theory of ambiguity-averse MDPs, which treats the uncertain transition probabilities as random variables and evaluates a policy via a risk measure applied to its random return. This ambiguity-averse MDP framework unifies several models of MDPs with epistemic uncertainty for specific choices of risk measures. We extend the concepts of value functions and Bellman operators to our setting. Based on these objects, we establish the consequences of dynamic programming principles in this framework (existence of stationary policies, value and policy iteration algorithms), and we completely characterize law-invariant risk measures compatible with dynamic programming. Our work draws connections among several variants of MDP models and fully delineates what is possible under the dynamic programming paradigm and which risk measures require leaving it.

paragraphs: A decision maker may be uncertain about the transition probabilities governing an environment. This paper represents those probabilities as random variables and evaluates policies through a risk measure applied to their resulting random return. The resulting ambiguity-averse framework expresses how uncertainty about the environment affects policy evaluation.

Different choices of risk measure recover several existing models of decision processes with epistemic uncertainty. The authors extend value functions and Bellman operators to this broader framework. These are the objects needed to express recursive decision making, where evaluating a current choice depends on the values of future situations.

The theory establishes the consequences of dynamic programming, including stationary policies and value- and policy-iteration algorithms, and completely characterizes which law-invariant risk measures are compatible with it. Such measures depend on a return's distribution. This compatibility question matters because choosing a risk measure also determines whether recursive solution methods remain available. The paper identifies both the models that fit this paradigm and the measures requiring methods outside it.
summary.tldr: The paper unifies risk-sensitive treatment of uncertain transition probabilities and characterizes which law-invariant risk measures permit dynamic programming.

title: Dynamic Programming for Epistemic Uncertainty in Markov Decision Processes

abstract: While deep learning is facing an homogenization across modalities led by Transformers, they are still challenged by shallow linear models in the time series forecasting task. Our hypothesis is that models should learn a direct link from past to future data points, which we identify as a learning dynamics capability. We develop an original $\texttt{PRO-DYN}$ nomenclature to analyze existing models through the lens of dynamics. Two observations thus emerge: 1. under-performing architectures learn dynamics at most partially, 2. the location of the dynamics block at the model end is of prime importance. Our systemic and empirical studies both confirm our observations on a set of performance-varying models with diverse backbones. We propose a simple plug-and-play methodology guiding model designs and improvements.

paragraphs: Complex forecasting architectures do not automatically outperform shallow linear models on time series. This paper investigates that puzzle through the hypothesis that a useful forecasting model should learn a direct link between past and future data points. The authors call this ability learning dynamics and develop the PRO-DYN nomenclature to analyze how existing models provide it.

Their analysis identifies two patterns. Underperforming architectures learn dynamics only partially, at most, and placing the dynamics block at the end of a model is especially important. This shifts attention from the broad choice of backbone to the specific computation that turns historical information into future predictions, including where that computation occurs.

Systemic and empirical studies support these observations across models with different backbones and varying performance. The authors use the findings to propose a simple plug-and-play methodology for designing or improving forecasting models. The contribution is an architectural perspective grounded in the studied models: examining the direct past-to-future link can help explain performance differences and guide changes without making model complexity itself the organizing principle.
summary.tldr: PRO-DYN links forecasting performance to how models learn past-to-future dynamics and where that computation sits in the architecture.

title: Time Series Forecasting Through the Lens of Dynamics

abstract: In this work, we show that Latent Flow-Matching (LFM) models are robust to different types of perturbations, including data reduction and model capacity shrinkage. We characterize this stability by these models’ tendency to generate similar outputs under identical noise seeds. We provide a perspective relating this phenomenon to flow matching theory, which indicates that this stability is inherent to the FM objective. We further exploit this stability to derive practical algorithms for more efficient training and inference. Concretely, first, we show that by training LFM models on significantly reduced datasets, performance is preserved, and in compute-constrained regimes, the model converges faster while maintaining quality. This yields multiple advantages, including savings in the training time due to faster convergence, and alleviating annotation effort when training conditional models. Second, LFM stability under architectural shrinkage gives rise to a two-model coarse-to-fine approach, one using a light-weight architecture for the first phase of the FM trajectory, and one with higher capacity for the second, thereby reducing the inference cost substantially. To determine which samples are informative, we introduce three sample-scoring criteria and evaluate them under standard metrics for generative models. Our results are thoroughly evaluated on multiple datasets, demonstrating the practical advantage of this stability, including data savings and a more than two-fold inference speedup while generating comparable outputs.

This paper studies that stability and connects it to the flow-matching objective. The authors then use the observation to develop ways of reducing both training and generation costs.

For training, they show that substantially smaller datasets can preserve performance. Under compute constraints, these models converge faster while maintaining quality, reducing training time and potentially the annotation effort required for conditional models. The paper introduces three scoring criteria for identifying informative samples and evaluates them using standard generative-model metrics.

For inference, the authors divide generation between two models. A lightweight architecture handles the first part of the flow trajectory, and a larger model handles the later part. Stability under architectural shrinkage makes this coarse-to-fine strategy useful in the tested settings. Evaluations across multiple datasets show data savings and more than a twofold inference speedup with comparable outputs, demonstrating practical uses of the observed stability.
summary.tldr: Latent flow-matching stability enables smaller training datasets and a two-model generation strategy that more than doubles inference speed in reported evaluations.

title: Exploring and Exploiting Stability in Latent Flow Matching

abstract: Embedding methods are among the most efficient approaches for learning to reason about relational knowledge. In this paper, we focus on the framework of region-based embeddings, where relations are encoded as geometric regions. The spatial arrangement of these regions allows such models to capture symbolic rules, enabling them to simulate some forms of symbolic reasoning. A crucial consideration is how the regions are parameterized, as this affects which rule bases can be captured. Most methods use convex regions which are defined in terms of coordinate-wise comparisons. This makes them highly efficient, but the implications of this choice have thus far remained unclear. We present a series of results that shed light on this issue, showing that convex coordinate-wise models indeed have important limitations, while at the same time showing that there is still room for pushing the expressivity of existing coordinate-wise models.

paragraphs: Region-based embeddings represent relations as geometric regions. Their spatial arrangement can encode symbolic rules, allowing a learned geometric model to carry out some forms of relational reasoning. This paper asks how the choice of region shapes and parameterization affects the rules that such a model can faithfully represent.

The focus is on convex regions described through comparisons along individual coordinates. These designs are computationally efficient and common in existing methods, but efficiency alone does not establish their expressive power. The authors analyze the implications of restricting relational representations to this family, connecting geometric design choices to the rule bases the models can capture.

The resulting theory identifies important limitations of convex coordinate-wise models while also showing that existing coordinate-wise approaches have room to become more expressive. These two findings matter together: some restrictions belong to the broader geometric framework, while current designs do not exhaust its possibilities. The work provides a basis for understanding what these efficient embeddings can represent and where improving their parameterization may expand their reasoning capabilities.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes expressive limitations and remaining opportunities in efficient relational embeddings built from convex, coordinate-wise regions.

title: Faithful Relational Reasoning with Region-based Embeddings: Expressivity of Convex Coordinate-wise Models

abstract: Finding flat minima in the loss landscape is a key strategy for Domain Generalization (DG). However, its effectiveness is often limited by two crucial challenges. 1) Domain Shift: Existing methods like Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) apply a uniform optimization strategy across all domains, overlooking the differences of the learning difficulties among multiple domains and thus performing poorly on challenging domains. 2) Anisotropic Sharpness: By perturbing parameters along a single gradient direction, SAM and its variants ignore multi-directional flatness, making the model converge to minima that remain sharp in other directions. The combined challenges make it more difficult for the model to find truly robust solutions in multi-domain scenarios. To overcome these limitations, we propose the Dual Adaptive Sharpness-Aware Minimization (DA-SAM), which comprises two key modules: Dynamic Adaptive Scaling (DAS) module and Adaptive Multi-Directional Flattening (AMDF) module. First, to tackle the domain shift problem, the DAS module computes the real-time loss on each domain to adaptively generate domain-specific scaling factors that guide the generation of perturbation directions. Second, the AMDF module calculates local flatness by generating multiple directions to simulate perturbations in the parameter space. Based on the learned local flatness metric, it dynamically adjusts the perturbation step size to guide the model parameters to be away from anisotropic sharp regions. Crucially, DAS provides domain-level guidance that makes AMDF’s multi-directional geometric exploration more targeted and effective. Extensive experiments on five DG benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our DA-SAM algorithm.

abstract: While recent Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have attained significant strides in multimodal reasoning, their reasoning processes remain predominantly text-centric and fail to visualize and track intermediate visual states during the reasoning process, leading to suboptimal performance in complex long-horizon, vision-centric tasks. Moving beyond the constraints of text-centric reasoning, we establish Generative Multimodal Reasoning as a novel paradigm and introduce DiffThinker, a diffusion-based reasoning framework. Conceptually, DiffThinker reformulates multimodal reasoning as a native generative image-to-image task, where the iterative denoising trajectory naturally serves as a visual reasoning path. This enables the model to track the evolution of visual information throughout the reasoning process. We perform a systematic comparison between DiffThinker and MLLMs, providing the first in-depth investigation into the intrinsic characteristics of this paradigm, revealing four core properties: efficiency, controllability, native parallelism, and collaboration. Extensive experiments across seven tasks demonstrate that DiffThinker significantly outperforms leading closed-source models, including GPT-5 (+314.2%) and Gemini-3-Flash (+111.6%), as well as the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-32B baseline (+39.0%), highlighting Generative Multimodal Reasoning as a promising approach for vision-centric reasoning.

paragraphs: Many multimodal language models handle visual reasoning mainly through text, which can make it difficult to track changing visual states over a long task. DiffThinker approaches this problem by making image generation itself the reasoning process. It frames multimodal reasoning as an image-to-image task performed by a diffusion model.

In this framework, successive denoising stages form a visual reasoning trajectory. Intermediate visual information can evolve within that trajectory instead of being represented predominantly through textual reasoning. The authors systematically compare this approach with multimodal language models and identify efficiency, controllability, native parallelism, and collaboration as core properties of the proposed paradigm.

Across seven evaluated tasks, the authors report improvements over GPT-5, Gemini-3-Flash, and a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-32B baseline of 314.2%, 111.6%, and 39.0%, respectively. These are reported comparative gains within the evaluation, rather than absolute accuracy values. The findings support generative image-based reasoning as a promising approach for vision-centric tasks, particularly when solving the problem involves maintaining and changing visual information through multiple stages.
summary.tldr: DiffThinker uses a diffusion model’s evolving images as a visual reasoning process and reports strong gains across seven vision-centric tasks.

title: DiffThinker: Towards Generative Multimodal Reasoning with Diffusion Models

abstract: Taxonomies provide key information about the semantic relationships between concepts and the inherent organization of vision and language. Despite their impressive capabilities, large multimodal models (LMMs) often lack taxonomic knowledge, leading to low hierarchical visual recognition (HVR) consistency. These models typically only rely on language modeling objectives during fine-tuning and lack explicit taxonomy-aware regularization. To address this, we propose Hierarchical Representation Regularization (HiR$^2$), a simple plug-and-play regularizer that improves hierarchical consistency in LMMs. Specifically, we introduce a semantic-aware visual tree construction framework that extracts coarse-to-fine visual features from intermediate LLM layers guided by textual cues. The regularizer combines two complementary objectives: a taxonomic entailment loss that enforces hierarchy via hyperbolic entailment cones in the Lorentz model, and a discriminative dispersive loss that promotes angular separation of semantically similar embeddings on the unit sphere without disturbing the radial hierarchical structure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HiR$^2$ effectively captures taxonomic structures across diverse LMMs and fine-tuning methods. Code is available at https://github.com/PKUICST-MIPL/HiR2_ICML2026.

paragraphs: Recognizing concepts hierarchically requires a multimodal model to respect relationships between broad categories and their more specific members. The paper argues that ordinary language-modeling objectives do not explicitly teach this taxonomic organization, contributing to inconsistent hierarchical visual recognition. HiR² adds a regularizer intended to make those relationships visible in learned representations.

The method first constructs a visual tree using textual guidance to extract coarse-to-fine features from intermediate language-model layers. It then combines two geometric objectives. A taxonomic entailment loss uses hyperbolic entailment cones in the Lorentz model to encode hierarchical relationships. A discriminative dispersive loss separates semantically similar embeddings by angle on a unit sphere while preserving their radial hierarchical organization.

The two objectives address complementary needs: representing category relationships and keeping related concepts distinguishable. Experiments across multiple large multimodal models and fine-tuning approaches show that the regularizer captures taxonomic structure effectively. The contribution is a plug-and-play way to supplement fine-tuning with explicit hierarchy-aware supervision, encouraging representations that retain both broad-to-specific organization and distinctions among nearby semantic concepts.
summary.tldr: HiR² adds complementary geometric losses that help multimodal models represent taxonomic hierarchies while distinguishing related concepts.

title: Learning Taxonomic Trees with Hierarchical Representation Regularization for Large Multimodal Models

abstract: Online link recommendation on evolving graphs is performative: by choosing which candidate links to show users, the system changes which links form and what feedback it later observes. Consequently, fairness estimates from logged outcomes can be misleading and may drift after deployment when the recommendation policy is updated. We introduce COPF (Counterfactual Online Performative Fairness), a decision-layer framework for deployment-stable fairness monitoring and control in online link recommendation. COPF (i) defines group-level opportunity gaps over exposure (shown vs. not shown) counterfactuals, (ii) makes them estimable by explicit exploration and by logging the probability (propensity) that each candidate is shown, and (iii) audits and controls fairness using residual outcome indistinguishability (OI) over a configurable auditor family with graph-aware doubly robust (GA-DR) estimators. We provide a noisy transfer theorem showing that Residual-OI on estimated GA-DR residuals implies bounds on exposure-counterfactual group gaps under temporal mixing and bounded local interference, and we instantiate an online multicalibration auditor together with a primal-dual controller. Experiments on two TGB streams and a controlled synthetic bipartite stream show that COPF reduces worst-case spikes in exposure-counterfactual group disparities with modest impact on ranking utility. Our code is available at https://github.com/lsnnnnnnnn/COPF.

paragraphs: A link recommendation system helps shape the network it later learns from: showing a potential connection changes whether that connection forms. Consequently, observed outcomes can give a misleading picture of fairness, and fairness can shift when the recommendation policy changes. COPF addresses this feedback problem at the recommendation decision layer.

The framework defines group opportunity gaps using counterfactual comparisons between showing and withholding candidate links. It introduces explicit exploration and records each candidate's probability of being shown so those comparisons can be estimated. Graph-aware doubly robust estimators support an auditor that checks residual outcome indistinguishability, alongside a controller that adjusts decisions.

A transfer theorem connects these residual checks to bounds on counterfactual group gaps under temporal mixing and bounded local interference. These assumptions qualify the theoretical guarantee. Experiments on two TGB streams and a controlled synthetic stream find that COPF reduces the worst disparity spikes with a modest effect on ranking utility. The contribution therefore combines a measurable fairness target, conditions supporting its interpretation, and an online mechanism for controlling it.
summary.tldr: COPF monitors and controls counterfactual fairness in evolving link recommendations, reducing disparity spikes with modest ranking impact in experiments.

title: COPF: An Online Framework for Deployment-Stable Counterfactual Fairness in Evolving Graphs

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) struggles to scale to large, combinatorial action spaces common in many real-world problems. This paper introduces a novel framework for training discrete diffusion models as highly effective policies in these complex settings. Our key innovation is an efficient online training process that ensures stable and effective policy improvement and . By leveraging policy mirror descent (PMD) to define an ideal, regularized target policy distribution, we frame the policy update as a distributional matching problem, training the expressive diffusion model to replicate this stable target. This decoupled approach stabilizes learning and significantly enhances training performance. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results and superior sample efficiency across a diverse set of challenging combinatorial benchmarks, including DNA sequence generation, RL with macro-actions, and multi-agent systems. Experiments demonstrate that our diffusion policies attain comparable or superior performance compared to other baselines. Crucially, our extensive empirical analysis reveals a key trade-off: FKL demonstrates superior sample efficiency and faster initial convergence, whereas RKL ensures stable training and higher asymptotic performance on challenging tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when actions are combinations drawn from a very large space. This paper trains discrete diffusion models as policies for such problems. The central challenge is making their expressive action distributions compatible with stable, efficient policy improvement during online learning.

The method uses policy mirror descent to define an ideal regularized target policy. It then trains the diffusion model to match that distribution, separating target construction from the task of representing it. This formulation turns policy updating into distribution matching and is intended to stabilize learning while improving training performance.

Experiments cover DNA sequence generation, macro-actions, and multi-agent systems, reporting state-of-the-art results and strong sample efficiency across the evaluated combinatorial benchmarks. The analysis also identifies a trade-off between forward and reverse KL matching. Forward KL gives better sample efficiency and faster early convergence, while reverse KL supports stable training and higher eventual performance on challenging tasks. Thus, the choice of matching objective affects both how quickly the policy learns and how well it performs later in training.
summary.tldr: Discrete diffusion policies learn combinatorial actions by matching regularized target policies, with forward and reverse KL offering different learning trade-offs.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Discrete Diffusion Policies for Combinatorial Action Spaces

abstract: Antimicrobial peptide discovery is challenged by the astronomical size of peptide space and the relative scarcity of active peptides. While generative models provide latent maps of this space, they typically ignore decoder-induced geometry and rely on flat Euclidean metrics, making exploration distorted and inefficient. Existing manifold-based approaches assume fixed intrinsic dimensionality, which fails for real peptide data. We introduce PepCompass, a geometry-aware framework based on a Union of $\kappa$-Stable Riemannian Manifolds that captures local decoder geometry while maintaining computational stability. PepCompass performs global interpolation via Potential-minimizing Geodesic Search (PoGS) to bias discovery toward promising seeds and enables local exploration through Second-Order Riemannian Brownian Efficient Sampling and Mutation Enumeration in Tangent Space, which together form Local Enumeration Bayesian Optimization (LE-BO). PepCompass achieves a 100% in-vitro validation rate: PoGS identifies four novel seeds and LE-BO optimizes them into 25 highly active, broad-spectrum peptides, demonstrating that geometry-informed exploration is a powerful paradigm for antimicrobial peptide design.

title: PepCompass: Navigating Peptide Embedding Spaces Using Riemannian Geometry

abstract: Existing approaches for watermarking AI-generated images often rely on post-hoc methods applied in pixel space, introducing computational overhead and potential visual artifacts. In this work, we explore latent space watermarking and introduce DistSeal, a unified approach for latent watermarking that works across both diffusion and autoregressive models. Our approach works by training post-hoc watermarking models in the latent space of generative models. We demonstrate that these latent watermarkers can be effectively distilled either into the generative model itself or into the latent decoder, enabling in-model watermarking. The resulting latent watermarks achieve competitive robustness while offering similar imperceptibility and up to 20x speedup compared to pixel-space baselines. Our experiments further reveal that distilling latent watermarkers outperforms distilling pixel-space ones, providing a solution that is both more efficient and more robust.

paragraphs: Image watermarks are often added after generation by modifying pixels, which can introduce extra computation and visible artifacts. DistSeal moves watermark learning into the generative model’s latent space, the internal representation used before the final image is produced. The framework works across both diffusion and autoregressive image generators.

The approach first trains separate watermarking models on these latent representations. It then distills their behavior into either the image generator itself or the decoder that converts latent representations into images. This creates a route from a separately trained watermarking component to watermarking embedded within the generation process, reducing the need for an additional pixel-space operation.

The authors report competitive robustness and similar imperceptibility compared with pixel-space baselines, together with speedups reaching twentyfold. Their experiments also find that distilling latent watermarkers gives better results than distilling pixel-space watermarkers. The findings support latent space as a useful place both to learn image watermarks and to integrate them efficiently into generative models.
summary.tldr: DistSeal learns image watermarks in latent space and distills them into generators or decoders, delivering competitive robustness with up to twentyfold speedups.

title: Learning to Watermark in the Latent Space of Generative Models

abstract: In this work, we present the first theoretical analysis of multi-agent imitation learning (MAIL) in linear Markov games where both the transition dynamics and each agent’s reward function are linear in some given features. We demonstrate that by leveraging this structure, it is possible to replace the state-action level all policy deviation concentrability coefficient (Freihaut et al., 2025b) with a concentrability coefficient defined at the feature level which can be much smaller than the state-action analog when the features are informative about states’ similarity. Furthermore, to circumvent the need for any concentrability coefficient, we turn to the interactive setting. We provide the first, computationally efficient, interactive MAIL algorithm for linear Markov games and show that its sample complexity depends only on the dimension of the feature map $d$. Building on these theoretical findings, we propose a deep MAIL interactive algorithm which clearly outperforms BC on games such as Tic-Tac-Toe and Connect4.

paragraphs: This paper studies the theory of learning multiple agents’ behavior from demonstrations using shared features. Its formal setting is a linear Markov game: both transition dynamics and each agent’s reward are linear functions of given features. The authors examine how this structure changes the data-coverage requirements of multi-agent imitation learning.

They replace a coverage coefficient defined over individual states and actions with one defined at the feature level. The feature-level coefficient can be much smaller when the features capture similarities between states. This makes the usefulness of the representation explicit: informative features can improve the theoretical coverage requirement without treating every state–action combination separately.

The authors then move to an interactive setting to avoid requiring any such coefficient. They provide a computationally efficient algorithm whose sample complexity depends only on feature dimension. Building on the analysis, they develop a deep interactive imitation-learning algorithm that clearly outperforms behavioral cloning on games including Tic-Tac-Toe and Connect4. The work connects guarantees under linear structure to a practical deep-learning approach.
summary.tldr: Feature structure and interaction improve theoretical guarantees for multi-agent imitation learning, motivating a deep algorithm that outperforms behavioral cloning in evaluated games.

title: Multi-agent imitation learning with function approximation: linear Markov games and beyond

abstract: Recent work shows that chain based sampling for power shaped trajectory distributions can deliver large test time gains from a fixed base LLM and can approach RL trained reasoners such as GRPO. Deployment is the bottleneck. Autoregressive Metropolis Hastings is inherently serial, limits GPU utilization, and exhibits extreme tail latency at high budgets, reaching p95 $=1318$s on MATH500 at $128\times$. We propose Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo (ASMC), a parallel particle inference method that targets power shaped trajectory distributions while adapting particle populations to problem hardness. To make resampling practical for Transformers, we introduce cache coherent resampling, which realizes ancestry updates by reordering KV caches and other particle bound tensors, avoiding prefix recomputation. On MATH500 at the same budget, ASMC attains 80.6% exact-match accuracy with p95 = 73.7s, substantially reducing the tail latency of sequential MCMC and providing additional high-accuracy operating points beyond the saturation of best-of-n. We further analyze particle degeneracy and find that collapse severity, measured by low $\mathrm{ESS}_{\min}/N$, strongly predicts failures, while sensitivity to the resampling scheme is limited.

paragraphs: Spending more computation at inference can improve reasoning from a fixed language model, but the sampling procedure determines whether that improvement is practical. Sequential Metropolis Hastings sampling is difficult to parallelize and can produce very long waits. The paper reports a 95th-percentile latency of 1,318 seconds on MATH500 at a 128× budget for this approach.

Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo maintains parallel candidate trajectories, called particles, and adjusts their population to problem hardness. Its cache coherent resampling mechanism makes this practical for Transformers. When particles inherit previous trajectories, the system rearranges their key-value caches and associated tensors, preserving already computed prefixes instead of calculating them again.

At the same MATH500 budget, the method achieves 80.6% exact-match accuracy with a 95th-percentile latency of 73.7 seconds. It also offers high-accuracy settings beyond where best-of-n sampling saturates. The analysis finds that severe particle collapse strongly predicts failures, while changing the resampling scheme has limited influence. This connects useful reasoning gains to both efficient execution and the health of the particle population.
summary.tldr: Parallel adaptive sampling with cache reuse substantially reduces reasoning tail latency while supporting high-accuracy inference from a fixed language model.

title: Cache Coherent Resampling for Efficient Test Time Scaling in LLM Reasoning via Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: Representation intervention has emerged as a promising paradigm for aligning large language models toward desired behaviors without modifying model weights. Existing methods typically apply a fixed intervention uniformly across all inputs. However, we find that the appropriate intervention direction and strength vary substantially across samples, and such indiscriminate intervention leads to degradation of general capabilities on benign inputs. To address these challenges, we propose Multi-Adapter Representation Interventions via Energy Calibration (MARI). Specifically, we introduce a competitive multi-adapter mechanism in which specialized experts capture non-linear correction patterns and adaptively determine the appropriate intervention direction and strength for different samples. Furthermore, we design an energy-based gating module that leverages internal propagation dynamics to distinguish inputs that are applicable for intervention. Extensive experiments across diverse model families and parameter scales demonstrate that MARI achieves state-of-the-art alignment performance. Our method significantly improves performance on TruthfulQA, BBQ, and safety benchmarks, while maintaining and even improving general capabilities on tasks such as MMLU and ARC. Our code is available at https://github.com/V1centNevwake/MARI.

paragraphs: Representation intervention aims to steer language-model behavior through internal representations without changing the underlying model weights. This paper finds that applying the same correction to every input can damage general capabilities on benign requests. Different samples need different correction directions and strengths, and some inputs should not receive an intervention.

MARI addresses those decisions through specialized adapters and an energy-based gate. The adapters compete to capture nonlinear correction patterns and determine how to steer each sample. The gate uses internal propagation dynamics to identify inputs for which intervention is applicable, adding an adaptive decision about whether correction is appropriate.

Experiments across multiple model families and sizes report state-of-the-art alignment performance. MARI improves results on TruthfulQA, BBQ, and safety benchmarks while maintaining or improving performance on general tasks including MMLU and ARC. These findings support making both the form and applicability of intervention responsive to the input, allowing behavioral alignment to coexist with preserved general capabilities in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: MARI adapts when and how to intervene in language-model representations, improving alignment while preserving or improving evaluated general capabilities.

title: Multi-Adapter Representation Interventions via Energy Calibration

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) faces a tension between semantic understanding and image reconstruction. High-level semantic SSL methods such as DINO encourage transformation-invariant global representations for augmentation alignment, while reconstruction-oriented methods such as MAE preserve dense feature grids for spatial grounding but often yield weaker semantic abstractions. We introduce STELLAR, a framework that alleviates this tension by factorizing visual features into a low-rank product of semantic concepts and their spatial distributions. This disentanglement allows us to perform augmentation alignment on semantic tokens while maintaining spatial localization through a localization matrix for reconstruction. We demonstrate that as few as 16 sparse tokens under this factorized form can simultaneously support high-quality reconstruction (2.60 FID) and strong semantic transfer (79.10% ImageNet accuracy). Our results highlight STELLAR as a versatile sparse representation that bridges discriminative and generative vision by separating semantic identity from spatial geometry. Code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/STELLAR.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning must balance recognizing what an image contains with retaining where its details occur. Methods emphasizing semantic consistency across transformations can lose spatial information, while reconstruction-focused methods retain dense spatial features but often learn weaker semantic abstractions. STELLAR addresses this tension by separating semantic identity from spatial organization inside the representation.

The framework expresses visual features as a low-rank product of semantic concepts and their spatial distributions. Semantic tokens can be aligned across augmented views, while a localization matrix preserves the information needed to place those concepts during reconstruction. This division lets the same compact representation support both semantic learning and spatially grounded image recovery.

The authors demonstrate that as few as 16 sparse tokens can support reconstruction with 2.60 FID alongside 79.10% ImageNet accuracy for semantic transfer. These reported results show that strong reconstruction and semantic usefulness can coexist in the proposed factorized representation. The broader contribution is a shared sparse format connecting discriminative and generative vision through an explicit separation of meaning and location.
summary.tldr: STELLAR separates semantic concepts from their spatial distributions, enabling sparse visual tokens to support both reconstruction and semantic transfer.

title: Learning Sparse Visual Representations via Spatial-Semantic Factorization

abstract: Deep hypergraph clustering exhibits compelling capacity for node representation learning via modeling high-order relationships. However, most existing methods adopt fixed propagation mechanisms and implicitly assume homophily, which presumes that adjacent nodes possess similar characteristics. This assumption might deviate from real-world situations, particularly under heterophilic conditions, thereby degrading clustering performance. To address this limitation, we propose a Unified Framework for Deep Hypergraph Clustering (Uni-DHC). Specifically, we design a learnable high-order hypergraph propagation strategy that fuses multi-order information and adaptively learns their importance derived from raw data. To stabilize unsupervised training and eliminate structural redundancy caused by high-order aggregation, we additionally enforce node-level consistency and hyperedge-level decorrelation constraints. From the spectral perspective, we demonstrate that conventional HGNN-style propagation corresponds to a fixed low-pass filter, whereas our designed method induces a learnable polynomial spectral filter. Extensive experiments on homophilic and heterophilic datasets illustrate that Uni-DHC consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving prominent performance improvement in heterophilic settings.

paragraphs: Hypergraph clustering learns groups of nodes using relationships that can connect multiple nodes at once. Many existing methods propagate information through these relationships in a fixed way, implicitly expecting connected nodes to have similar characteristics. That expectation can be misleading in heterophilic data, where connected nodes differ, and can weaken the resulting clusters.

Uni-DHC makes the propagation process learnable. It combines information from multiple orders of relationships and learns how much each should contribute from the data itself. Two additional constraints support unsupervised learning: consistency at the node level stabilizes training, while decorrelation at the hyperedge level addresses redundant structure introduced by higher-order aggregation.

The paper explains the difference through spectral filtering. Conventional propagation acts like a fixed low-pass filter, whereas Uni-DHC learns a polynomial filter with more adaptable behavior. Experiments cover both homophilic and heterophilic datasets and report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with especially strong gains in heterophilic settings. These findings support adapting propagation to the relationship structure rather than fixing it in advance.
summary.tldr: Uni-DHC learns how to combine hypergraph relationships, improving clustering especially when connected nodes have different characteristics.

title: A Unified Framework for Deep Hypergraph Clustering Beyond Homophily

abstract: Slot Attention (SA) lies at the heart of mainstream Object-Centric Learning (OCL). Image features can be aggregated into object-level representations by SA iteratively refining cold-start query slots. For video, such aggregation proceeds by SA recurrently shared across frames, with queries cold-started on the first frame while transitioned from the previous frame’s slots thereafter. However, cold-start queries lack sample-specific cues thus hindering precise aggregation on image or video’s first frame; Non-first frames’ queries are already sample-specific thus requiring aggregation transforms different from the first frame. We address these issues with our SmoothSA: (1) To smooth SA iterations on image or video’s first frame, we preheat cold-start queries with rich input-feature information, by a tiny module self-distilled inside OCL; (2) To smooth SA recurrences across video’s first and non-first frames, we differentiate the homogeneous aggregation transforms by using full and single iterations respectively. Comprehensive experiments on object discovery, recognition and visual reasoning validate our method’s effectiveness. Further visual analyses illuminate the underline mechanisms. Our source code, model checkpoints and training logs are provided on https://github.com/Genera1Z/SmoothSA.

paragraphs: Slot Attention groups image features into object-level representations by repeatedly refining query slots. For an image or the first video frame, those queries begin without information specific to the input. Later video frames are different: their queries inherit information from previous slots. The paper argues that these distinct starting conditions call for different aggregation behavior.

SmoothSA first prepares cold-start queries using rich input-feature information. A small module, trained through self-distillation within the object-centric learning system, supplies this preparation. For video, the method then uses the full set of refinement iterations on the first frame and a single iteration on subsequent frames, reflecting their already informed starting points.

Experiments on object discovery, recognition, and visual reasoning validate the method's effectiveness, and visual analyses examine its mechanisms. The contribution is to adjust both initialization and recurrence to the information already available. Better prepared initial queries address the first-frame difficulty, while differentiated iteration schedules address the transition to frames that already have object-specific context.
summary.tldr: SmoothSA prepares Slot Attention queries with input features and uses different refinement schedules for initial and subsequent video frames.

title: Smoothing Slot Attention Iterations and Recurrences

abstract: In this work, we study Human-Object Interaction Video Generation (HOIVG), which aims to synthesize high-quality human-object interaction videos conditioned on text, reference images, audio, and pose. We present OmniShow, the first all-in-one model tailored for this practical yet challenging task, capable of harmonizing multimodal conditions and delivering industry-grade performance. To overcome the trade-off between controllability and quality, we introduce Unified Channel-wise Conditioning for efficient image and pose injection, and Gated Local-Context Attention to ensure precise audio-visual synchronization. To effectively address data scarcity, we develop a Decoupled-Then-Joint Training strategy that leverages a multi-stage training process with model merging to efficiently harness heterogeneous sub-task datasets. Furthermore, to fill the evaluation gap in this field, we establish HOIVG-Bench, a dedicated and comprehensive benchmark for HOIVG. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniShow achieves overall state-of-the-art performance across various multimodal conditioning settings, setting a solid standard for the emerging HOIVG task.

paragraphs: Generating human-object interaction videos requires coordinating what a person does with objects while respecting multiple kinds of instructions. OmniShow tackles this task using text, reference images, audio, and pose as conditioning inputs. The challenge is to combine those controls while maintaining video quality and keeping sound and visual behavior synchronized.

The model uses Unified Channel-wise Conditioning to introduce image and pose information efficiently. Gated Local-Context Attention handles audio-visual synchronization. To address scarce training data, a Decoupled-Then-Joint strategy combines multiple training stages with model merging, drawing on heterogeneous datasets for related subtasks before bringing their capabilities together.

The authors also introduce HOIVG-Bench, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating human-object interaction video generation. Across different combinations of conditioning inputs, experiments report overall state-of-the-art performance. The work contributes both an integrated generation system and an evaluation resource, with its training strategy addressing how a model can learn coordinated multimodal control from datasets that cover different parts of the overall task.
summary.tldr: OmniShow combines text, images, audio, and pose to generate human-object interaction videos and introduces a dedicated evaluation benchmark.

title: OmniShow: Unifying Multimodal Conditions for Human-Object Interaction Video Generation

abstract: Lens flare removal is challenging due to the large spatial extent of flare artifacts and their entangle-ment with scene structures, while existing meth-ods heavily rely on large-scale paired data. We propose a semi-supervised flare removal frame-work that enables stable learning from unlabeled images by jointly addressing pseudo-label relia-bility and representation discrimination. We pro-pose an adaptive pseudo-label repository that pro-gressively refines pseudo supervision through no-reference quality assessment, momentum-based updates, and invalid label filtering, effectively mit-igating error accumulation. Moreover, we pro-pose a flare-aware contrastive loss that explic-itly treats flare-contaminated inputs as negatives and performs patch-level contrastive learning, en-couraging representations that are discriminative against flare patterns while remaining consistent with reliable pseudo targets. Extensive experi-ments on multiple flare benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed framework is model-agnostic and consistently improves performance and ro-bustness.

paragraphs: Semi-LAR removes nighttime lens flares while reducing reliance on large collections of paired training images. Flares are difficult to separate from genuine scene structure because they can cover extensive regions and overlap with meaningful content. The framework uses unlabeled images, concentrating on the reliability of generated training targets and the ability to distinguish flare patterns.

An adaptive pseudo-label repository progressively improves the supervision supplied by those generated targets. It combines quality assessment without a reference image, momentum-based updates, and filtering of invalid labels to limit accumulating errors. A flare-aware contrastive loss also treats contaminated inputs as negative examples and compares image patches, encouraging representations that resist flare patterns while agreeing with reliable pseudo targets.

Experiments across multiple flare benchmarks show consistent improvements in performance and robustness. The authors describe the framework as model-agnostic, making its supervision and representation-learning mechanisms applicable across restoration models. The central contribution is the combination: unlabeled data becomes more useful when its training targets are refined and its flare-specific distinctions are explicitly learned.
summary.tldr: Semi-LAR improves nighttime flare removal using refined pseudo-labels and flare-aware contrastive learning on unlabeled images.

abstract: In this paper, we propose a probabilistic kernel approach to preference learning based on Gaussian processes. A new likelihood function is proposed to capture the preference relations in the Bayesian framework. The generalized formulation is also applicable to tackle many multiclass problems. The overall approach has the advantages of Bayesian methods for model selection and probabilistic prediction. Experimental results compared against the constraint classiﬁcation approach on several benchmark datasets verify the usefulness of this algorithm.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we propose a probabilistic kernel approach to preference learning based on Gaussian processes. A new likelihood function is proposed to capture the preference relations in the Bayesian framework. The generalized formulation is also applicable to tackle many multiclass problems. The overall approach has the advantages of Bayesian methods for model selection and probabilistic prediction. Experimental results compared against the constraint classiﬁcation approach on several benchmark datasets verify the usefulness of this algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper develops a probabilistic approach to learning preferences using Gaussian processes and kernels. The learning signal consists of preference relations, and the aim is to represent those relations within a Bayesian model. This connects the observed preferences to a framework that supports probabilistic predictions and model selection.

A central contribution is a new likelihood function designed to capture preference relations. The likelihood supplies the connection between those observations and the Bayesian formulation. The authors also give a generalized version that applies to many multiclass problems, extending the scope of the approach beyond its initial preference-learning motivation.

Experiments compare the method with a constraint-classification approach on several benchmark datasets. The reported results support the algorithm’s usefulness. The contribution is thus a combination of a preference-specific probabilistic formulation and evidence that it works in benchmark comparisons. Its Bayesian treatment also provides the stated advantages for selecting models and expressing predictions probabilistically, making those capabilities part of the proposed learning approach.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process preference learner introduces a likelihood for preference relations and supports Bayesian model selection and probabilistic prediction.

title: Preference learning with Gaussian processes

abstract: The four-level pachinko allocation model (PAM) (Li & McCallum, 2006) represents correlations among topics using a DAG structure. It does not, however, represent a nested hierarchy of topics, with some topical word distributions representing the vocabulary that is shared among several more specific topics. This paper presents hierarchical PAM —an enhancement that explicitly represents a topic hierarchy. This model can be seen as combining the advantages of hLDA’s topical hierarchy representation with PAM’s ability to mix multiple leaves of the topic hierarchy. Experimental results show improvements in likelihood of held-out documents, as well as mutual information between automatically-discovered topics and humangenerated categories such as journals.

paragraphs: The paper extends the pachinko allocation model to represent a nested hierarchy of topics. The earlier four-level model represents correlations among topics through a directed acyclic graph, but does not explicitly provide broader topics whose word distributions capture vocabulary shared by more specific topics. Hierarchical PAM adds that capability.

The resulting model combines a topical hierarchy with the ability to mix multiple leaves of that hierarchy. Broad and specific topics can therefore coexist in the representation, while a document can draw on multiple specific topics. This brings together the hierarchical organization associated with hLDA and the flexible topic mixing associated with PAM.

Experiments show improvements in the likelihood assigned to held-out documents and in mutual information between discovered topics and human-created categories, such as journals. These findings address two different aspects of the model: how well it accounts for unseen documents and how closely its learned topics relate to external categories. Both results support the added hierarchical representation in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical PAM combines nested topics with flexible topic mixtures, improving held-out likelihood and alignment with human categories in experiments.

title: Mixtures of hierarchical topics with Pachinko allocation

abstract: We describe an algorithm for constructing a set of acyclic conjunctive relational features by combining smaller conjunctive blocks. Unlike traditional level-wise approaches which preserve the monotonicity of frequency, our block-wise approach preserves a form of monotonicity of the irreducibility and relevancy feature properties, which are important in propositionalization employed in the context of classification learning. With pruning based on these properties, our block-wise approach efficiently scales to features including tens of first-order literals, far beyond the reach of state-of-the art propositionalization or inductive logic programming systems.
originalAbstract: We describe an algorithm for constructing a set of acyclic conjunctive relational features by combining smaller conjunctive blocks. Unlike traditional level-wise approaches which preserve the monotonicity of frequency, our block-wise approach preserves a form of monotonicity of the irreducibility and relevancy feature properties, which are important in propositionalization employed in the context of classification learning. With pruning based on these properties, our block-wise approach efficiently scales to features including tens of first-order literals, far beyond the reach of state-of-the art propositionalization or inductive logic programming systems.

paragraphs: Relational classification can require features that combine several statements about objects and their relationships. This paper constructs such features by joining smaller conjunctive blocks, meaning groups of conditions that must hold together. The resulting features are acyclic. The goal is to make richer relational descriptions available to classification through propositionalization, which turns relational information into features.

The key contribution is how the construction process supports pruning. Traditional level-wise methods preserve a monotonicity property related to frequency. The proposed block-wise method instead preserves a form of monotonicity for irreducibility and relevance. These properties concern whether features contain reducible structure and whether they are useful for the classification setting, giving the search different grounds for discarding candidates.

Pruning with these properties allows the method to scale efficiently to features containing tens of first-order literals, the individual logical statements making up a feature. The authors describe this scale as beyond the reach of existing propositionalization and inductive logic programming systems. The significance is a larger practical search space for complex relational features.
summary.tldr: Building relational features from blocks enables pruning based on irreducibility and relevance, making substantially larger acyclic features tractable.

title: Block-wise construction of acyclic relational features with monotone irreducibility and relevancy properties

abstract: Dual supervision refers to the general setting of learning from both labeled examples as well as labeled features. Labeled features are naturally available in tasks such as text classification where it is frequently possible to provide domain knowledge in the form of words that associate strongly with a class. In this paper, we consider the novel problem of active dual supervision, or, how to optimally query an example and feature labeling oracle to simultaneously collect two different forms of supervision, with the objective of building the best classifier in the most cost effective manner. We apply classical uncertainty and experimental design based active learning schemes to graph/kernel-based dual supervision models. Empirical studies confirm the potential of these schemes to significantly reduce the cost of acquiring labeled data for training high-quality models
