paragraphs: Dual supervision trains a model using both labeled examples and labeled features. In text classification, feature labels can express domain knowledge through words strongly associated with a class. This paper studies how an active learner should request these two kinds of information while aiming to build a strong classifier at low labeling cost.

The resulting problem involves choosing queries to both an example-labeling oracle and a feature-labeling oracle. The authors apply uncertainty-based selection and experimental-design methods to graph- and kernel-based dual-supervision models. This brings established active-learning ideas into a setting where supervision can arrive in two different forms.

Empirical studies confirm that these schemes have the potential to substantially reduce the cost of acquiring labels for high-quality models. The finding matters because labeling effort can be directed across examples and features, rather than being considered only within one source of supervision. The reported evidence supports the cost-saving potential of this combined querying approach, without making an unconditional guarantee about every classification task.
summary.tldr: Active selection of both example labels and feature labels can substantially reduce the supervision cost of training strong classifiers.

title: Uncertainty sampling and transductive experimental design for active dual supervision

abstract: Variable selection for cluster analysis is a difficult problem. The difficulty originates not only from the lack of class information but also the fact that high-dimensional data are often multifaceted and can be meaningfully clustered in multiple ways. In such a case the effort to find one subset of attributes that presumably gives the ``best'' clustering may be misguided. It makes more sense to facilitate variable selection by domain experts, that is, to systematically identify various facets of a data set (each being based on a subset of attributes), cluster the data along each one, and present the results to the domain experts for appraisal and selection. In this paper, we propose a generalization of the Gaussian mixture model, show its ability to cluster data along multiple facets, and demonstrate it is often more reasonable to facilitate variable selection than to perform it.

In such a case the effort to find one subset of attributes that presumably gives the ``best'' clustering may be misguided. paragraphs: Choosing variables for clustering is difficult because there are no class labels to identify the desired grouping. This paper highlights a further complication: high-dimensional data can have several meaningful structures, each visible through a different subset of attributes. Searching for a single supposedly best subset may therefore overlook useful ways to understand the data.

The authors propose helping domain experts select among clustering alternatives. The system identifies different facets of a dataset, clusters observations along each facet, and presents those results for expert appraisal. To support this approach, the paper introduces a generalization of the Gaussian mixture model and shows that it can cluster data along multiple facets.

The contribution changes the role of variable selection from producing one final answer to exposing meaningful alternatives. Different attribute subsets become ways of revealing different structures that experts can assess. The authors demonstrate that facilitating selection is often more reasonable than performing it automatically. This is a qualified argument about multifaceted data, rather than a claim that automatic variable selection is never appropriate.
summary.tldr: A generalized Gaussian mixture model reveals multiple clustering facets so domain experts can choose among meaningful attribute subsets and groupings.

title: Variable Selection in Model-Based Clustering: To Do or To Facilitate

abstract: The hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP) is a Bayesian nonparametric mixed membership model---each data point is modeled with a collection of components of different proportions. Though powerful, the HDP makes an assumption that the probability of a component being exhibited by a data point is positively correlated with its proportion within that data point. This might be an undesirable assumption. For example, in topic modeling, a topic (component) might be rare throughout the corpus but dominant within those documents (data points) where it occurs. We develop the IBP compound Dirichlet process (ICD), a Bayesian nonparametric prior that decouples across-data prevalence and within-data proportion in a mixed membership model. The ICD combines properties from the HDP and the Indian buffet process (IBP), a Bayesian nonparametric prior on binary matrices. The ICD assigns a subset of the shared mixture components to each data point. This subset, the data point's ``focus'', is determined independently from the amount that each of its components contribute. We develop an ICD mixture model for text, the focused topic model (FTM), and show superior performance over the HDP-based topic model.

paragraphs: Mixed-membership models describe each data point using several components in different proportions. The paper identifies a coupling in the hierarchical Dirichlet process: whether a component appears is positively related to its proportion within a data point. For topic modeling, that can be undesirable when a topic is rare across documents but dominates the few documents where it appears.

The authors introduce the IBP compound Dirichlet process to separate prevalence across data points from proportion within a data point. It combines properties of the hierarchical Dirichlet process and the Indian buffet process. Each data point receives a subset of shared components, called its focus, selected independently of how much those selected components contribute.

The paper applies this prior to text through a focused topic model and reports superior performance over an HDP-based topic model. The modeling contribution is the separation of two questions: which topics belong in a document and how strongly each contributes. That separation accommodates the stated rare-but-dominant topic pattern without imposing the original coupling.
summary.tldr: The IBP compound Dirichlet process separates component occurrence from contribution, enabling a focused topic model with improved reported performance.

title: The IBP Compound Dirichlet Process and its Application to Focused Topic Modeling

abstract: In this paper we propose a simple yet powerful method for learning representations in supervised learning scenarios where each original input datapoint is described by a set of vectors and their associated outputs may be given by soft labels indicating, for example, class probabilities. We represent an input datapoint as a mixture of probabilities over the corresponding set of feature vectors where each probability indicates how likely each vector is to belong to an unknown prototype pattern. We propose a probabilistic model that parameterizes these prototype patterns in terms of hidden variables and therefore it can be trained with conventional approaches based on likelihood maximization. More importantly, both the model parameters and the prototype patterns can be learned from data in a discriminative way. We show that our model can be seen as a probabilistic generalization of learning vector quantization (LVQ). We apply our method to the problems of shape classification, hyperspectral imaging classification and people's work class categorization, showing the superior performance of our method compared to the standard prototype-based classification approach and other competitive benchmark methods.

We propose a probabilistic model that parameterizes these prototype patterns in terms of hidden variables and therefore it can be trained with conventional approaches based on likelihood maximization. More importantly, both the model parameters and the prototype patterns can be learned from data in a discriminative way. We apply our method to the problems of shape classification, hyperspectral imaging classification and people's work class categorization, showing the superior performance of our method compared to the standard prototype-based classification approach and other competitive benchmark methods.

paragraphs: Some supervised learning problems describe each input as a collection of feature vectors rather than a single vector. Their target labels may also be soft, expressing class probabilities instead of one definite class. This paper proposes a representation-learning method that accommodates both features of this setting through probabilistic prototype patterns.

An input is represented using a mixture of probabilities over its feature vectors. Each probability expresses how likely a vector is to belong to an unknown prototype pattern. Hidden variables parameterize those patterns, making likelihood-based training possible. Crucially, the prototypes and the other model parameters can both be learned discriminatively, so the representation is shaped by the supervised prediction task.

The authors show that the model is a probabilistic generalization of learning vector quantization. They evaluate it on shape classification, hyperspectral image classification, and categorization of people's work classes. Across these applications, they report superior performance relative to a standard prototype classifier and other competitive methods. The findings support learning task-sensitive probabilistic prototypes for inputs composed of sets of vectors.
summary.tldr: The method learns probabilistic prototypes discriminatively for set-valued inputs, supporting soft labels and improving classification in the reported applications.

title: Discriminative Probabilistic Prototype Learning
Knowledge Acquisition and Learning in EXPERT
